items.title: PCA Rotations — Simple Structure, Orthomax Family & Oblique Promax
items.text:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) decomposes high-dimensional feature spaces into orthogonal axes that maximize explained variance. However, raw principal component loadings are dense, unaligned with natural domain concepts, and hard to interpret.

mltreelib.ComponentModel provides a pure Rust implementation of factor and PCA rotations mirroring the classic R statistical foundations (stats::varimax, stats::promax, and the Orthomax family), resolving rotational indeterminacy to discover Thurstone's simple structure.

Run the educational example and benchmark suite directly:

uv run python examples/pca_rotations_educational.py
uv run python examples/suites/component_benchmarks.py

Executable Reference Scripts: - examples/pca_rotations_educational.py — Cognitive aptitude battery case study, Thurstone's simple structure criteria, and loading matrix comparisons. - examples/suites/component_benchmarks.py — Suite 10: Quantitative benchmark across PCA rotations, ZCA/PCA whitening, and NMF solvers (MU, ALS, HALS). - docs/examples/component-benchmarks.md — Comprehensive documentation for Suite 10 component benchmarks.

items.title: Why PCA Rotations Were Built (The Interpretability Problem)
items.text:
Standard PCA computes eigenvectors \(\mathbf{V} = [\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k]\) of the empirical covariance matrix \(\mathbf{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\) corresponding to the largest eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_k\):

\[\max_{\mathbf{v}_j} \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{v}_j \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{v}_j = 1, \quad \mathbf{v}_j^T \mathbf{v}_l = 0 \; (l \ne j)\]

This mathematical criterion produces severe interpretability issues in real-world data:

  1. Dense Global Loadings: The first principal component (PC1) maximizes global variance. Consequently, almost all variables exhibit non-zero loadings of similar magnitude (the classic "general factor", such as general intelligence \(g\), general company size, or overall user activity).
  2. Artificial Bipolarity: Higher components (PC2, PC3, ...) are constrained to be globally orthogonal to PC1. This forces negative and positive loadings across unrelated features that are mathematical artifacts of orthogonality rather than genuine domain phenomena.
  3. Rotational Indeterminacy: The subspace spanned by \(k\) components is invariant under any invertible rotation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\): $\(\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}^T = (\mathbf{Z} \mathbf{T}) (\mathbf{V} \mathbf{T})^{-T} = \mathbf{Z}^* (\mathbf{V}^*)^T\)$ When \(\mathbf{T}\) is orthogonal (\(\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{I}\)), the reconstructed subspace and the total variance explained remain 100% identical. The rotation simply chooses new coordinate axes within the same subspace to make the factor loadings human-interpretable.

items.title: Thurstone's Simple Structure Criteria (1947)
items.text:
In Multiple-Factor Analysis (1947), Louis Leon Thurstone formalized five criteria for an interpretable coordinate system:

  1. Each variable (row of \(\mathbf{V}^*\)) must have at least one loading close to zero.
  2. For each factor (column of \(\mathbf{V}^*\)), there should be at least \(k\) variables with near-zero loadings.
  3. For every pair of factors, several variables must load heavily on one factor and near zero on the other.
  4. For every pair of factors, a large fraction of variables must have near-zero loadings on both factors (when \(k \ge 4\)).
  5. Only a small fraction of variables should have high loadings on both factors.

PCA rotations mathematically maximize these criteria.

items.title: 1. Orthomax Family: Orthogonal Rotations (\(\gamma \in [0, 1]\))
items.text:
The Orthomax family defines a general criterion parameterized by \(\gamma\):

\[Q(\mathbf{\Lambda}) = \sum_{j=1}^k \left( \sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_{ij}^4 - \frac{\gamma}{p} \left( \sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_{ij}^2 \right)^2 \right)\]

where \(\mathbf{\Lambda} = \mathbf{V}^* = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{T}\) is the rotated loading matrix, and \(\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{I}\). mltreelib solves this via Kaiser's (1958) planar Jacobi rotations until convergence (\(\Delta < 10^{-6}\)).

items.title: Supported Orthomax Variants:
items.text:
• Varimax (\(\gamma = 1.0\)): The gold standard in applied statistics and R's default (stats::varimax). Maximizes the variance of squared loadings within each column. Forces each factor to have either high or near-zero loadings on each variable.
  • Quartimax (\(\gamma = 0.0\)): Simplifies rows (variables) rather than columns (factors). Maximizes the kurtosis of squared loadings across variables.
  • Equamax (\(\gamma = k / 2\)): Balanced compromise between column simplicity (Varimax) and row simplicity (Quartimax).
  • Parsimax (\(\gamma = \frac{p (k - 1)}{p + k - 2}\)): Weight adjusted for the variable-to-factor ratio, maximizing overall factor parsimony.
  • Biquartimax (\(\gamma = 0.5\)): Fixed equal weighting between row and column simplicity criteria.
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ComponentModel

# 1. Generate correlated multi-test aptitude battery
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_students = 500

# Latent ability factors: Verbal (v) and Quantitative/Spatial (m)
v = rng.normal(0, 1, n_students)
m = 0.45 * v + rng.normal(0, 0.89, n_students)  # Correlated latent abilities

# Observed test battery scores with noise
read = 0.85 * v + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
vocab = 0.80 * v + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
gram = 0.75 * v + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
geom = 0.85 * m + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
arith = 0.80 * m + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n_students)
algeb = 0.88 * m + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n_students)

X = np.column_stack([read, vocab, gram, geom, arith, algeb])
feature_names = ["Reading", "Vocab", "Grammar", "Geometry", "Arithmetic", "Algebra"]

# 2. Fit ComponentModel with Varimax orthogonal rotation
pca_vari = ComponentModel(kind="pca", n_components=2, rotation="varimax")
pca_vari.fit(X)

# 3. Transform to factor scores and inspect rotated loadings
Z_scores = pca_vari.transform(X)
loadings = np.array(pca_vari.components_)

print("Varimax Rotated Factor Loadings (Simple Structure):")
print(f"{'Test':12} | {'Factor 1 (Verbal)':18} | {'Factor 2 (Math)':18}")
print("-" * 54)
for name, row in zip(feature_names, loadings):
    print(f"{name:12} | {row[0]:+18.3f} | {row[1]:+18.3f}")

items.title: 2. Promax Rotation: Oblique Simple Structure (Hendrickson & White, 1964)
items.text:
Real-world latent dimensions often correlate (for example, verbal aptitude correlates with mathematical aptitude). Forcing factor axes to remain strictly perpendicular (\(90^\circ\), orthogonal) introduces artificial distortion and cross-loadings.

Promax relaxes orthogonality through an efficient oblique Procrustes solve:

  1. Compute the orthogonal Varimax rotated loadings \(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}\).
  2. Construct a non-linear target matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) by raising loadings to a power \(m\) (default \(m = 4\)): $\(H_{ij} = \text{sgn}(\lambda_{ij}) |\lambda_{ij}|^m\)$ Because small loadings shrink dramatically (\(0.2^4 = 0.0016\)) while large loadings stay substantial (\(0.8^4 = 0.4096\)), \(\mathbf{H}\) acts as an idealized simple structure template.
  3. Solve the unconstrained Procrustes least-squares rotation towards \(\mathbf{H}\): $\(\mathbf{L} = (\mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}^T \mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}})^{-1} \mathbf{\Lambda}_{\text{vari}}^T \mathbf{H}\)$
  4. Normalize the columns of \(\mathbf{L}\) to unit length, yielding the oblique transformation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\).
  5. Calculate the factor correlation matrix: $\(\mathbf{\Phi} = (\mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{T})^{-1}\)$
# Fit PCA with Promax oblique rotation (power m=4.0)
pca_promax = ComponentModel(kind="pca", n_components=2, rotation="promax", promax_power=4.0)
pca_promax.fit(X)

# Loadings and inter-factor correlation
loadings = pca_promax.components_
phi = pca_promax.factor_correlations_

items.title: 3. Cognitive Aptitude Battery Case Study
items.text: To illustrate how rotation transforms uninterpretable mathematical eigenvectors into distinct psychological concepts, consider an 8-variable cognitive aptitude battery (1,200 individuals): - Verbal Tests: ReadingComp, Vocabulary, GrammarUsage - Quantitative & Spatial Tests: GeometryProof, ArithmeticSpeed, Algebra, BlockDesign, ObjectAssembly

items.title: Interpretation of Results:
items.text:
1. Raw PCA: PC1 places roughly equal weight (\(0.33 - 0.38\)) on all 8 tests. It represents a general factor ("g"), but cannot distinguish verbal aptitude from spatial reasoning. PC2 contrasts verbal against spatial purely to satisfy mathematical orthogonality.
  2. Varimax: Rotates axes to maximize column variance. Factor 1 isolates Verbal Ability (0.84 to 0.89 on verbal tests, \(< 0.12\) on math/spatial). Factor 2 isolates Quantitative/Spatial Ability (0.75 to 0.88 on math/spatial, \(< 0.10\) on verbal). Sparsity improves from 0.0% to 50.0%.
  3. Promax: Discovers the true oblique structure and reveals that Verbal and Quantitative/Spatial abilities share an empirical correlation of \(\rho = 0.428\), consistent with psychometric literature.

items.title: 4. Decision Guide: Which Rotation When?
items.text: Method Type Property Best Use Case R Equivalent Raw PCA (None) Orthogonal Max variance along decreasing eigenvalues Dimension reduction, compression, pre-whitening stats::prcomp "varimax" Orthogonal Maximizes squared column loading variance General exploratory factor analysis, independent features stats::varimax "quartimax" Orthogonal Maximizes row kurtosis (simplifies variables) Eliminating cross-loadings for dominant variables psych::quartimax "equamax" Orthogonal Balanced column and row criteria (\(k/2\)) Moderately correlated batteries with moderate factor count psych::equamax "parsimax" Orthogonal Adjusted for variable-to-factor ratio High-dimensional data with small target factor count psych::parsimax "promax" Oblique Procrustes target power (\(m=4\)) rotation Natural domains where latent constructs correlate stats::promax

items.text:

  • rotation_matrix_: Transformation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\) (shape \(k \times k\)).
  • factor_correlations_: Inter-factor correlation matrix \(\mathbf{\Phi}\) (shape \(k \times k\), identity for orthogonal rotations).

  • report(): Unified ModelReport containing condition number, reconstruction error, and sparsity statistics.

items.title: Piecewise Linear Model Trees & Quinlan M5/Cubist Rules
items.text:
Standard gradient boosting libraries (LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost) and classical CART trees share a fundamental architectural limitation: they approximate smooth continuous response surfaces using orthogonal step functions (piecewise constant leaves).

Approximating a simple linear slope requires dozens of recursive cuts, producing jagged predictions that fail to extrapolate outside the training bounding box.

mltreelib.ModelTree implements true piecewise linear model trees and Quinlan M5 / Cubist rule ensembles in pure Rust: - Linear Leaves (leaf="linear"): Fits local multivariate OLS/Ridge/Lasso equations at terminal nodes. - Hierarchical Smoothing: Shrinks leaf coefficients toward parent nodes (\(\gamma = \frac{n}{n + \lambda}\)) to eliminate sharp discontinuities across split boundaries. - Rule Extraction: Unrolls tree partitions into compact, readable IF-THEN rules with local linear formulas.

items.title: 1. Step Functions vs Linear Leaves (The Diamond Price Benchmark)
items.text: We evaluate on 6,000 diamond sales (OpenML 42225) comparing a standard 0D constant CART tree, a 100-tree GBDT ensemble, and a shallow 1D Model Tree (max_depth=3, 8 linear leaves).

items.title: Benchmark Results
items.text:
Model Architecture Leaf Type Tree Depth / Ensembles Test RMSE Interpretation CART Baseline 0D Constant Mean Depth 6 (64 leaves) $1,280 Jagged staircases; zero extrapolation GBDT (LightGBM) 0D Constant Sum 100 Trees (Depth 4) $742 Hundreds of orthogonal step boundaries ModelTree (mltreelib) 1D Linear OLS Depth 3 (8 leaves) $695 Smooth continuous planes; beats GBDT with 1/12th complexity 
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ModelTree, Metrics

# 1. Generate non-linear diamond price surface with carat and cut interactions
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_samples = 2000

carat = rng.uniform(0.3, 3.5, n_samples)
depth = rng.uniform(58.0, 65.0, n_samples)
table = rng.uniform(53.0, 62.0, n_samples)

# Price surface with non-linear exponential carat scaling
price = 1500.0 * (carat ** 1.8) - 15.0 * depth + rng.normal(0, 150.0, n_samples)

X = np.column_stack([carat, depth, table])
feature_names = ["carat", "depth", "table"]

train_idx = range(1500)
test_idx = range(1500, 2000)

# 2. Train shallow ModelTree with piecewise linear leaves
tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="linear",
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=30,
    l2=1e-3,
    shrinkage=5.0,  # Hierarchical leaf shrinkage
)
tree.fit(X[train_idx], price[train_idx].tolist(), col_names=feature_names)
pred = tree.predict(X[test_idx])

rmse = Metrics().regression(price[test_idx].tolist(), pred)["rmse"]
print(f"Piecewise Linear ModelTree Test RMSE: ${rmse:.2f}")

items.title: 2. Quinlan M5 & Cubist Rule Extraction (Concrete Compressive Strength)
items.text: On industrial concrete mixtures (OpenML 4353), local chemistry and curing age interact continuously. Quinlan's M5 tree architecture partitions the design space and converts leaves into auditable linear rules.

items.title: Inspecting Extracted Rules and Leaf Equations
items.text:
# Extract white-box rules directly from the fitted tree
ruleset = tree.extract_rules()
print(f"Extracted {len(ruleset.rules)} Transparent Rules:")
for r in ruleset.rules:
    print(f"  RULE #{r.id} (Cover: {r.cover} samples, Confidence: {r.confidence:.2f}):")
    print(f"    IF {' AND '.join(r.conditions)}")
    print(f"    THEN Leaf #{r.leaf_id} prediction = {r.prediction:.2f}")

RULE #1 (n=382, coverage=46.4%):
  WHEN Age <= 28.00 AND Cement <= 380.00
  THEN y = -14.25 + 0.08*Cement + 0.06*BlastFurnaceSlag + 0.28*Age - 0.12*Water

RULE #2 (n=195, coverage=23.7%):
  WHEN Age > 28.00 AND Water <= 180.00
  THEN y = +18.42 + 0.12*Cement + 0.15*Superplasticizer + 0.14*Age - 0.05*FineAggregate

items.title: 3. Hierarchical Leaf Shrinkage
items.text:
In small leaf partitions (\(N < 50\)), unregularized OLS fits are vulnerable to high variance. mltreelib stabilizes leaf parameters by shrinking them toward the parent node's equation:

\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_\text{leaf}^* = \gamma \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_\text{leaf} + (1 - \gamma) \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_\text{parent}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{n}{n + \lambda}\]

Setting shrinkage=10.0 prevents overfitting in sparse leaves while retaining sharp local adaptation in data-rich regimes.

items.title: Decision tree regression with linear leaves: a worked diamond price example
items.text: Consider a 0.95-carat and a 0.99-carat diamond with the same grades. If they reach the same constant leaf, a conventional regression tree predicts the same price for both. A linear leaf can assign different prices inside that region. We can test whether that flexibility improves predictions by changing only the leaf type.
path: Decision tree regression with linear leaves: a worked diamond price example

items.title: How do constant and linear leaves work?
items.text:
A mean leaf predicts the average training outcome in its region. A linear leaf fits a local equation. For two features, that equation can look like intercept + b1 * carat + b2 * width. Routing still happens first. The tree determines which local equation applies.

The trade-off is fit versus support. A shallow mean tree needs enough splits to approximate a curved price surface. A linear leaf needs enough data to estimate coefficients, particularly when carat and physical dimensions are correlated. Predictions on opposite sides of a split can still jump.
path: Decision tree regression with linear leaves: a worked diamond price example

items.title: Train both trees on real data
items.text:
Download OpenML diamonds 46923 to datasets/diamonds.parquet. Clone the repo, run uv sync, then run this code from its root. The seed fixes the random split. It keeps 6,000 training and 2,000 test observations. The input carries cut, color and clarity as raw labels.

from statistics import mean

from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

df = load("diamonds", 46923).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
train, test = df.iloc[:6000], df.iloc[6000:8000]
features = df.columns.drop("price").tolist()
types = ["categorical" if c in {"cut", "color", "clarity"} else "numeric"
         for c in features]
x_train, x_test = rows(train, features), rows(test, features)
y_train, y_test = train.price.tolist(), test.price.tolist()
metric = Metrics()
print("global mean", metric.regression(y_test, [mean(y_train)] * len(test))["rmse"])

for leaf in ("mean", "linear"):
    tree = ModelTree(leaf=leaf, max_depth=2, min_rows=40, prune="none")
    tree.fit(x_train, y_train, col_names=features, dtypes=types)
    predicted = tree.predict(x_test)
    print(leaf, metric.regression(y_test, predicted)["rmse"])
    print(tree.splits()[0], tree.leaves()[0])
path: Decision tree regression with linear leaves: a worked diamond price example

items.title: Where do the models make mistakes?
items.text:
Prediction Test RMSE Global training mean 3,998 Mean leaves 1,712 Linear leaves 1,367

Both trees include a split on carat at 0.87. The linear leaves reduced test RMSE by about 20% compared with the mean leaves in this run. The first leaf had 3,582 training records.

The residual plot puts observed price on the horizontal axis and prediction minus observed price on the vertical axis. Large negative values are underestimates. Horizontal bands and repeated patterns can reveal that the model gives common predictions to very different records. A falling cloud at the high end can matter even if the average error improves.

Check support before reading a coefficient. A local carat coefficient describes the fit within a leaf while its other inputs stay fixed. The data may contain few plausible combinations where width stays constant as carat changes. Inspect actual cases and the training range before using the coefficient for a pricing decision.
path: Decision tree regression with linear leaves: a worked diamond price example

items.title: Does this beat gradient boosting?
items.text:
This experiment compares two leaf types at the same depth and support setting. A comparison with gradient boosting needs the same data split, tuning budget and metrics. Include train time, inference time and failed runs if those matter. Use validation to choose the configuration. A cheaper model can be useful if its residuals are acceptable where the business acts.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py diamonds

items.title: Cubist-style model trees in Python: explain a concrete strength prediction
items.text:
Concrete strength depends on the recipe and curing age. It is plausible that those relationships differ across mixtures. A model tree divides the measurements into regions and fits a local equation in each region. We can inspect those regions and test whether the local equations improve held-out predictions.

Cubist and M5 motivate this combination of partitions and linear models. C5.0 belongs to a related lineage for classification and rule sets. Here we use ModelTree in mltreelib, whose tree fit runs in Rust and is exposed through Python. The exercise compares its mean and linear leaves. It does not reproduce every Cubist or C5.0 rule and committee feature.
path: Cubist-style model trees in Python: explain a concrete strength prediction

items.title: Prepare real concrete measurements
items.text:
Download OpenML concrete compressive strength 46917 to datasets/concrete_compressive_strength.parquet. The UCI source describes the eight inputs and the response in MPa. The dataset includes 1,030 experiments. This tutorial uses 824 for training and 206 for testing. Similar recipes can appear in both parts of this random split. Use grouped recipe or batch splits for claims about new mixes.

Clone the repo, run uv sync, and run this code from the root.

from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

target = "ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
df = load("concrete_compressive_strength", 46917).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
train, test = df.iloc[:824], df.iloc[824:]
features = df.columns.drop(target).tolist()
for leaf in ("mean", "linear"):
    tree = ModelTree(leaf=leaf, max_depth=2, min_rows=40, prune="none")
    tree.fit(rows(train, features), train[target].tolist(), col_names=features)
    prediction = tree.predict(rows(test, features))
    print(leaf, Metrics().regression(test[target].tolist(), prediction)["rmse"])

print("Split", tree.splits()[0])
print("Example leaf", tree.leaves()[0])
print(tree.to_dot())

The last tree uses linear leaves. Its DOT export records the fitted split structure. To create a diagram, save the DOT text to a file and run Graphviz. Use the same feature names for fitting, diagrams and the review worksheet.
path: Cubist-style model trees in Python: explain a concrete strength prediction

items.title: What can you read from a leaf?
items.text:
Test RMSE was 18.34 MPa for the global training mean, 11.63 MPa for mean leaves, and 6.85 MPa for linear leaves. Both trees split first on curing age at 14 days and include a cement split at 350 kg/m³. The linear tree's first leaf had 180 training rows. Its fitted age coefficient was about 1.18 MPa per day with other inputs held fixed inside that leaf.

Start with the root split. Check which training records a branch covers, then read the support n and the leaf's coefficient columns. The split and the coefficients answer different questions. The split chooses a local region. The coefficients describe how the fitted prediction changes within it.

A condition on curing age can expose a useful region for an experiment. Treat the coefficient as predictive until a controlled study estimates the effect of changing the process. A large residual for a particular recipe is often a better place to investigate than the largest global importance bar.
path: Cubist-style model trees in Python: explain a concrete strength prediction

items.title: How does a rule become a useful handoff?
items.text:
Use the diagram to read the structure. Check boundary routing before transcribing the displayed conditions.

Record the feature name, input unit, threshold, missing direction, leaf support and final prediction. Use the exported representation to review a few rows on both sides of each boundary. If you extract a separate rule set, compare its predictions with the tree and check how overlapping and unmatched rules behave.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py concrete

items.title: Comprehensive Regression Methods & Regularizers Showcase
items.text:
A single regression loss cannot serve every problem. Real datasets exhibit physical non-linearities, heavy-tailed claim distributions, overdispersed counts, and grouped dummy encodings.

This showcase provides an empirical benchmark across four distinct regression regimes, comparing constant 0D leaves, piecewise linear leaves, robust M-estimators, asymmetric quantile envelopes, adaptive splines, generalized linear models (GLMs), and structured group penalties.

All benchmarks run from a single reproducible script with zero scikit-learn dependency:

uv run python -u examples/regression_methods_showcase.py

items.title: Regression Architecture Taxonomy
items.text:
mltreelib unifies tree partitioning with heterogeneous local leaf solvers:

Family Architecture Optimization Objective Primary Use Case 0D Constant LeafKind::Mean, Median, Huber SSE, SAE (\(L_1\)), Huber Location Fast step-function baselines 1D Linear LeafKind::Linear (OLS / Ridge / Lasso) \(\frac{1}{2n}\|X\beta - y\|_2^2 + \lambda_1\|\beta\|_1 + \lambda_2\|\beta\|_2^2\) Piecewise linear trends with coordinate sparsity Robust M-Estimation LeafKind::Linear (loss="huber") Piecewise quadratic/linear with iterative \(\hat{\sigma}_\text{MAD}\) scale Outlier-contaminated responses and heavy tails Asymmetric Quantiles LeafKind::Linear (loss="quantile", \(\tau\)) Pinball loss \(\rho_\tau(r) = r(\tau - \mathbb{1}(r < 0))\) Conditional risk boundaries & prediction intervals Smooth Asymmetric LeafKind::Linear (loss="expectile", \(\tau\)) Asymmetric squared \(\rho_\tau^\text{exp}(r) = \|\tau - \mathbb{1}(r < 0)\| r^2\) Differentiable asymmetric loss without pinball kinks Constrained Bounded LeafKind::Linear (nnls=True) Lawson-Hanson active-set \(\beta \ge 0\) Non-negative price, dosage, or mixing mixtures Structured Groups LeafKind::Linear (group_l2 > 0) Block soft-thresholding \(\sum_g \sqrt{p_g} \|\beta_g\|_2\) One-hot dummy blocks and multi-channel features Count & Bounded GLM LeafKind::Glm (Poisson, NegBinomial, Beta) Maximum deviance with canonical/log link Overdispersed counts and rates in \((0, 1)\) Adaptive Splines MarsRegressor Forward hinge basis expansion + backward pruning Piecewise linear continuous basis functions Penalized Spline GAM GamRegressor B-splines with second-difference roughness penalty Smooth additive non-linear response curves

items.title: Study 1: Physical Continuous Process (Concrete Compressive Strength)
items.text:
• Dataset: Industrial Concrete Mixtures (OpenML 4353)
  • Structure: 1,030 samples, 8 continuous physical ingredients (Cement, Blast Furnace Slag, Fly Ash, Water, Superplasticizer, Coarse Aggregate, Fine Aggregate, Age).
  • Core Question: Can local linear leaves, hierarchical leaf shrinkage, or smooth splines beat piecewise constant CART?

items.title: Empirical Results
items.text: Model Architecture Test RMSE Test MAE Complexity Fit Time CART Mean Leaf (0D SSE) 9.947 7.656 15 leaves 12.7 ms Binned Histogram Split (0D SSE) 10.029 7.709 15 leaves 2.0 ms Median Leaf (0D \(L_1\) Location) 9.971 7.642 15 leaves 3.3 ms OLS Linear Tree (shrinkage=0.0) 6.589 4.790 15 leaves 11.4 ms Hierarchical Shrunk Tree (\(\lambda=10.0\)) 6.503 4.842 15 leaves 5.5 ms Huber Robust Linear Tree 6.594 4.684 15 leaves 231.9 ms NNLS Non-Negative Linear Tree 6.785 4.944 15 leaves 3.2 ms Expectile Linear Tree (\(\tau=0.75\)) 7.235 5.377 15 leaves 33.7 ms MARS Adaptive Spline (max_terms=15) 6.586 5.423 12 terms 28.4 ms Penalized B-Spline GAM (n_knots=8) 5.533 4.428 65 terms 28.9 ms

items.title: Key Findings
items.text:
1. Piecewise linear leaves crush 0D CART: Moving from constant leaves to local linear leaves reduces test RMSE from \(9.947\) to \(6.589\) (a 33.8% error reduction).
  2. Hierarchical leaf shrinkage prevents local overfitting: Shrinking leaf equations toward parent nodes via \(\gamma = \frac{n}{n + \lambda}\) drops test RMSE from \(6.589\) to \(6.503\).
  3. Smooth additive B-splines dominate physical mixtures: The Penalized B-spline GAM achieves the lowest overall error (\(5.533\) RMSE), capturing smooth monotonic physical interactions across curing ages and cement ratios.

• Dataset: US Healthcare Expenses (OpenML 43894)

  • Core Question: How do Huber M-estimators, Group Lasso dummy penalties, and asymmetric quantile envelopes handle heavy-tailed financial data?

items.title: Multi-Tau Quantile Crossing Diagnostics
items.text:
Fitting independent quantile surfaces across \(\tau \in [0.10, 0.50, 0.90]\) can cause quantile crossing when lines invert. mltreelib includes native diagnostic verification:

from mltreelib import detect_quantile_crossings

diag = detect_quantile_crossings(
    predictions=[pred_q10, pred_q50, pred_q90],
    taus=[0.10, 0.50, 0.90]
)
print("Violations:", diag["n_violations"], "Max Dollar Inversion:", diag["max_violation"])

The Negative Binomial GLM tree models conditional variance as \(V(\mu) = \mu + \alpha \mu^2\), outperforming both constant CART (\(0.750\)) and Gaussian OLS (\(0.725\)).

items.title: Study 4: Controlled Ground Truth & Structured Group Sparsity
items.text: • Setup: Controlled simulation with 12 features split into two structured 4-column blocks plus individual coordinates and a non-linear sine component: $\(\mathbf{x}_\text{signal} \in \mathbb{R}^4, \quad \mathbf{x}_\text{noise} \in \mathbb{R}^4, \quad x_\text{sine} \sim \mathcal{U}(-3, 3), \quad y = \mathbf{x}_\text{signal}^\top \boldsymbol{\beta} + 2.5 \sin(x_\text{sine}) + \epsilon\)$

items.text: Model Configuration Test RMSE Test MAE Fit Time Standard OLS Linear Tree 0.756 0.643 2.4 ms Coordinate Lasso Tree (\(L_1=2.0\)) 0.920 0.776 0.8 ms Group Lasso Tree (\(\text{group\_l2}=5.0\)) 0.925 0.779 0.8 ms Sparse-Group Lasso (\(L_1=1.5, \text{group\_l2}=4.0\)) 1.168 0.959 0.8 ms Penalized B-Spline GAM on Sine Feature 0.209 0.161 0.7 ms

items.title: Block Zeroing Verification
items.text: Under Group Lasso, the block norm of the uninformative noise features \(\|\beta_\text{noise}\|_2\) is driven exactly to \(0.0\), selecting only the active signal group. The B-spline GAM smoothly recovers the true sine curve with an RMSE of \(0.209\).

items.title: Code Example: Running the Benchmark Suite
items.text:
from mltreelib import (
    ModelTree,
    GamRegressor,
    MarsRegressor,
    detect_quantile_crossings,
)

# 1. Fit an OLS ModelTree with Hierarchical Leaf Shrinkage
tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="linear",
    max_depth=4,
    min_rows=20,
    shrinkage=10.0,  # Empirical Bayes leaf-to-parent shrinkage
)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_shrunk = tree.predict(X_test)

# 2. Fit a Smooth Penalized B-Spline GAM
gam = GamRegressor(
    n_knots=8,
    spline_order=3,
    l2_penalty=1.0,
    fit_intercept=True,
)
gam.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_gam = gam.predict(X_test)

# 3. Fit a Huber Robust Linear Tree
huber_tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="linear",
    loss="huber",
    huber_delta=1.345,
    max_depth=4,
)
huber_tree.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_huber = huber_tree.predict(X_test)

items.text:
Three classical capabilities modernizing Quinlan's C5.0 and Cubist lineage in Rust: 1. R / statsmodels Leaf Regression Summaries: Exact goodness-of-fit tables, degrees of freedom, standard errors, \(t\)-values, \(p\)-values, \(R^2\), and \(F\)-statistics computed via closed-form covariance matrix \((X^T X)^{-1}\) inversion. 2. C5.0 Rule-Set Extraction: Transforming decision paths into standalone IF-THEN rules with interval simplification and Quinlan's pessimistic binomial error pruning (\(CF=0.25\)). 3. Cubist \(k\)-NN Sample Neighbor Adjustments: Adjusting terminal leaf predictions at inference time using distance-weighted training residuals.

items.title: 1. R summary(lm) & Python statsmodels Leaf Summaries

items.title: 2. C5.0 Rule-Set Extraction with Pessimistic Pruning
items.text:
A decision tree forces disjoint, hierarchical branching. C5.0 extracts root-to-leaf paths into standalone IF-THEN rules, simplifies multi-condition bounds on the same feature, and greedily prunes preconditions using Quinlan's pessimistic error upper bound (\(U_{CF}(E, N)\)):

# Extract and prune rules with confidence factor cf=0.25
ruleset = tree.extract_rules(X_train, y_train, prune=True, cf=0.25)
print(ruleset)

# Predict directly using the extracted rule set
predictions = ruleset.predict(X_test)

Output:

items.title: 3. Cubist \(k\)-NN Sample Neighbor Adjustments
items.text:
Cubist's signature technique corrects model tree predictions by finding the \(k\) nearest training samples in normalized feature space and adjusting the prediction by their weighted residuals:

\[\hat{y}_{\text{adj}}(x) = \hat{y}(x) + \sum_{i=1}^k w_i (y_i - \hat{y}(x_i)), \quad w_i = \frac{1}{D(x, x_i) + \epsilon}\]

where distance is scaled Manhattan distance: $\(D(x, z) = \frac{1}{p} \sum_{j=1}^p \frac{|x_j - z_j|}{\sigma_j}\)$

# Standard ModelTree prediction
base_preds = tree.predict(X_test)

# Cubist k-NN adjusted prediction with 5 neighbors
adj_preds_5 = tree.predict(X_test, neighbors=5)

items.title: 4. Native Leaf-KNN & DW-KNN Architecture
items.text:
Beyond post-hoc inference adjustments, mltreelib implements native Leaf-KNN models where each partitioned terminal node fits a localized, metric-weighted \(k\)-NN regressor or classifier directly inside the tree structure (leaf="knn" or leaf="dwknn").

Script: examples/knn_leaf_showcase.py.
path: Rules, Leaf Regression Summaries & k-NN Adjustments

items.title: Weighting Variants
items.text:
• uniform: Standard unweighted majority vote / mean over \(k\) nearest leaf samples.
  • distance: Inverse-distance weighting (Dudani, 1976), \(w_i = 1 / (d_i + \epsilon)\).
  • exponential: Radial / kernel exponential decay, \(w_i = \exp(-\gamma \cdot d_i^2)\).
  • dual: Distance \(\times\) local compactness weighting (Gou et al., 2012).
  • double / dwknn: Double-Weighted KNN (Pathak, Karthik, Madan, Kapila; arXiv:2512.08956). Precomputes neighbor validity \(v_i\) for each training instance within its neighborhood, dampening label noise and boundary anomalies before query voting: $\(w_i = \frac{1}{d_i + \epsilon} \times v_i\)$
path: Rules, Leaf Regression Summaries & k-NN Adjustments

items.title: Proximity & Distance Metrics
items.text: Supports 10 distance metrics via knn_metric: - Continuous geometry: euclidean, manhattan, chebyshev, minkowski(p) - Directional & correlation: cosine, correlation - Normalized & relative: canberra, braycurtis - Mixed / Missing data: gower (range-normalized across numerical and categorical features; handles missing None values without imputation) - Scale-invariant: mahalanobis (diagonal variance-scaled)
path: Rules, Leaf Regression Summaries & k-NN Adjustments

items.title: Usage Example
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Train a ModelTree with DW-KNN leaves and Gower distance
tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="dwknn",
    knn_k=7,
    knn_metric="gower",
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=15,
)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Predictions invoke localized DW-KNN within the targeted leaf node
y_pred = tree.predict(X_test)

You can also dynamically retrain tree leaves using LeafControl: 

from mltreelib import LeafControl

# Retrain existing tree partitions to DW-KNN without rebuilding the tree topology
tree.retrain(
    X_train,
    y_train,
    leaf_control=LeafControl(leaf="knn", knn_variant="double", knn_k=5, knn_metric="manhattan"),
)

items.text:
Consolidated Flagship Guide

items.title: Explainable Decision Stumps & Leaf Retraining
items.text:
A single decision stump (max_depth=1) splits feature space into two transparent regimes, then fits independent models inside each leaf. This pattern replicates the high-explainability output of Quinlan's Cubist and C5.0 — models senior executives, actuaries, and clinical leaders understand in seconds.

With tree.retrain(...), leaf models can be refitted across families (linear, huber, quantile, binomial, poisson) on frozen partitions in milliseconds (~2.2 ms on 1,000 rows across 1,000 runs), completely decoupling split finding from leaf estimation.

Script: examples/practical_stump_showcase.py.

items.title: Real-World Case: Healthcare Insurance Expenses
items.text:
Using the TabArena healthcare_insurance_expenses benchmark (1,338 patients with age, bmi, children, smoker predicting medical charges):

from mltreelib import ModelTree, LeafControl
from mltreelib.datasets import load_dataset

d = load_dataset("healthcare_insurance_expenses")
cols = ["age", "bmi", "children", "smoker"]
x = [[d["columns"][c][i] for c in cols] for i in range(d["n_rows"])]
y = d["columns"]["charges"]

stump = ModelTree(max_depth=1, min_rows=20, leaf="linear", l2=1e-3, leaf_digest=True)
stump.fit(x, y, dtypes=["numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "categorical"])

items.title: Practical Insights Delivered Instantly
items.text:
1. Identical Aging Velocity:
  2. Non-smokers: +$265.29 / year
  3. Smokers: +$264.93 / year

  4. Both populations accumulate baseline medical risk at identical rates (~$265 annually).

  5. Compounding Metabolic Risk:

  6. Non-smokers: +$5.28 / BMI unit (essentially flat).
  7. Smokers: +$1,438.73 / BMI unit (270× steeper!).

  8. In smokers, high BMI triggers catastrophic cardiovascular and pulmonary claims. A flat linear model would average these slopes (~$330/BMI) and miss the entire interaction.

  9. Base Claim Shift:

  10. Non-smoker average: $8,434
  11. Smoker average: $32,050 (nearly 4× higher).

items.title: Frozen-Topology Retraining (tree.retrain)
items.text:
Re-partitioning 1,338 rows across feature candidates takes ~38 ms. But once split boundaries are set, leaf models can be swapped and refitted in < 1 ms:

# 1. Robust Huber M-estimator (outlier bill resistance)
stump.retrain(x, y, leaf="huber")

# 2. Actuarial Quantile Bands (10th, 50th, 90th percentile reserves)
stump.retrain(x, y, leaf="linear", l2=1e-3, leaf_digest=True)
q10 = stump.quantile(test_cases, 0.10)
q50 = stump.quantile(test_cases, 0.50)
q90 = stump.quantile(test_cases, 0.90)

# 3. Regularized Ridge Leaves (shrinkage under small sample partitions)
stump.retrain(x, y, leaf="linear", l2=10.0)

# 4. Piecewise Constant CART baseline
stump.retrain(x, y, control=LeafControl(leaf="mean"))

items.title: Architectural Extensibility
items.text: By decoupling routing from leaf estimation: - The tree handles global discrete partitioning (discovering regime boundaries). - The leaves handle local estimation (OLS, GLM, Huber, Quantiles, and future kNN, SVM, or Neural leaves). - Leaf models can be updated in production or fine-tuned on recent data without altering approved business rules.

items.title: Tobit & Censored Regression Trees
items.text:
Tobit models a latent response censored at a known boundary. A natural lower bound or a real zero alone does not establish censoring. Latent-normal and censoring assumptions must fit the application.

ModelTree provides native Tobit regression leaves (leaf_family="tobit") fitted via iterative reweighted least squares (IRLS / EM) inside tree partitions.

Script: - examples/tobit_benchmark.py (python3 examples/tobit_benchmark.py)

======================================================================
1. TOBIT VS OLS: OVERCOMING ATTENUATION BIAS ON CENSORED DATA
======================================================================
Sample size: N=1500 | Censored at zero: 38.5%
True Latent Model: y* = 0.5 + 2.0 * x + N(0, 1)

Fitted Parameters:
  OLS (Gaussian) : Intercept = +0.8850 | Slope = +1.3257 (Attenuated by 33.7%)
  Tobit (Censored): Intercept = +0.4458 | Slope = +2.0920 (Recovery error: 0.0920)

items.title: 1. The Tobit Model Formulation
items.text:
The standard formulation assumes a latent continuous variable \(y^*_i\): $\(y^*_i = x_i' \beta + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\)$

Observed outcomes are left-censored at threshold \(c\) (default \(c = 0\)): $\(y_i = \begin{cases} y^*_i & \text{if } y^*_i > c \\ c & \text{if } y^*_i \le c \end{cases}\)$

The log-likelihood consists of discrete probability mass at \(c\) and continuous Gaussian density for uncensored observations: $\(\ln L = \sum_{y_i = c} \ln \left[ 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{x_i' \beta - c}{\sigma}\right) \right] + \sum_{y_i > c} \left[ -\frac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{(y_i - x_i' \beta)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right]\)$

items.title: 2. ModelTree Tobit Usage
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Fit a piece-wise linear Tobit tree
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=2,
    min_rows=30,
    leaf="linear",
    leaf_family="tobit",
    l2=1e-3,
    tobit_threshold=0.0,
)
tree.fit(X, y)

# Predict latent expected response
predictions = tree.predict(X_test)

items.title: 3. Econometric Benchmark: Mroz (1987)
items.text: On the classic Mroz female labor supply dataset (datasets/external/mroz.csv): - 43.2% of women in the survey reported 0 hours worked. - OLS attenuates the disincentive effect of infant children (kidslt6), giving \(-403.61\) hours. - The fitted Tobit tree leaf coefficient is of \(-436.19\) hours.

items.title: Tree Architecture, Growth Knobs & Structural Constraints
items.text:
Decision trees are notorious for high variance and unconstrained overfitting when grown without structural bounds. Conversely, over-constraining a tree can cause underfitting and miss localized non-linear interactions.

mltreelib solves this with a Two-Control Decoupling Architecture that cleanly separates how the tree grows its topology from how local leaves solve their objectives.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Growth [GrowthControl: Tree Topology & Search]
        G1[max_depth: Maximum recursive height]
        G2[min_rows: Minimum node partition support]
        G3[min_gain: Minimal deviance improvement]
        G4[max_leaves: Best-first leaf budget]
        G5[criterion: SSE, Deviance, Tweedie, etc.]
    end

    subgraph Structural [StructuralControl: Domain & Legal Constraints]
        S1[monotone_constraints: Directional sign enforcement]
        S2[interaction_groups: Restricted split pairs]
        S3[honesty: Independent sample splitting]
        S4[pruning: Cost-complexity CCP validation]
    end

    Growth --> T["Fitted ModelTree Topology\nValid White-Box Partitions"]
    Structural --> T
    T --> L["Leaf Solvers: 0D Mean / 1D OLS / Huber / Quantile"]

    classDef blueBox fill:#1e3a8a,stroke:#3b82f6,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef greenBox fill:#14532d,stroke:#22c55e,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;

    class G1,G2,G3,G4,G5 blueBox;
    class S1,S2,S3,S4 greenBox;

items.title: 1. The Growth Knob Grid (Depth, Min Rows, and Pruning)
items.text:
The balance between model bias and variance is tuned via recursive growth controls:

Parameter Type Default Operational Effect max_depth int 6 Hard ceiling on recursive partitioning depth. min_rows int 20 Minimum sample count required to attempt a split. min_gain float 0.0 Minimum reduction in split deviance required to accept a partition. prune str "none" Cost-complexity pruning ("cost_complexity" via holdout cross-validation). 

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Regularized tree growth configuration
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=4,
    min_rows=35,
    min_gain=1e-4,
    prune="cost_complexity",
    ccp_alpha=0.015,
)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

items.title: 2. Monotone & Interaction Constraints
items.text:
In regulated domains such as insurance rating and credit underwriting, legal and physical rules dictate that increasing risk indicators (e.g. debt ratio, past delinquencies, or vehicle speed) must never decrease predicted default probability or claim cost.

mltreelib enforces strict monotonicity along split paths: - +1: Monotonically non-decreasing (\(\frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial x_j} \ge 0\)). - -1: Monotonically non-increasing (\(\frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial x_j} \le 0\)). - 0: Unconstrained split behavior.

import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ModelTree, Metrics

# 1. Generate credit applicant data with natural risk relationships
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_applicants = 1200

# Predictors: Revolving Utilization (%), Borrower Age (Years), Monthly Income ($k)
utilization = rng.uniform(0.05, 1.20, n_applicants)
age = rng.uniform(21.0, 75.0, n_applicants)
income = rng.uniform(2.0, 20.0, n_applicants)

# Default risk increases with utilization, decreases with age and income
risk_score = 0.45 * utilization - 0.005 * age - 0.02 * income + rng.normal(0, 0.05, n_applicants)

X = np.column_stack([utilization, age, income])
feature_names = ["revolving_utilization", "borrower_age", "monthly_income"]

# 2. Enforce domain monotonicity: +1 (increasing), -1 (decreasing)
# Utilization must increase risk (+1), Age must decrease risk (-1), Income must decrease risk (-1)
monotone_spec = [1, -1, -1]

tree = ModelTree(
    leaf="linear",
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=30,
    monotone=monotone_spec,     # Enforces sign constraints along every split path
    honesty=True,               # Disjoint sample splitting for structure vs leaf estimation
    honesty_fraction=0.5,
    seed=2026,
)
tree.fit(X, risk_score.tolist(), col_names=feature_names)

print("Monotone & Honest Tree Fit Successfully.")
print(f"Total Leaves: {len(tree.leaves())}")
for s in tree.splits():
    print(f"  Split: Feature '{s['col']}' <= {s['threshold']:.3f}")

Related Suites and Documents

  • Suite 2: Structural Constraints & Honesty for mathematical proofs of monotone projection.
  • Suite 1: Core Tree Architecture for allocator-free growth benchmarks.

items.title: Two-Control Architecture & 0D Leaf Formulations
items.text:
Consolidated Flagship Guide

This topic is now part of the comprehensive flagship guide: Tree Architecture, Growth Knobs & Structural Constraints.

items.title: Two-Control Architecture & 0D Leaf Formulations
items.text:
ModelTree decouples tree growth from leaf modeling and provides rich 0D statistical profiles across terminal nodes:

  1. Model configuration:
  2. GrowthControl configures split search, stopping, and pruning.
  3. LeafControl configures the leaf form, family, solver, penalties, and local slope constraints.
  4. Pass each control to ModelTree as an object or a dictionary.
  5. Rich 0D Formulations:
  6. Produce exact 0D statistics across leaves: prob, odds, log_odds, majority_class, var, skew, kurtosis, median, mad, iqr, entropy, gini, zero_fraction, dispersion.
  7. Access directly via leaf["stats"] or tree.leaf_stats().
  8. Predict 0D formulations row-wise on test data: predict(x, kind="prob"|"odds"|"log_odds"|"median"|"stats").
  9. Dual Monotonicity:
  10. tree_monotone: Enforces directional ordering across tree splits: \((\bar{y}_L - \bar{y}_R) \cdot m \le 0\).
  11. leaf_monotone: Enforces directional sign bounds on local linear leaf slopes (\(\beta_j \ge 0\) for +1, \(\le 0\) for -1).
  12. Row & Column Weights:
  13. sample_weight / row_weights / w: Row-level importance weighting.
  14. col_weights: Feature-level split priorities scaling candidate split gains and weighting feature subsampling during col_sample.
  15. Interaction Groups with Column Names:
  16. Restrict root-to-leaf paths using semantic column names (e.g. interaction_groups=[["age", "income"], ["city_tier"]]).

Run the full example.

uv run python examples/two_controls_and_0d_showcase.py

items.title: 1. Configure growth and leaf controls
items.text:
Give the tree a global split constraint on the first feature. Give each local linear model slope constraints on both features.

from mltreelib import GrowthControl, LeafControl, ModelTree

leaves = LeafControl(
    leaf="linear",
    leaf_family="gaussian",
    l1=0.0,
    l2=1e-3,
    leaf_monotone=[1, -1],  # local feature slope constraints
)

growth = GrowthControl(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=10,
    tree_monotone=[1, 0],   # global split ordering
    col_weights=[2.0, 0.5], # feature split priorities
)
model = ModelTree(growth_control=growth, leaf_control=leaves)

Use the constructor examples to pass the same settings through a configuration dictionary or flat keywords.

items.title: 2. 0D Leaf Formulations & Stats Dictionary
items.text:
Train a tree with 0D probability leaves:

clf = ModelTree(leaf="prob", max_depth=2, min_rows=10)
clf.fit(X, y, sample_weight=weights)

# Inspect the full 0D statistics dictionary on every leaf:
for i, leaf in enumerate(clf.leaves()):
    st = leaf["stats"]
    print(f"Leaf {i}: prob={st['prob']:.4f}, odds={st['odds']:.4f}, entropy={st['entropy']:.4f}")
    print(f"         median={st['median']:.4f}, mad={st['mad']:.4f}, iqr={st['iqr']:.4f}")

# Or get the list of leaf stats directly:
all_stats = clf.leaf_stats()

items.title: 3. Flexible Prediction Kinds
items.text:
Predict response values, probabilities, odds ratios, log-odds, medians, or full per-row stats dictionaries:

# Specific 0D formulations:
preds_prob = clf.predict(X_test, kind="prob")
preds_odds = clf.predict(X_test, kind="odds")
preds_lo   = clf.predict(X_test, kind="log_odds")
preds_med  = clf.predict(X_test, kind="median")

# Full 0D stats profile per observation:
preds_stats = clf.predict(X_test, kind="stats")
# Returns a list of dicts: [{"prob": ..., "odds": ..., "entropy": ..., ...}, ...]

items.title: 4. Interaction Groups with Column Names
items.text:
Enforce LightGBM-style interaction constraints using column name lists:

tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=5,
    interaction_groups=[["age", "income"], ["city_tier"]],
)

# Column names resolve automatically during fit:
tree.fit(X, y, col_names=["age", "income", "city_tier"])

# Verify split paths respect the groups:
paths = tree.split_paths()
for path in paths:
    print("Path:", path)

items.title: Unsupervised Density Trees: Clustering & Anomaly Detection
items.text:
Unsupervised learning in high-dimensional tabular data is plagued by the curse of dimensionality: traditional distance-based methods like k-means and DBSCAN degrade when noisy or irrelevant features distort Euclidean distances.

mltreelib provides a clean, unified unsupervised API surface through two high-level facades: - AnomalyModel (or AnomalyTree): Pure Rust tree-based anomaly detection engines (kind="eif" for oblique hyperplanes, kind="det" for piecewise density, kind="hst" for streaming half-spaces, kind="rct" for random cut trees). - ClusterModel (or ClusterTree): Divisive and density-based tree clustering (kind="cltree" for bounding-box density partitions, kind="hdbscan" for reachability MST hierarchies, kind="pct" for predictive clustering trees).

flowchart LR

    B -- "Outlier & Anomaly Ranking" --> C["AnomalyModel(kind='eif')\nRecursive Oblique Hyperplane Isolation"]
    B -- "White-Box Density Clustering" --> D["ClusterModel(kind='cltree')\nSynthetic Reference Partitioning"]
    B -- "Hierarchical Density Clustering" --> E["ClusterModel(kind='hdbscan')\nMutual Reachability Minimum Spanning Tree"]

    C --> F["Continuous Anomaly Score s(x) in [0, 1]\nCalibrated Binary Outlier Flag (0 or 1)"]
    D --> G["Discrete Cluster Labels\nOrthogonal White-Box Bounding Boxes"]
    E --> H["Condensed Tree Cluster Hierarchy\nVariable-Density Cluster Extraction"]

items.title: 1. High-Level Anomaly Detection: AnomalyModel
items.text:
In operations, fraud detection, and hardware monitoring, review budgets are strictly limited. Engineers need an anomaly model that ranks true failures into the top 1% to 5% triage queue.

AnomalyModel(kind="eif") evaluates random oblique hyperplanes through feature space, isolating anomalies with significantly shorter recursive path lengths than normal instances.

items.title: Complete End-to-End Example
items.text:
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import AnomalyModel, Metrics

# 1. Generate realistic multi-sensor telemetry with injected failure anomalies
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_normal = 2000
n_anomalies = 60

# Normal operational cluster (engine cruise telemetry)
normal_sensor1 = rng.normal(loc=120.0, scale=12.0, size=n_normal)
normal_sensor2 = rng.normal(loc=85.0, scale=8.0, size=n_normal)
normal_vibration = rng.exponential(scale=2.5, size=n_normal)

# Injected anomalous sensor drift (bearing failure and thermal spikes)
outlier_sensor1 = rng.uniform(low=180.0, high=240.0, size=n_anomalies)
outlier_sensor2 = rng.uniform(low=130.0, high=160.0, size=n_anomalies)
outlier_vibration = rng.uniform(low=15.0, high=30.0, size=n_anomalies)

X = np.column_stack([
    np.concatenate([normal_sensor1, outlier_sensor1]),
    np.concatenate([normal_sensor2, outlier_sensor2]),
    np.concatenate([normal_vibration, outlier_vibration]),
])
y_true = np.array([0] * n_normal + [1] * n_anomalies)

feature_names = ["temp_primary", "temp_secondary", "vibration_rms"]

# 2. Instantiate and fit AnomalyModel using oblique hyperplane isolation
model = AnomalyModel(
    kind="eif",             # Extended isolation tree
    contamination=0.03,     # Anticipated 3% anomaly prevalence
    max_depth=10,
    seed=2026,
)
model.fit(X, col_names=feature_names)

# 3. Extract continuous anomaly scores and binary classifications
scores = model.score_samples(X)  # Normalized anomaly score in [0, 1]
is_anomaly = model.predict(X)    # Calibrated binary flag: 1 = anomaly, 0 = inlier

# 4. Measure triage efficiency at 5% inspection budget
budget = int(0.05 * len(X))
ranked_indices = np.argsort(-np.array(scores))[:budget]
caught = sum(y_true[i] for i in ranked_indices)

print(f"Total Rows: {len(X)} | True Anomalies: {sum(y_true)}")
print(f"Reviewed Top {budget} Cases (5% Operational Budget):")
print(f"  Captured: {caught}/{sum(y_true)} anomalies ({caught / sum(y_true):.1%} recall)")
print(f"  Precision: {caught / budget:.1%}")

# 5. Review top anomaly profiles
print("\nTop 3 Flagged Anomalies:")
for rank, idx in enumerate(ranked_indices[:3], 1):
    vals = dict(zip(feature_names, [round(v, 2) for v in X[idx]]))
    print(f"  Rank #{rank} (Score: {scores[idx]:.4f}) -> {vals}")

Total Rows: 2060 | True Anomalies: 60
Reviewed Top 103 Cases (5% Operational Budget):
  Captured: 58/60 anomalies (96.7% recall)
  Precision: 56.3%

Top 3 Flagged Anomalies:

items.title: 2. High-Level Density Clustering: ClusterModel
items.text: Rather than tuning distance metrics across noisy dimensions, ClusterModel(kind="cltree") builds an adaptive spatial partition that separates high-density data regions from low-density noise.

items.title: Complete End-to-End Example
items.text:
import numpy as np
from mltreelib import ClusterModel

# 1. Generate multi-modal synthetic customer segments with background noise
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_per_cluster = 300

# Segment A: High frequency, low ticket
seg_a = rng.normal(loc=[15.0, 25.0], scale=[2.0, 4.0], size=(n_per_cluster, 2))
# Segment B: Moderate frequency, high ticket
seg_b = rng.normal(loc=[5.0, 180.0], scale=[1.0, 15.0], size=(n_per_cluster, 2))
# Segment C: Enterprise accounts
seg_c = rng.normal(loc=[30.0, 450.0], scale=[3.0, 30.0], size=(n_per_cluster, 2))
# Uniform background noise
noise = rng.uniform(low=[0.0, 0.0], high=[40.0, 600.0], size=(80, 2))

X_customers = np.vstack([seg_a, seg_b, seg_c, noise])
feature_names = ["monthly_orders", "avg_order_value"]

# 2. Fit ClusterModel using CLTree density partitioning
clusterer = ClusterModel(
    kind="cltree",
    min_rows=25,       # Minimum points to form an independent cluster partition
    max_depth=5,
)
clusterer.fit(X_customers, col_names=feature_names)

# 3. Extract cluster assignments (None represents unassigned background noise)
cluster_ids = clusterer.predict(X_customers)

valid_clusters = [c for c in cluster_ids if c is not None]
unique_clusters = set(valid_clusters)

print(f"Total Customers: {len(X_customers)}")
print(f"Identified {len(unique_clusters)} Cohesive Density Clusters: {sorted(unique_clusters)}")
print(f"Background Noise Points Rejected: {cluster_ids.count(None)}")

# 4. Inspect discovered cluster centroids
for cid in sorted(unique_clusters):
    members = [X_customers[i] for i, c in enumerate(cluster_ids) if c == cid]
    mean_orders, mean_ticket = np.mean(members, axis=0)
    print(f"  Cluster #{cid} (n={len(members)}): Orders = {mean_orders:.1f}/mo, Spend = ${mean_ticket:.2f}")

Total Customers: 980
Identified 3 Cohesive Density Clusters: [0, 1, 2]
Background Noise Points Rejected: 64
  Cluster #0 (n=298): Orders = 15.1/mo, Spend = $24.89
  Cluster #1 (n=296): Orders = 5.0/mo, Spend = $180.12
  Cluster #2 (n=302): Orders = 29.8/mo, Spend = $449.65

ClusterModel (or ClusterTree) "cltree", "hdbscan", "pct", "urf" fit, predict, cluster_profiles Divisive density trees, bounding boxes, and mutual reachability MST. items.title: Review a fitted tree before handing it off
items.text:
Use this checklist after you run a modeling pathway. The example uses the concrete strength tree to show what to deliver with a fitted regression model.

Download OpenML concrete strength 46917 to datasets/concrete_compressive_strength.parquet. Run this code from the repository root after uv sync.

from pathlib import Path

from examples.real_tree_studies import load, rows
from mltreelib import ModelTree

df = load("concrete_compressive_strength", 46917).sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
target = "ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
features = df.columns.drop(target).tolist()
train, test = df.iloc[:824], df.iloc[824:]
tree = ModelTree(leaf="linear", max_depth=2, min_rows=40, prune="none")
tree.fit(rows(train, features), train[target].tolist(), col_names=features)
pred = tree.predict(rows(test, features))

review = test[features + [target]].assign(predicted_mpa=pred)
review["error_mpa"] = review["predicted_mpa"] - review[target]
largest_error = review["error_mpa"].abs().nlargest(5).index
print(review.loc[largest_error].to_string(index=False))
print(tree.split_paths())
print([(leaf["id"], leaf["n"]) for leaf in tree.leaves()])
Path("concrete-tree.dot").write_text(tree.to_dot(), encoding="utf-8")

If Graphviz is installed, render that file with dot -Tsvg concrete-tree.dot -o concrete-tree.svg.

Use the diagram to read the structure. Check boundary routing before transcribing the displayed conditions.

items.title: Prepare the handoff
items.text:
1. Inputs. Record feature order, units, allowed categories and the prediction time. Keep a sample with a missing value.
  2. Evaluation. Report errors for the intended decision. Include the baseline, split method and examples of large errors.
  3. Structure. Export the DOT diagram and keep the structured splits and leaves. Check the support behind the smallest leaves.
  4. Deployment. Compare scores on a fixed set of reference rows after moving the model into the serving environment. Include rows near a split and ones with absent fields.

The concrete strength reference compares the tree with constant leaves. The serving contract lists the checks needed when you move from an example to a service. For the original churn exercise, see the secondary case on the dataset page.

items.title: Extend a model tree
items.text:
Start with a regression or classification pathway. Then choose the change that matches the modeling problem. These options are different decisions, not a checklist to enable together.

Need Technique Read next Outcome is censored at a known bound Tobit leaves Tobit example Domain limits on direction or combinations Monotone or interaction constraints Constraint example Preserve segments while updating leaf models Leaf retraining Retraining examples Control fit complexity and flexibility Growth and leaf settings Growth knob tour Different outcome distributions Distributional families Distributional leaves Predict only from approved input columns Feature and interaction controls Parameters

items.title: Censored outcomes: Tobit
items.text:
Tobit is a model for a latent response observed only above a censoring boundary. Structural zeros, truncation and missing outcomes are different problems. Its interpretation depends on the assumed latent model and censoring mechanism.

from random import Random
from mltreelib import ModelTree

rng = Random(12)
x = [[rng.uniform(-2, 2)] for _ in range(160)]
y = [max(0.0, 0.5 + 2 * row[0] + rng.gauss(0, 1)) for row in x]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=0, min_rows=10, leaf="linear",
                  leaf_family="tobit", tobit_threshold=0.0)
model.fit(x[:120], y[:120], col_names=["signal"])
print("Latent predictions:", model.predict(x[120:])[:3])

The response above is the fitted latent expectation, so negative values are possible even though observations are censored at zero. Evaluate the desired observed outcome separately. Correct censoring assumptions do not guarantee an unbiased result on every dataset. See Tobin (1958).

items.title: Constrain shape and interactions
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

x = [[float(i)] for i in range(40)]
y = [float(i // 10) for i in range(40)]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=5, leaf="mean", monotone=[1])
model.fit(x, y, col_names=["volume"])
print("Predictions:", model.predict([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]]))

A positive constraint encodes a domain requirement. Check predictions on meaningful grids and held-out data. A check on the healthcare example found two decreases with linear leaves when age increased. The same check found no decreases with mean leaves. This is a tracked behavior gap; a finite grid does not prove monotonicity elsewhere. Do not assume local coefficient signs guarantee global monotonicity. Interaction constraints restrict paths and should also be checked with split_paths().

items.title: Retrain leaves with fixed partitions
items.text:
from mltreelib import LeafControl, ModelTree

x = [[float(i)] for i in range(40)]
y = [float(i // 10) for i in range(40)]
model = ModelTree(max_depth=1, min_rows=5, leaf="mean")
model.fit(x, y, col_names=["volume"])
before = model.splits()
model.retrain(x, [v + 1 for v in y], control=LeafControl(leaf="mean"))
print("Splits preserved:", before == model.splits())
print("Updated prediction:", model.predict([[5.0]]))

This example mutates the model. Use appropriate independent data for evaluation and check that each leaf has sufficient new observations. Fixed partitions can become stale when the population changes. See the hierarchical retraining guide for alternative feature sets and routing.

items.title: Tune deliberately
items.text: Start with max_depth and min_rows to control partition size. Compare mean and linear leaves only when their assumptions and interpretation fit the outcome. Tune on a validation set and keep a final test set untouched. The knob tour is a parameter reference, not a recommended sequence or a substitute for evaluation.

items.title: 1. Domain Context & The Ghost Anomaly Problem
items.text:
Standard Isolation Forests construct trees by sampling orthogonal, axis-aligned cuts. On correlated or multi-modal feature distributions, axis-aligned splits produce artificial rectangular bands of low average path length, creating false-positive "ghost" anomalies in empty spaces between normal clusters.

AnomalyTree(kind="eif") implements Extended Isolation Forest (EIF), sampling random oblique hyperplanes with uniformly distributed normal vectors. This achieves rotationally invariant scoring contours that isolate true anomalies without axis-aligned artifacts.
path: Anomaly detection in Python: operational triage review queues

items.title: 2. Fit the Reference Model and Score New Rows
items.text:
You can evaluate on industrial telemetry using load_dataset("APSFailure") or the UCI Statlog Shuttle benchmark:

from mltreelib import Metrics, load_dataset
from mltreelib.anomaly import AnomalyTree

# 1. Load industrial sensor telemetry
data = load_dataset("APSFailure")
target = "AirPressureSystemFailure"
features = ["aa_000", "ab_000", "ac_000", "ad_000", "ae_000", "af_000"]
n_sample = 10000

y_raw = data["columns"][target][:n_sample]
y = [1 if v in ("pos", "1", 1) else 0 for v in y_raw]
X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in features] for i in range(n_sample)]

split = 7000
X_train = [X[i] for i in range(split) if y[i] == 0]  # Fit reference on normal operating states
X_test, y_test = X[split:], y[split:]

# 2. Fit Extended Isolation Forest (oblique cuts, depth=10)
tree = AnomalyTree(kind="eif", max_depth=10, extension_level=1, seed=42)
tree.fit(X_train, col_names=features)

# 3. Score held-out telemetry
scores = tree.predict(X_test, kind="score")

# 4. Allocate fixed 5% operational review budget
budget = round(0.05 * len(scores))
order = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: (-scores[i], i))

hits = sum(y_test[i] for i in order[:budget])
total_anomalies = sum(y_test)
print(f"Review Budget Size : {budget} records (Top 5%)")
print(f"Precision at Budget: {hits / budget:.4f}")
print(f"Recall at Budget   : {hits / max(1, total_anomalies):.4f}")

metrics = Metrics()
print(f"ROC-AUC            : {metrics.roc_curve(y_test, scores)['auc']:.4f}")

kind="binary" returns labels from the fitted threshold, and kind="score" returns the same scores as score_samples(). The extended isolation tree and its aliases also expose kind="path_length".

For a fitted EIF, tree.save("anomalies.json") stores the model and fitted threshold. Use AnomalyTree.load("anomalies.json") to restore scoring and labels. The API reference lists the JSON and byte methods.
path: Anomaly detection in Python: operational triage review queues

items.text:

Engine (kind) Core Mechanism Best Used For "eif" Oblique random hyperplanes with uniform normals Multi-modal, correlated continuous telemetry without ghost artifacts "isolation" Standard axis-aligned recursive bisection Fast baseline on uncorrelated low-dimensional features "det" Density Estimation Trees (piecewise constant density) Estimating exact probability density distributions "hst" Streaming Half-Space Trees with mass-based scoring Online, real-time sliding window data streams "rct" Robust Random Cut Trees (co-displacement scoring) Dynamic time-series streams with concept drift "active" Active learning tree with expert feedback loops Human-in-the-loop analyst triage queues

items.title: Binary classification in Python: predict financial distress
items.text: Use the Give Me Some Credit dataset to estimate financial distress within two years. The tutorial fits a decision tree classifier, then uses validation data to decide which scores enter a review queue.
path: Binary classification in Python: predict financial distress

items.title: 1. Get the data and define the decision
items.text:
Download OpenML 46929 to datasets/GiveMeSomeCredit.parquet. The target is FinancialDistressNextTwoYears. The published table has 150,000 labeled rows. This example uses a shuffled 12,000-row subset. Keep the last 2,000 sampled rows for the final report.

Use observed values as supplied. In the sample, monthly income and number of dependents can be missing. Pass them through to the tree. The input schema is numeric and needs no encoder.
path: Binary classification in Python: predict financial distress

items.title: 2. Fit and choose a threshold
items.text:
import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

df = pd.read_parquet("datasets/GiveMeSomeCredit.parquet")
df = df.sample(frac=1, random_state=2026).iloc[:12000]
target = "FinancialDistressNextTwoYears"
features = df.columns.drop(target).tolist()

def input_data(frame):
    x = [[None if pd.isna(v) else v for v in row]
         for row in frame[features].itertuples(index=False, name=None)]
    return x, (frame[target] == "Yes").astype(int).tolist()

x_train, y_train = input_data(df.iloc[:8000])
x_val, y_val = input_data(df.iloc[8000:10000])
x_test, y_test = input_data(df.iloc[10000:])

tree = ModelTree(leaf="mean", leaf_family="binomial", gain="deviance",
                 max_depth=3, min_rows=100, prune="none")
tree.fit(x_train, y_train, col_names=features, dtypes=["numeric"] * len(features))

val_scores = tree.predict_proba(x_val)
def cost(threshold):
    return sum(5 if y and p < threshold else 1 if not y and p >= threshold else 0
               for y, p in zip(y_val, val_scores))

threshold = min([.02, .05, .10, .20, .40, 1.01], key=cost)
scores = tree.predict_proba(x_test)
alerts = [int(score >= threshold) for score in scores]
print(Metrics().classification(y_test, alerts)["confusion"])

The costs are illustrative. A missed event costs five units and a false alert costs one. A threshold above 1 represents no alerts. The full script also compares probability error with the training event rate.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py credit
path: Binary classification in Python: predict financial distress

items.title: 3. Read the result
items.text:
The validation threshold was 0.20. It flagged 159 of 2,000 test rows. Of the 155 observed distress events, 73 were flagged and 82 were missed. The remaining 86 alerts were false positives.

Test metric Tree Reference Average precision 0.3310 0.0775 event prevalence Brier score 0.0577 0.0717 constant training rate

The root uses revolving utilization. A later split uses the count of payments 60 to 89 days past due. The training sample contains 1,616 missing income values and 222 missing dependent counts.

Average precision measures how well the scores rank the positive cases. Compare it with test prevalence as a reference. Brier score measures squared probability error. Compare it with the constant training-rate model. The probability plot is a diagnostic. Review bin counts and treat sparsely populated bins with care.
path: Binary classification in Python: predict financial distress

items.title: 4. Review the model before acting
items.text:
Use tree.splits() to see the original feature names and tree.leaves() to check support. Evaluate calibration, decision cost and review volume on realistic future records. This random historical split demonstrates a workflow. An underwriting decision needs time-based validation, group analysis, documented data provenance and governance.

Read the credit article for a deeper walkthrough of explanation and threshold choice. Use the evaluation guide for the differences between probability, ranking and decision metrics.
path: Binary classification in Python: predict financial distress

items.title: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry
items.text: Use a predictive clustering tree to group wines by measurements a lab can inspect. The output is a leaf ID, a rule and a profile. A lab could investigate an unexpected shift in the size of a segment across production batches.
path: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry

items.title: 1. Get the data and choose the features
items.text:
Save OpenML Wine Quality 46964 to datasets/wine_quality.parquet. The 6,497 records come from the UCI Wine Quality collection. Use four numeric measurements. Keep median_wine_quality and wine_color out of fitting. Those columns can help interpret groups later.

PCT splits to reduce the variation of numeric features inside its leaves. The measurements have different units, so give them comparable scales using training means and standard deviations. Keep the original units for the report. Scaling is an explicit choice for this similarity objective.
path: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry

items.title: 2. Fit, assign and profile
items.text:
Run this from the repository root. The second split supports a refit check. Assign the review records with both models before comparing them.

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib.cluster import ClusterTree

df = pd.read_parquet("datasets/wine_quality.parquet").sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
features = ["residual_sugar", "volatile_acidity", "alcohol", "chlorides"]
train, review = df.iloc[:2500], df.iloc[5000:].copy()
center = train[features].mean()
scale = train[features].std()

def design(frame):
    return ((frame[features] - center) / scale).to_numpy().tolist()

tree = ClusterTree(kind="pct", max_depth=2, min_rows=150)
tree.fit(design(train), col_names=features)
review["segment"] = tree.predict(design(review), kind="cluster")
print(review.groupby("segment")[features].median().round(3))
print(review["segment"].value_counts().sort_index())
print(tree.rules())

labels_ stores the training assignments and n_clusters_ gives the number of assigned clusters. The full script refits on the other 2,500 wines and draws the figure.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py wine
path: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry

items.title: 3. Read the profiles and check stability
items.text:
Leaf Review rows Median residual sugar (g/L) Median volatile acidity (g/L) Median alcohol (%) 0 715 2.1 0.260 10.9 1 303 2.2 0.580 10.0 2 350 12.0 0.265 9.3 3 129 9.7 0.280 11.0

The two lower-sugar groups differ on acidity. The higher-sugar groups differ on alcohol. Pairwise Jaccard agreement on the 1,497 review wines was 0.841 after refitting at depth two on the second training sample. This is one check with a shared training scale.

A scatter plot only shows two of the four input features. Use the profile panel to see how the segments differ across the full feature list. It displays each segment's median in units of the training standard deviation. For a rule review, convert a standardized threshold back to lab units using threshold * scale + center.

Report pairwise Jaccard agreement after refitting. It counts pairs assigned together in both fits as a fraction of pairs assigned together in either fit. It avoids matching arbitrary leaf IDs and excludes the usually large number of pairs separated by both fits. This tests the stability of one partition with fixed scaling. Before using the groups operationally, repeat with independent batches and compare against a simpler lab rule.
path: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry

items.title: 4. Choose an engine through ClusterTree
items.text:
The following observations are from a small numeric, two-group synthetic check. They establish the interface paths exercised, not comparative model quality.

kind Training and prediction output checked rules() in that check pct Training labels and new-row labels Conditions, prototypes and support cltree Labels can include None for unassigned rows Bounding boxes and support hdbscan Training and new-row labels Empty list urf Training and new-row labels Empty list

The sample check returned 8 PCT leaves, 3 CLTree groups plus unassigned points, 2 HDBSCAN groups, and a highly imbalanced URF assignment. These results depend on the data and settings. They do not rank the engines. Check whether a segment is stable and useful before assigning an action to it.

For URF, tree.predict(x, kind="distances") returns one row per query and one column per training row in fit order. Each distance is the square root of one minus the fraction of trees in which the two rows share a leaf.

For a fitted PCT, tree.save("clusters.json") stores the model, training assignments, and rules. Use ClusterTree.load("clusters.json") to restore the fitted tree. The API reference lists the JSON and byte methods.
path: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry

items.title: Missing values and categories: product gaps
items.text:
The wrapper currently converts None to 0.0 for cltree, hdbscan and urf during fitting and prediction. This is implicit imputation and conflicts with the package's missing-data goal. Track it as a product gap. Do not assume those engines distinguish missing from a real zero. They also reject raw strings in the checked inputs.

PCT accepted raw categorical labels and missing numeric entries in a separate check. Its returned rules displayed category codes rather than the original labels. In that check, an unseen category and a missing category went to different leaves. Category-label rendering and unseen-category routing need further investigation before those rules become a business handoff.

For density and proximity methods, check scaling, distance choice and the meaning of an unassigned or noise label. For all kinds, test the actual new-row behavior and input schema that your workflow uses.
path: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry

items.title: 5. Run the controlled stability example
items.text:
The synthetic clustering workflow lets you change the overlap between known generating groups. It uses 1,000 independent review rows and illustrates how a tree can split a single generating group into several leaves.

See Blockeel et al. on predictive clustering and the engine comparison.
path: Clustering in Python: profile wines by chemistry

items.title: Prepare data for modeling
items.text:
Path: Define the prediction time → Split rows → Inspect types and missingness → Fit transformations on training data → Apply the same schema to new data.

Decision Check Split Keep future observations, customers or groups out of training when they define the deployment setting. Numeric Check units, impossible values, missingness and whether scaling is appropriate for the chosen model. Categorical Preserve the distinction between labels and ordered numeric measurements. Fit any mapping on training data. Target Exclude the outcome and features that become available only after the prediction time. New data Preserve column order, names, types and the fitted mapping. Test unknown levels and missing values.
