ModelTree accepts categorical labels and missing predictors without a separate encoder or imputation step. Declare the feature types and preserve the same column order at prediction time.

from mltreelib import ModelTree

x = [["north", 1.0], ["north", None], ["south", 1.0], ["south", None]] * 10
y = [1.0, 2.0, 9.0, 10.0] * 10
model = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=4, leaf="mean")
model.fit(x, y, dtypes=["categorical", "numeric"],
          col_names=["region", "amount"])
print(model.predict([["north", None], ["south", None]]))
print(model.splits())

Use a separate encoder only when another downstream workflow needs it. If you use one, fit it on training data only.

items.title: Inspect before fitting
items.text:
The data and metrics example creates a synthetic mixed dataset and splits it into training, validation and test rows. It counts missing values on the training rows before fitting. It passes the original categorical labels and missing numeric entries directly to both models.

For the fixed seed, 239 of 2,000 training rows have a missing volume. The chart shows where to investigate collection and data quality. It does not imply that those values need imputation. Also check missingness by source, group and time when those fields are available.

uv run python examples/data_metrics_pathway.py

The example requires matplotlib to render the charts. Graphviz is optional for rendering the tree. The package plotting extra installs the chart dependencies; Graphviz also requires its system executable.

items.title: Choose the preparation
items.text:
Use native categorical inputs for ModelTree. Use an encoder when the downstream estimator requires it. Target-based encoders need leakage-safe training representations and an independently fitted evaluation pipeline. Missing-value behavior varies by operation. Test missing predictors, targets and unknown categories for the exact estimator before deployment.

  • Missing routing explains ModelTree routing.
  • Categorical encoders explains training leakage.
  • Data processing shows typed ingestion, summaries and time features.
  • Time series forecasting shows prior-day features and a time split.
  • Data API catalogs builders, encoders and transforms.

items.title: What remains
items.text: The existing references do not yet give a checked missing and unseen-value matrix for every model and encoder. They also need a single end-to-end example that carries a fitted schema through deployment. In a checked two-category example, an unseen category routed differently from a missing value. This conflicts with the stated unseen-as-missing contract and is recorded as a product gap for investigation. A checked IndexMapper maps an unseen label to missing. In a separate check, OneHotEncoder mapped missing and unseen labels to all-zero vectors, CountEncoder mapped them to missing and zero respectively, and TargetEncoder mapped them to missing and the fitted prior.

items.title: Evaluate and monitor a model
items.text:
Path: Choose a baseline → Choose the split → Select metrics and costs → Tune on validation data → Report once on test data → Monitor outcomes and drift.

Task Start with Also check Regression MAE and RMSE against a mean or operational baseline Residuals, large errors, segments, time periods Classification Confusion matrix and precision/recall at a chosen threshold Probability calibration, PR curve, costs, subgroup outcomes Clustering Segment sizes, profiles and stability Out-of-sample assignment, usefulness and sensitivity to scaling Anomaly Reviewed precision at a fixed review budget Score drift, alert volume, missed cases when labels are available Survival Censoring-aware discrimination and calibration Risk sets and reliability at the chosen horizon Uplift Randomized held-out policy value Arm counts, uncertainty, cost and overlap

items.title: A complete held-out example
items.text:
The data and metrics example uses the same raw mixed inputs for regression and classification. It generates 4,000 synthetic rows with a fixed seed: 2,000 for training, 1,000 for validation and 1,000 for test. It uses raw category labels and missing numeric values without encoding or imputation.

uv run python examples/data_metrics_pathway.py

items.title: Regression: compare with a baseline
items.text: The script compares test MAE with a constant equal to the training outcome mean. For this synthetic run, model MAE is 2.505 and baseline MAE is 5.098. Those numbers describe this generated sample, not a general benchmark. Use residual plots to look for error patterns rather than relying only on an average.

items.title: Classification: ranking, calibration and decisions
items.text:
The script chooses among four thresholds on validation data. Its illustrative cost assigns three units to a missed event and one unit to a false alert. The selected threshold is 0.2. The test confusion matrix is [[6, 486], [1, 507]], with actual classes in rows and predicted classes in columns. Test average precision is 0.643.

A precision–recall curve shows the tradeoff as the score threshold changes. Compare it with the positive event rate and the capacity of the review team. It does not establish calibration.

Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed event frequencies in bins. Small bins make the plot unstable. The 1,000 test rows come from a synthetic distribution; the plot alone does not establish calibration in production.

Use IsotonicCalibrator to fit a monotone mapping for binary event probabilities. Fit the mapping on validation or out-of-fold probabilities. Compare Brier scores on independent test rows.

from mltreelib import Metrics
from mltreelib.calibration import IsotonicCalibrator

calibrator = IsotonicCalibrator.fit(y_val, model.predict_proba(X_val))
raw = model.predict_proba(X_test)
calibrated = calibrator.predict(raw)
metrics = Metrics()
print(metrics.brier_score(y_test, raw), metrics.brier_score(y_test, calibrated))

The confusion matrix describes decisions at one chosen threshold. Change the cost assumptions or capacity and repeat threshold selection on validation data. Keep the test set independent of that selection.

items.title: Inspect the tree
items.text:
The tree is rendered from ModelTree.to_dot(). Node conditions describe the fitted partitions. Check feature names, missing routing and leaf support before using them in a report. Categorical conditions can display internal codes, so check their meaning before sharing a rule. A prediction path does not establish the effect of an intervention.

Split importance summarizes gain used by the fitted tree. It is not a causal effect and does not measure every source of predictive value. The visualization guide shows how to select and render each view.

items.title: What remains
items.text:
The current metrics guide catalogs many report functions, but it does not provide a complete task-by-task evaluation workflow. Survival, uplift, clustering and anomaly examples still need validated task-specific evaluation and uncertainty examples. Check the API before assuming that a recommended metric is implemented by this package.

Metrics and plots · Metrics reference · Model pathways

items.text:
Use OpenML 46911 at datasets/Bank_Customer_Churn.parquet to compare three interfaces on the same mixed feature schema. The script fits a churn classifier, a cluster tree and an anomaly tree. Only the classifier uses churn labels.

The unsupervised outputs describe this customer table. A churn outcome cannot validate an anomaly ranking or determine whether a segment is actionable.

items.title: Decision tree regression in Python: estimate diamond prices
items.text: Predict the listed price of a diamond from its measurements and grading labels. Compare a simple baseline and two tree configurations. Inspect the largest errors before using the score for a pricing decision.
path: Decision tree regression in Python: estimate diamond prices

items.title: 1. Get the data and make the split
items.text:
Save the OpenML diamonds dataset 46923 to datasets/diamonds.parquet. It contains 53,940 records. Use 6,000 rows to fit and 2,000 independent rows to evaluate. A production pricing study needs a split that respects listing date, seller and repeated items where available.

The input includes numeric measurements such as carat and raw labels for cut, color and clarity. Keep those labels as strings. Select the target and feature order once.
path: Decision tree regression in Python: estimate diamond prices

items.title: 2. Fit and compare
items.text:
from statistics import mean

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree

df = pd.read_parquet("datasets/diamonds.parquet").sample(frac=1, random_state=2026)
features = df.columns.drop("price").tolist()
types = ["categorical" if c in {"cut", "color", "clarity"} else "numeric"
         for c in features]
train, test = df.iloc[:6000], df.iloc[6000:8000]

def rows(frame):
    return [[None if pd.isna(v) else v for v in row]
            for row in frame[features].itertuples(index=False, name=None)]

x_train, x_test = rows(train), rows(test)
y_train, y_test = train["price"].tolist(), test["price"].tolist()
metrics = Metrics()
print("baseline", metrics.regression(y_test, [mean(y_train)] * len(test))["rmse"])

for leaf in ("mean", "linear"):
    tree = ModelTree(leaf=leaf, max_depth=2, min_rows=40, prune="none")
    tree.fit(x_train, y_train, col_names=features, dtypes=types)
    predictions = tree.predict(x_test)
    print(leaf, metrics.regression(y_test, predictions)["rmse"])
    print(tree.splits()[:1], tree.leaves()[0])

Run the complete study to regenerate the chart.

uv run python examples/real_tree_studies.py diamonds
path: Decision tree regression in Python: estimate diamond prices

items.title: 3. Interpret the errors
items.text:
Prediction Test RMSE Global training mean 3,998 Mean leaves 1,712 Linear leaves 1,367

Both trees include a split on carat at 0.87. The linear leaves reduced test RMSE by about 20% compared with the mean leaves in this run. The first leaf had 3,582 training records.

The left panel summarizes error with RMSE. The right panel shows prediction minus observed price. Look for systematic underpricing below the zero line and overpricing above it. Add MAE if you need the average absolute error in price units. Review residuals by cut, price band and support. A shallow linear tree can follow a trend inside a leaf. Check for extrapolation and sudden changes at split boundaries before relying on that trend.

Use splits() to review named feature conditions and leaves() to inspect support and coefficients. Category conditions can display internal codes. Keep that mapping available before showing a rule to a reviewer.
path: Decision tree regression in Python: estimate diamond prices

items.title: 4. Repeat the comparison with missing inputs
items.text:
The regression comparison first generates 5,000 records with raw category labels and 15% missing numeric inputs. It fits four ModelTree configurations on 3,000 rows, selects one using 1,000 validation rows, then checks it on 1,000 separate test rows. The test set contains 169 missing numeric values. No imputation or categorical encoder is applied.

uv run python examples/regression_real_and_synthetic.py
Synthetic configuration Validation RMSE Mean leaves, depth 2 3.594 Mean leaves, depth 4 2.704 Linear leaves, depth 2 2.770 Linear leaves, depth 4 2.633

For this seed and simulated data, linear leaves at depth 4 had the lowest validation RMSE. Its test RMSE was 2.933, against 6.385 for a training-mean baseline. This chooses among four settings on one synthetic problem. It does not establish the best model for other datasets.

The same configuration then fits 6,000 rows from the real OpenML diamonds dataset 46923 and predicts 2,000 separate rows. The data has 53,940 total records. Download its parquet file to datasets/diamonds.parquet; see the dataset manifest. The example needs pandas, pyarrow and matplotlib.

On the fixed random split, test RMSE was 1,225.052 versus 3,982.039 for the training-mean baseline. Test MAE was 641.615 versus 3,012.514. These values use the dataset's price units and describe this split, not a benchmark result. The selected real training columns contained no missing values, so the synthetic check supplies the missing-data exercise.

The real tree splits on named size measurements, including x and y, and exposes leaf support and coefficients. Inspect the feature definitions and leaf sample sizes before drawing business conclusions. Category values in fitted structures can appear as internal codes. Coefficients and paths describe the prediction model; they do not establish what happens if a business changes a feature.

For more on local slopes and the fair comparison setup, see the model tree regression reference.

items.title: Prepare a model for prediction
items.text: Record the fitted model's prediction contract, then save the model and check predictions after reloading.

items.title: Record the prediction contract
items.text:
Item Record before handing off the model Decision Outcome, units, prediction horizon and when features are available. Inputs Feature names, order, types, units and allowed values. Missingness Which fields can be missing and how the fitted model routes them. Categories Training vocabulary and how the workflow handles an unseen value. Output Prediction kind, scale, class ordering and any decision threshold. Evidence Training data period, split, baseline, metrics and known model gaps. 
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Ingestion Client / API Gateway
    participant Guard as Schema Guard & Validator
    participant Normalizer as Sentinel Normalizer (None / NaN)
    participant Core as mltreelib-core Tree Route
    participant Leaf as Local Leaf Solver (Linear / GLM)
    participant Decision as Threshold & Policy Post-Processor

    Client->>Guard: Submit Raw Record (JSON Payload)
    Note over Guard: Check required keys, field order, and valid types
    Guard->>Normalizer: Verified Named Features
    Note over Normalizer: Treat unobserved keys, NaNs, and unseen category levels as missing
    Normalizer->>Core: Fast Vector Traversal [x1, x2, ..., xk]
    Note over Core: Traverse internal split nodes using learned missing_left and surrogates
    Core->>Leaf: Deliver to Terminal Leaf Node
    Note over Leaf: Evaluate local linear model: y_hat = b0 + sum(bj * xj)
    Leaf->>Decision: Continuous Raw Score / Probability
    Note over Decision: Apply calibrated threshold (e.g. p >= 0.20 -> Review Queue)
    Decision-->>Client: Final Actionable Prediction & Audit Path

ModelTree accepts raw categorical strings and missing predictor values. Preserve the fitted feature order. A row-based input does not carry column names at prediction time, so your application needs to check the schema before constructing rows.

items.title: Fit and predict with named records
items.text:
The following example checks names before converting a record to the fitted order. It passes category labels and missing values directly to the tree.

from mltreelib import ModelTree

names = ["region", "volume"]
dtypes = ["categorical", "numeric"]
x_train = [["north", 1.0], ["north", None], ["south", 1.0], ["south", None]] * 10
y_train = [1.0, 2.0, 9.0, 10.0] * 10
model = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=4, leaf="mean")
model.fit(x_train, y_train, col_names=names, dtypes=dtypes)

record = {"region": "north", "volume": None}
if set(record) != set(names):
    raise ValueError("Input fields do not match the model schema")
row = [record[name] for name in names]
print("Prediction:", model.predict([row])[0])

Check types, units, ranges and batch sizes at the application boundary as well. The short example checks field names only. It does not provide a complete serving validator.

items.title: Persist a fitted model
items.text:
ModelTree.save() writes a versioned UTF-8 JSON file. ModelTree.load() restores the fitted tree, including the state used for inference.

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

expected = model.predict([row])
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / "model.json"
    model.save(path)
    restored = ModelTree.load(path)
    assert restored.predict([row]) == expected

Use model.to_json() and ModelTree.from_json(text) for JSON strings. Use model.to_bytes() and ModelTree.from_bytes(data) when the transport requires bytes. The bytes contain the same JSON encoded in UTF-8. Standard Python pickle uses the same model state.

import pickle

assert ModelTree.from_json(model.to_json()).predict([row]) == expected
assert ModelTree.from_bytes(model.to_bytes()).predict([row]) == expected
assert pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(model)).predict([row]) == expected

Persistence rejects Python callbacks in the model configuration. Keep the package version with each artifact and check predictions before upgrading the serving environment. Use extract_rules() for rule inspection and load pickle data only from trusted sources.

The artifact contains the training rows and targets retained for neighbor adjustments. Apply the same access controls you use for training data.

items.title: Checks before release
items.text:
1. Compare a known in-process prediction with the intended serving path.
  2. Check missing values, unseen categories, invalid types and changed column order.
  3. Check the output scale and confirm the decision threshold uses independent validation data.
  4. Record the model and package versions, data period and evaluation results.
  5. Monitor input missingness, category changes, output distributions and observed outcomes.

The following gaps were reproduced in the current worktree and are tracked for investigation:

  • A short or extra-long row was accepted in one test. Do not assume the model rejects a schema mismatch.
  • An unseen category routed differently from a missing category in a tested tree, despite the stated unseen-as-missing rule.
  • break_down rejected a raw string category in a tested row, although predict accepted it.

Do not present the checks above as complete deployment coverage. See the data guide, evaluation guide, and documentation audit for further work.

items.title: Check split boundaries
items.text: The DOT export in the checked build labels numeric branches as < and >=. In a one-feature reproduction with a threshold of zero, the fitted tree routed zero with lower values. It routed positive values to the other leaf. Use the fitted model to check predictions below, at, and above a threshold before translating a diagram into executable rules.

items.title: Survival trees in Python: FLCHAIN mortality follow-up
items.text: Use baseline measurements to estimate survival at one, three and five years. The event is death. If follow-up ends first, the row is right-censored.
path: Survival trees in Python: FLCHAIN mortality follow-up

items.title: 1. Get the data and define the evaluation
items.text:
The survival package's FLCHAIN cohort contains 7,874 people and right-censored follow-up. futime is follow-up in days and death=1 records a death. We use age, sex, kappa, lambda and creatinine as predictors. We exclude chapter, which describes cause of death and is unavailable at prediction time. Creatinine is missing for 952 of the 5,500 training records and 398 of the 2,374 test records; values enter the tree without imputation.

Download FLCHAIN CSV from Rdatasets to datasets/external/real_eval/flchain.csv. The checked file SHA-256 is a96bcc58addb4c127e5012c5974aec8c7daf66123ddb104f309a78f158daa563. Run the shared real-data evaluation script.

uv run python examples/real_survival_uplift.py survival
path: Survival trees in Python: FLCHAIN mortality follow-up

items.title: 2. Fit leaf survival curves
items.text:
futime is the time to death or last observation. Keep the event flag next to it. For example, someone censored at day 600 survived beyond day 365, but their status at day 1,095 is unknown. Do not replace the censored outcome with an event at day 600.

Run this Python block from the repository root. The evaluation helpers are part of the example script.

from random import Random

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import ModelTree
from examples.real_survival_uplift import brier, censor_km

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/external/real_eval/flchain.csv")
features = ["age", "sex", "kappa", "lambda", "creatinine"]
types = ["numeric", "categorical", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric"]
ids = list(range(len(df)))
Random(2026).shuffle(ids)

def inputs(indices):
    part = df.iloc[indices]
    x = [[None if pd.isna(v) else v for v in row]
         for row in part[features].itertuples(index=False, name=None)]
    return x, part.futime.astype(float).tolist(), part.death.astype(float).tolist()

x_train, t_train, e_train = inputs(ids[:5500])
x_test, t_test, e_test = inputs(ids[5500:])
grid = [365.0, 1095.0, 1825.0]
censor = censor_km(t_train, e_train)

for depth in (0, 2):
    tree = ModelTree(leaf_family="survival", max_depth=depth,
                     min_rows=100, prune="none")
    tree.fit(x_train, (t_train, e_train), col_names=features, dtypes=types)
    curves = tree.predict(x_test, kind="survival", times=grid)
    print("depth", depth, "first survival curve", curves[0])
    for j, horizon in enumerate(grid):
        print(horizon, brier(t_test, e_test, [curve[j] for curve in curves],
                             horizon, censor))
    print(tree.splits()[:1])

The depth-zero tree estimates one Kaplan–Meier curve for everyone. The deeper tree assigns a separate curve to each leaf. Inspect early and late horizons separately because each has a different set of known outcomes.

items.title: 3. Interpret the held-out results
items.text:
Horizon, days Test at risk Censoring survival, training estimate Tree IPCW Brier Global baseline 365 2,270 0.9930 0.0329 0.0343 1,095 2,144 0.9834 0.0671 0.0731 1,825 2,043 0.9737 0.0884 0.1026

The right panel shows two held-out feature rows routed through the training tree. They were selected by their predicted five-year survival, without using their outcomes. Their five-year predictions are 0.321 and 0.948. These are leaf estimates. The left panel measures error across all 2,374 test rows, which include 644 recorded deaths and 1,730 censored observations over the available follow-up.

The example uses a seeded random split and estimates the marginal censoring distribution from training data only. A marginal censoring model assumes censoring is independent of the outcome in the relevant population. This observational cohort and one split do not establish clinical usefulness. Check conditional censoring, calibration, discrimination and uncertainty with the intended deployment population before interpreting the comparison.

items.title: 4. Controlled check with synthetic truth
items.text:
The survival and uplift evaluation script simulates 5,000 people. It fits 3,000 and evaluates 2,000 independent records, including 1,391 observed events and 609 censored observations. A global survival model provides the baseline.

uv run python examples/survival_uplift_evaluation.py
Horizon Tree IPCW Brier Global baseline IPCW Brier 10 0.2417 0.2509 20 0.2000 0.2102 30 0.1226 0.1316

The Brier score compares predicted survival probabilities with event outcomes at a fixed horizon. Inverse probability of censoring weights (IPCW) account for records censored before that horizon. Lower is better. This simulation uses the known censoring distribution. Real data requires a justified censoring model estimated without using the test outcomes for model selection, adequate follow-up, and positive censoring survival at each evaluated horizon. Conditional censoring requires appropriate conditional weights; a single global curve can be wrong.

The script also compares predictions with the known synthetic survival probability. Real individual survival probabilities are not observed. Check discrimination and horizon-specific calibration on real held-out data, with uncertainty and risk-set sizes. This example implements the evaluation calculation locally; it does not claim an IPCW metric API exists in the package. See Graf et al. (1999).
path: Survival trees in Python: FLCHAIN mortality follow-up

items.title: 5. Competing risks and multi-cause endpoints
items.text:
When subjects can experience mutually exclusive event causes (e.g. disease relapse vs treatment-related mortality), treating competing events as ordinary censoring violates the independent censoring assumption and overestimates cumulative incidence by 20–50%.

mltreelib implements native competing risks trees: - Split Criterion: Gray's subdistribution log-rank test (gain="gray", target_cause=j) maintaining subjects who experienced competing events in the risk set. - Leaf Estimators: Aalen-Johansen multi-state estimator guaranteeing the probability simplex identity: \(\sum_{c=1}^J \hat{F}_c(t) + \hat{S}(t) = 1.0\). - Unified Prediction API: tree.predict(X, kind="cif", times=times, cause=1) and tree.predict(X, kind="risk"). - Validation: Metrics().competing_risks(...) computing cause-specific Harrell's C, Uno's IPCW C-index, and time-dependent Brier score matrices.

from mltreelib import ModelTree, Metrics

# Events: 0 = censored, 1 = relapse (primary), 2 = toxicity (competing)
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=25, gain="gray", target_cause=1)
tree.fit(X_train, (durations_train, events_train))

# Evaluate Aalen-Johansen CIF at specified horizons
times = [2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0]
cif_cause1 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=times, cause=1)
cif_cause2 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=times, cause=2)
surv = tree.predict(X_test, kind="survival", times=times)

# Compute full IPCW competing risks performance report
metrics = Metrics()
report = metrics.competing_risks(
    durations=durations_test,
    events=events_test,
    cif_curves={1: cif_cause1, 2: cif_cause2},
    times=times,
)
print("Cause 1 Harrell C:", report["cause_c_indices"][1])
print("Cause 1 Uno IPCW C:", report["cause_uno_c_indices"][1])
print("Cause 1 IBS:", report["cause_ibs"][1])

items.title: Uplift modeling in Python: the Hillstrom email experiment
items.text: Decide whether to send a campaign email to everyone, a subset, or nobody. Compare incremental visits on a randomized holdout.
path: Uplift modeling in Python: the Hillstrom email experiment

items.title: 1. Get the data and define the evaluation
items.text:
The Hillstrom email experiment randomly assigned 64,000 customers to a men's email, women's email or no email. This example compares women's email versus no email, using a website visit within two weeks as the outcome. It excludes the men's arm and uses only pre-treatment features. A visit is not a purchase or profit.

The publisher's original download endpoint failed HTTPS certificate validation in our environment. We used this public mirror, SHA-256 0e5893329d8b93cefecc571777672028290ab69865718020c78c7284f291aece. The mirror matches published row and arm counts; independent byte equivalence with the original is not established. Save the CSV as datasets/external/real_eval/hillstrom.csv. It is excluded from Git.

uv run python examples/real_survival_uplift.py uplift
path: Uplift modeling in Python: the Hillstrom email experiment

items.title: 2. Fit a causal tree and choose an email policy
items.text:
Use treatment as part of the target. The columns below describe customers before the campaign. Use validation to choose a threshold. Keep the randomized test outcomes sealed until after the policy is fixed.

flowchart TD
    subgraph HonestSplit["Honest Causal Partitioning (Athey & Imbens 2016)"]
        direction TB
        Sample["Randomized Trial Data (Y, W, X)"] --> Partition{"Random Subsample Split"}

        Partition -->|"Estimation Sample S_est"| LeafEstimator["Leaf CATE Estimation\ntau_hat = E[Y | W=1] - E[Y | W=0]"]
        TreeStructure --> FixedNodes["Fixed Partition Topology"]
        FixedNodes & LeafEstimator --> UnbiasedModel["Unbiased Honest Causal Tree"]
    end

    classDef dataBox fill:#1e293b,stroke:#475569,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef gateBox fill:#b45309,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef treeBox fill:#4338ca,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef leafBox fill:#065f46,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;
    classDef causalBox fill:#0f766e,stroke:#14b8a6,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff;

Run this Python block from the repository root. group_value comes from the example script.

from random import Random

import pandas as pd
from mltreelib import ModelTree
from examples.real_survival_uplift import group_value

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/external/real_eval/hillstrom.csv")
df = df[df.segment.isin(["Womens E-Mail", "No E-Mail"])]
features = ["recency", "history", "mens", "womens", "newbie", "zip_code", "channel"]
types = ["numeric"] * 5 + ["categorical"] * 2
ids = list(range(len(df)))
Random(2026).shuffle(ids)
a, b = int(.6 * len(ids)), int(.8 * len(ids))

def inputs(indices):
    part = df.iloc[indices]
    x = [[None if pd.isna(v) else v for v in row]
         for row in part[features].itertuples(index=False, name=None)]
    return x, part.visit.tolist(), (part.segment == "Womens E-Mail").astype(int).tolist()

x_train, y_train, w_train = inputs(ids[:a])
x_val, y_val, w_val = inputs(ids[a:b])
x_test, y_test, w_test = inputs(ids[b:])
tree = ModelTree(gain="causal", leaf="mean", max_depth=2, min_rows=250,
                 prune="none", honesty=True, seed=42)
tree.fit(x_train, (y_train, w_train), col_names=features, dtypes=types)

val_scores = tree.predict(x_val, kind="uplift")
def value_at(threshold):
    return group_value(y_val, w_val, [score > threshold for score in val_scores])[0]

threshold = max([min(val_scores) - 1, *sorted(set(val_scores))], key=value_at)
test_scores = tree.predict(x_test, kind="uplift")
for selected in ([score > threshold for score in test_scores],
                 [True] * len(y_test), [False] * len(y_test)):
    print(group_value(y_test, w_test, selected))

The helper estimates the visit-rate difference between treatment and control among selected customers. It multiplies that difference by the selected fraction. The result measures incremental visits per eligible customer. Check arm support in each candidate group. If the treatment has a cost, use net value in threshold selection and reporting.
path: Uplift modeling in Python: the Hillstrom email experiment

items.title: 3. Interpret the held-out results
items.text:
The seeded split contains 25,615 training, 8,539 validation and 8,539 test rows. An honest causal tree ranks customers. Validation selects the policy threshold, and the randomized test set estimates incremental visits. This example assumes zero treatment cost because campaign costs are not in the data.

Test policy Selected Treated / control Incremental visits per eligible customer Approximate 95% interval Validation-selected policy 8,539 4,270 / 4,269 0.04517 0.03108 to 0.05927 Treat all 8,539 4,270 / 4,269 0.04517 0.03108 to 0.05927 Treat none 0 — 0 —

The chosen policy treats everyone. This run therefore supplies no evidence that targeting improves on treat-all. The interval is a normal approximation conditional on the selected population and excludes model-selection uncertainty. The data is from a historical campaign; repeat evaluation in a new experiment, include costs and use the outcome the business actually values before applying a policy.
path: Uplift modeling in Python: the Hillstrom email experiment

items.title: 4. Controlled check with synthetic truth
items.text:
The survival and uplift evaluation script simulates a randomized trial. It uses 3,000 training, 1,000 validation and 2,000 independent test observations. It selects a threshold on validation data and evaluates the fixed policy on test data. The example assigns a treatment cost of 0.5 outcome units per treated person.

uv run python examples/survival_uplift_evaluation.py
Test policy Selected Treated / control among selected Estimated net outcome per person Selected policy 967 471 / 496 0.7072 Treat all 2,000 972 / 1,028 -0.0478 Treat none 0 0 / 0 0

Within the selected subgroup, the script compares observed treated and control outcomes. It subtracts the cost and multiplies by the selected fraction to report value per person in the whole test population. The selected policy's approximate 95% interval is [0.6438, 0.7706]. It uses a normal approximation conditional on the selected fraction; it does not include model-selection uncertainty. Randomized assignment and independent test data support this comparison. Check arm counts and use a suitable uncertainty method for the actual design.

Synthetic truth is available here: the selected policy's true net value is 0.7252 per person and PEHE is 0.2347. Real records do not reveal both potential outcomes, so individual-effect error and PEHE cannot be calculated directly from ordinary real-world outcomes. These calculations are example code, not a claim that the package already exposes uplift evaluation metrics.

items.title: Visualize data, model behavior and decisions
items.text:
Use charts to answer a question at each step. The plots below come from the same reproducible data and metrics example. It uses synthetic mixed data, raw category labels and missing numeric inputs.

Question View How to use it Where are inputs missing? Missingness counts Compare fields, sources and time periods before deciding on data-quality work. Where are numeric predictions wrong? Residuals Look for patterns and large errors on held-out observations. How does a ranking trade precision for recall? Precision–recall Compare operating points with the event rate and review capacity. Do predicted probabilities match outcomes? Calibration Compare predicted and observed rates, with bin counts and sample size. What happens at the chosen threshold? Confusion matrix Read actual classes by row and predicted classes by column. How does the fitted tree partition data? Tree diagram and split importance Review conditions, names, support and missing routing.
path: Visualize data, model behavior and decisions

items.title: Reproduce the charts
items.text:
uv run python examples/data_metrics_pathway.py

The script needs matplotlib and writes SVG files to docs/assets/guides/. It uses the existing mltreelib.plots functions for model diagnostics. Install the project plotting extra for those dependencies. To render the DOT tree, install the Graphviz dot executable. The numerical metrics and tree DOT representation do not require Graphviz.
path: Visualize data, model behavior and decisions

items.title: Use the plotting API
items.text:
This complete example plots a small held-out regression result. The plotting layer is optional; Metrics returns numeric reports without matplotlib.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mltreelib import Metrics, plots

actual = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
predicted = [1.2, 1.8, 3.4, 3.7]
print("MAE:", Metrics().regression(actual, predicted)["mae"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plots.plot_residuals(actual, predicted, ax=ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.close(fig)
path: Visualize data, model behavior and decisions

items.title: Read a tree and explain one row
items.text:
model.to_dot() returns DOT text. Supply that text to Graphviz to render a diagram. model.splits() and model.leaves() expose structured information, while model.break_down(row) supports a path-based explanation for numeric rows. A test with raw string categories raised TypeError even though prediction accepted those rows. Mixed-category explanations are a product gap to investigate. Use tree inspection for examples. Verify category labels and missing routing before presenting a rule as actionable. A path explains a prediction; it does not by itself establish a causal intervention.

Split importance summarizes gain in a particular fitted tree. It is not a causal effect. Compare it with held-out errors and domain knowledge.

items.title: Evaluate a classification decision
items.text: The evaluation pathway explains the validation threshold, baseline and synthetic results. The catalog below covers the remaining plot functions.
path: Visualize data, model behavior and decisions

items.title: Complete plot catalog
items.text:
The public mltreelib.plots module exposes the functions below. y_true is the observed outcome. scores are model scores for the positive class. Classification plots expect aligned binary outcomes and scores. Use held-out data for assessment. The linked images come from the earlier metrics showcase and are illustrative; run the showcase to regenerate them.

Question Function View How does ranking separate positives and negatives? plot_roc(y_true, scores) ROC What precision accompanies each recall? plot_pr(y_true, scores) Precision–recall How many events do the top-scored cases capture? plot_cumulative_gain(y_true, scores) Cumulative gain How much better is targeting than the base event rate? plot_lift(y_true, scores) Lift Where is class separation largest? plot_ks(y_true, scores) KS How do outcome rates and capture vary by score band? plot_decile(y_true, scores, n_buckets=10) Decile profile Do predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies? plot_calibration(y_true, scores, n_bins=10) Calibration How does observed response vary by score band? plot_response(y_true, scores, n_buckets=10) Response How do two sets of predictions compare? plot_double_lift(y_true, scores_a, scores_b) Double lift How did a score or numeric feature distribution change? plot_psi(reference, current, n_bins=10) PSI What decisions were correct or incorrect? plot_confusion_matrix(confusion, class_names=None) Confusion matrix Where do numeric predictions miss? plot_residuals(y_true, y_pred) Residuals Which features contributed split gain? plot_importance(model.feature_importance()) Importance How does one prediction decompose along its path? plot_breakdown(model.break_down(row)) Break-down What signal components did the generator realize? plot_variance_shares(shares) Variance shares How does a series decompose? plot_decomposition(values, trend, detrended, deseason, residual, dates=None, axes=None) Decomposition

A calibration plot is a diagnostic. It does not fit a probability calibrator or change model predictions. Fitted post-hoc calibration is on the roadmap.

The chart functions accept an optional Matplotlib ax; plot_decomposition uses axes for its panels. When using your own axes, use the axes you supplied rather than relying on a return value. See examples/metrics_showcase.py for calls and chart generation. The evaluation pathway explains how to choose a threshold and interpret held-out results.

When exporting a decision as a rule, check split boundaries using the fitted model. The current DOT labels differ from prediction at an exact numeric split threshold in the checked example.

items.title: API reference — Data
items.text: The data & feature layer: everything that turns raw columns into numeric matrices. All names come from import mltreelib.

items.title: Dataset helpers
items.text:
• list_datasets() — the bundled benchmark sets (see DataSets).
  • load_dataset(name) — load one as a frame.
  • summarize(df) — per-column summary including n_missing by default.

items.title: Winnowing (column screening)
items.text: • winnow(x, y, min_relevance=0.05) → {"kept": [column indices], "relevance": [score per column]} — screen columns by univariate relevance against the target before training (the cheap pre-split screening LightGBM calls feature pre-filtering). The same screen runs inside ModelTree.fit when min_relevance is set.

items.title: Categorical encoders
items.text:
Encoder fit and transform signatures differ. Target-based encoders also need training targets. Missing and unseen-level behavior depends on the encoder. See the individual API and test the behavior required by your workflow.

encoder shape OneHotEncoder levels(), transform → {level: [0/1 column]} (missing → all-zero row) HashingEncoder(n_buckets) fixed-width hashing TargetEncoder(smoothing) smoothed target mean; prior() CatBoostEncoder(prior, permutations, seed) ordered target statistics WoEEncoder(prior) weight of evidence JamesSteinEncoder shrinkage estimator CountEncoder frequency encoding LeaveOneOutEncoder leave-one-out target mean MEstimatorEncoder(smoothing) m-estimate smoothing BaseNEncoder base-N numeric code SumEncoder sum (effect) coding QuantileEncoder quantile target statistics TfidfEncoder tf-idf over categories EmbeddingEncoder(dim, lr, epochs, seed, task) learned embeddings (Rust core)

items.title: Scalers & builders
items.text:
• VariableScaler(normalize) — per-column numeric scaling with invertible inverse_transform.
  • GroupedScaler — grouped/trended/windowed transforms; module functions grouped_transform, trended_transform, windowed_transform, lag_by_days, decomposed_transform, calendar_features.
  • DatasetBuilder — add_numeric(name, values) / add_categorical(name, values) / build() → schema summary.
  • IndexMapper — string ↔ code mapping: fit, transform, inverse_transform, get_index, get_name, get_all_names.

items.title: Missing-value semantics
items.text: None and NaN = missing (NaN normalized at ingestion). Missing in → missing out; imputation is opt-in; unseen categorical levels map to missing; degenerate scalings produce missing, not inf. Time-series transforms drop incomplete rows and warn with the count.

items.title: Generator
items.text:
generate(...) — the adjustable benchmark generator with known ground truth (group/hierarchy signal knobs). See docs/field-notes.md for the research context.

Next: Model for the tree itself, or Metrics for evaluation.

items.title: Class reference
items.text:
Full docstrings and every method: the full generated API.

DatasetBuilder(n_category=None, na_policy='allow', digits=None, add_intercept=False) — ingest any raw columns into the typed dataset. add_categorical(name, values), add_numeric(name, values), build() → {"columns", "dtypes", "na_counts", "n_rows", "n_cols"}.

Encoders — signatures, output shapes and handling of missing or unseen levels vary. Consult the individual API before constructing a pipeline.

VariableScaler(normalize) / GroupedScaler — fit / transform / inverse_transform (invertible by construction).

IndexMapper — fit, transform, inverse_transform, get_index, get_name, get_all_names.

items.title: A real example (churn)
items.text:
from mltreelib import DatasetBuilder, OneHotEncoder, load_dataset

d = load_dataset("churn")            # the typed dataset dict
cols = d["columns"]
print(f"churn: {d['n_rows']} rows x {d['n_cols']} cols; "
      f"na_counts (state) = {d['na_counts']['state']}")

b = DatasetBuilder(n_category=5, na_policy="impute")
b.add_categorical("state", [str(v) for v in cols["state"]])
b.add_numeric("account_length", [float(v) for v in cols["account_length"]])
b.add_numeric("total_day_charge", [float(v) for v in cols["total_day_charge"]])
d2 = b.build()
print(f"build(): {d2['n_rows']} rows x {d2['n_cols']} cols; "
      f"dtypes={d2['dtypes']}; na_counts={d2['na_counts']}")

enc = OneHotEncoder()
enc.fit([str(v) for v in cols["state"]])
X = enc.transform([str(v) for v in cols["state"]])
print(f"OneHotEncoder on state: fit -> {len(enc.levels())} levels; "
      f"transform -> dict of {len(X)} columns x {len(next(iter(X.values())))} rows")

churn: 5000 rows x 20 cols; na_counts (state) = 0
build(): 5000 rows x 3 cols; dtypes={'state': 'categorical',
  'account_length': 'numeric', 'total_day_charge': 'numeric'};
  na_counts={'state': 0, 'account_length': 0, 'total_day_charge': 0}
OneHotEncoder on state: fit -> 51 levels; transform -> dict of 51 columns
  x 5000 rows

load_dataset returns the built typed dataset (name, columns, dtypes, na_counts, n_rows, n_cols) — the same schema DatasetBuilder.build() produces, which is why the two interoperate.

items.title: API reference — Metrics
items.text:
Metrics — evaluation reports, curves, scorecards, stability and distances. Everything returns plain structures (numeric series + summary scalars); the library never plots — rendering lives in mltreelib.plots (matplotlib as an optional extra) and the Visualization guide. Charts on these docs are click-to-zoom.

Unless noted, classification inputs take scores/probabilities with positive class y > 0.5; ties sweep together in stable order.

items.title: Reports
items.text:
• Metrics().regression(y_true, y_pred) → n, n_missing, mean_error, bias, mae, mad, mape, rmse, r2, max_error, explained_variance, plus a deciles table (decile, n, mean_error, mae, mape) — calibration by tentile, not just accuracy. Missing-aware.
  • Metrics().classification(y_true, y_pred) — integer class labels — n, n_missing, n_classes, accuracy, macro_precision/recall/f1, per_class, confusion matrix.
  • Metrics().regression_by_group(keys, y_true, y_pred) — regression report per group key.

items.title: Ranking & calibration curves
items.text: call returns roc_curve(y, scores) {"points": [[fpr, tpr], ...], "auc"} — trapezoid over the empirical curve pr_curve(y, scores) {"points": [[recall, precision], ...], "average_precision"} — step-wise AP (sklearn convention) gain_curve(y, scores) {"points": [[population_fraction, capture_rate], ...]} lift_curve(y, scores) {"points": [[population_fraction, lift], ...]} — lift = capture / fraction ks_statistic(y, scores) {"points": [[fpr, tpr, score], ...], "ks", "score_at_ks", "tpr_at_ks", "fpr_at_ks"} decile_table(y, scores, n_buckets=10) [{"decile", "n", "avg_score", "events", "event_rate", "cum_capture", "cum_event_rate", "lift"}] — decile 1 = top scores (kds/PerfScoreCard profile; response + cumulative response at decile granularity) calibration(y, scores, n_bins=10) {"bins": [{"left", "right", "mean_score", "observed", "n"}]} — equal-width over [0, 1], edge-clipped, empty bins omitted

items.title: Probability & margin scores
items.text:
• log_loss(y, probs) — mean log loss (probabilities clip to (1e-15, 1−1e-15)).
  • brier_score(y, probs) — mean squared probability error.
  • hinge_loss(y, decision) — mean hinge over signed margins (labels map to ±1).

items.title: Classification scorecard
items.text:
Metrics().classification_scores(y_true, y_pred) — single-label binary or multiclass, labels = sorted distinct union of truth and predictions:

n, n_classes, accuracy, balanced_accuracy, precision/recall/f1 × (macro|micro|weighted), mcc (Gorodkin multiclass Matthews), jaccard × (macro|micro|weighted), hamming_loss, zero_one_loss.

items.title: Multilabel scorecard
items.text:
Metrics().multilabel_scores(y_true, y_scores) — rows are instances, columns labels, entries > 0.5 positive; the raw entries double as ranking scores:

subset_accuracy, hamming_loss, precision/recall/f1 × (micro|macro|samples), label_ranking_ap, coverage_error. Rows with no true labels are skipped in the samples averages and ranking metrics.

items.title: Agreement
items.text: Metrics().weighted_kappa(y_true, y_pred, weights="quadratic"|"linear"|"none") — Cohen's kappa over the sorted distinct labels; 1 = perfect agreement (PerfScoreCard's weighted kappas).

items.title: Stability (scorecard monitoring)
items.text: Metrics().stability_index(reference, current, n_bins=10) → {"psi": float, "bins": [{"left", "right", "reference_share", "current_share", "contribution"}]} — the Population Stability Index (equal-width bins over the reference range, zero shares floored at 1e-6). CSI is the same call on a feature column instead of scores.

items.title: Model comparison
items.text: Metrics().double_lift(y_true, scores_a, scores_b, n_buckets=10) → [{"bucket", "n", "actual", "pred_a", "pred_b"}] — equal-count buckets by model A's ranking (CAS monograph double-lift chart; the additive vs ratio display is a plotting concern — plots.plot_double_lift(model_type=...)).

items.title: Distances
items.text: Metrics().pairwise_distances(a, b, metric="euclidean", p=2.0) → len(a) × len(b) matrix. Metrics: euclidean, manhattan, chebyshev, minkowski (power p), cosine, correlation, hamming, jaccard (binary presence). Zero-variance rows → correlation distance 1.0; zero vectors → cosine distance 1.0; both-empty → jaccard 0.0.

items.title: Plotting (mltreelib.plots)
items.text:
Optional layer, installed with pip install mltreelib[plotting] (matplotlib + pygraphviz + seaborn; each function takes ax=None, returns Axes): plot_roc, plot_pr, plot_cumulative_gain, plot_lift, plot_ks, plot_decile, plot_calibration, plot_response, plot_double_lift, plot_psi.

from mltreelib import Metrics, plots
r = Metrics().roc_curve(y_test, scores)
plots.plot_ks(y_test, scores)          # click the figure in these docs to zoom

Time-series metrics (MAPE/SMAPE variants, MASE, pinball for quantiles, Tweedie/Poisson deviance with the GLM leaves) are parked with their feature work.

Next: Data or Model.

items.title: The Metrics class
items.text:
Metrics() — no constructor args; every method is a complete report. Missing pairs are dropped and counted in n_missing. Full docstrings: the full generated API.

family methods reports classification(y_true, y_pred, probabilities=None), classification_scores(y_true, scores), regression(y_true, y_pred), classification_by_group(keys, ...), regression_by_group(keys, y_true, y_pred) curves roc_curve, pr_curve, gain_curve, lift_curve, decile_table, calibration probability & margin log_loss, brier_score, hinge_loss scorecards ks_statistic, weighted_kappa(y_true, y_pred, rev, power) multilabel multilabel_scores(y_true, y_pred) distances pairwise_distances(a, b, metric, p=2) stability stability_index(reference, current, n_bins=10) model comparison double_lift(y_true, a, b, model_type)

items.title: A real example (churn)
items.text:
from mltreelib import Metrics, load_dataset

cols = load_dataset("churn")["columns"]
y = [1 if str(v) == "Yes" else 0 for v in cols["CustomerChurned"]]
print(f"churn: 5000 rows; event rate {sum(y)/len(y):.3f} ({sum(y)} churned)")
scores = [float(v) for v in cols["total_day_charge"]]   # a (silly) risk score
med = sorted(scores)[len(scores) // 2]
pred = [1 if s >= med else 0 for s in scores]

rep = Metrics().classification(y, pred,
                               probabilities=[min(1.0, s / 80.0) for s in scores])
print(f"classification: accuracy={rep['accuracy']:.3f} "
      f"macro_f1={rep['macro_f1']:.3f} auc={rep['auc']:.3f} "
      f"logloss={rep['logloss']:.3f} brier={rep['brier']:.3f}")
mins = [float(v) for v in cols["total_day_minutes"]]
fit = [s / 0.17 for s in scores]                        # charge = 0.17 * minutes
rr = Metrics().regression(mins, fit)
print(f"regression: n={rr['n']} rmse={rr['rmse']:.2f} mae={rr['mae']:.2f} "
      f"r2={rr['r2']:.3f} mape={rr['mape']:.2f}")
gr = Metrics().regression_by_group([str(v) for v in cols["state"]], mins, fit)
print(f"regression_by_group: {len(gr)} groups (keyed by group)")

churn: 5000 rows; event rate 0.141 (707 churned)
classification: accuracy=0.531 macro_f1=0.462 auc=0.640 logloss=0.545 brier=0.176
regression: n=5000 rmse=0.02 mae=0.01 r2=1.000 mape=0.01
regression_by_group: 51 groups (keyed by group)

The classification report carries accuracy, macro_precision/recall/f1, per_class, confusion and (with probabilities) auc, logloss, brier. The regression report carries n, n_missing, mean_error, bias, mae, mad, mape, rmse, r2, max_error, explained_variance and the deciles error profile; the grouped version returns one such report per group (dict keyed by group). Full output shapes on real data: the Metrics & plots showcase.

items.title: API reference — Model
items.text:
ModelTree finds partitions using the selected split criterion and fits a local model in each leaf. It supports raw categorical values and routes missing predictors through the fitted tree.

Scikit-Learn Compatibility

ModelTree provides familiar fit, predict, and predict_proba methods following standard Python estimator conventions. However, it is not fully scikit-learn compatible: it does not inherit from sklearn.base.BaseEstimator, does not implement get_params, set_params, or score, and does not pass sklearn.base.clone or sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.check_estimator.

items.title: Constructor
items.text: See the generated API reference for the constructor signature and the parameter reference for available settings.

items.title: Configure growth and leaves
items.text:
Use GrowthControl for partitioning, stopping, and pruning. Use LeafControl for the models fitted inside those partitions.

from mltreelib import GrowthControl, LeafControl, ModelTree

model = ModelTree(
    growth_control=GrowthControl(max_depth=4, min_rows=8),
    leaf_control=LeafControl(leaf="linear", solver="lbfgs", l2=0.01),
)

from_config = ModelTree(
    growth_control={"max_depth": 4, "min_rows": 8},
    leaf_control={"leaf": "linear", "solver": "lbfgs", "l2": 0.01},
)

from_flat = ModelTree(max_depth=4, min_rows=8, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="lbfgs", l2=0.01)

These calls show three ways to supply explicit settings. Dictionaries inherit the defaults of ModelTree for omitted keys. A typed LeafControl uses its own defaults. Existing flat keywords and the control= alias for leaf_control= are supported. Use solver inside a leaf control and leaf_solver in flat calls. Supply each setting once.

The leaf model and family determine which solvers can fit it. The built-in linear and GLM paths offer the choices listed in the parameter reference. Specialized leaves can use their own fitting methods. See persist a fitted model for JSON, file, byte, and pickle examples.

The gain family is sample-weight aware end to end: weighted class masses for entropy/gini/gain_ratio/twoing, weighted moments for sdr/SSE, fitted deviance for binomial/Poisson, and a custom gain_fn(left, right) receives lazy (y, w) pair slices of the two sides (higher = better). gain="deviance" scores the fitted leaf-family likelihood and is recommended for binomial and Poisson leaves.

Defaults are the arena bake-off winner (see Benchmarks) — linear leaves at shallow depth with a small ridge (l2) penalty. l1 (lasso/elastic) is available but off by default: coordinate descent is slow inside the split scan and the accuracy gain over ridge is marginal. Turning regularization fully off (l1=l2=0) on raw scales is a known blowup mode — keep the ridge unless you standardize your inputs.

items.title: Split search — per dtype, raw data in
items.text:
Categorical columns are levels as-is (dtypes declares "categorical"; string values and numeric level codes enter directly — identity, never order), NAs route as-is. Raw strings are ingested directly: the tree builds an internal identity dictionary on the fly without requiring an external encoder. Binary level partitions (cat_search) are built along cat_order ("frequency_desc", "target_mean", or custom); multiway partitions are reserved for a later build. gain picks the split-quality function: built-ins scan on summary stats or deviance; a custom gain_fn(left_y, right_y) -> float receives lazy y-slices per candidate. Numeric columns scan candidates on the split_precision grid (thresholds are grid values; prediction compares raw values), None restores the exact unique-value scan.

# Raw strings ingested directly in categorical columns:
m = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=2, cat_order="target_mean")
m.fit([["paris", 1.0], ["tokyo", 2.0], ["paris", 3.0], ["london", 4.0]],
      [10.0, 20.0, 15.0, 30.0], dtypes=["categorical", "numeric"])
m.predict([["paris", 1.5], ["london", 3.5]])

items.title: Significance gates & Honesty
items.text:
• split_test="chow": A Chow structural break F-test gates node splitting. The candidate split must demonstrate statistically significant parameter heterogeneity over the pooled node model at split_alpha (e.g. 0.05), optionally adjusted with bonferroni=True across evaluated split candidates.
  • honesty=True: GRF-style sample splitting partition. honesty_fraction (default 0.5) of rows select tree structure and splits; the held-out estimation rows fit leaf parameters, yielding unbiased honest predictions.

items.title: Distributional leaves — binomial & Poisson
items.text:
leaf_family switches the leaf distribution and link function: - "gaussian" (default): Identity link, least squares regression. - "binomial": Logit link for 0/1 binary targets. Coefficients are on the log-odds scale; predict and predict_proba return response probabilities P(Y=1). - "poisson": Log link for nonnegative counts or rates. Coefficients are on the log-rate scale; predict returns expected counts.

Pair with gain="deviance" so split search maximizes deviance reduction under the family.

items.title: Fitting & predicting
items.text: method returns notes fit(x, y, w=None, dtypes=None, ...) self rows of float/str/None (None = missing); w / sample_weight / row_weights = row weights; col_weights = column split priority; dtypes = per column "numeric"/"categorical" predict(x, kind="response") list[float] or list[dict] kind="response" (default), kind="prob", kind="odds", kind="log_odds", kind="median", or kind="stats" (full 0D stats dict per row) predict_proba(x) list[float] or matrix response probability P(Y=1) for binomial/probit, or (N, C) probability matrix for softmax cdf(x, value) list[float] conditional fitted-distribution CDF P(Y <= value) for binomial/Poisson quantile(x, tau) list[float] empirical conditional τ-quantile from leaf t-digests (leaf_digest=True)

items.title: Reading the model & 0D Leaf Formulations
items.text: method returns notes __repr__() str rpart-style text (print(model)); refuses to print an unfitted tree to_dot() str Graphviz DOT — render with pygraphviz/graphviz (layout is graphviz's job) splits() list[dict] {col, threshold, missing_left, gain} per split (col is the column name) leaves() list[dict] one flat dict per leaf: cols, coef, na_coef, intercept, n, mean, std, var, median, mad, iqr, min, max, skew, kurtosis, prob, odds, log_odds, majority_class, entropy, gini, zero_fraction, dispersion, stats, quantiles leaf_stats() list[dict] list of 0D stats dictionaries across all leaves: {mean, std, var, median, mad, iqr, min, max, skew, kurtosis, prob, odds, log_odds, majority_class, entropy, gini, zero_fraction, dispersion} split_paths() list[list[str]] split column names per root→leaf path (constraint verification) n_leaves() int terminal node count profile() list[dict] per-depth fit diagnostics: depth, nodes, rows, cols, candidates, group_ns, scan_ns, leaf_ns

items.title: Constraints & Weights
items.text:
• Dual Monotonicity:
  • tree_monotone: Enforces directional ordering on split child target means across tree splits: \((\bar{y}_L - \bar{y}_R) \cdot m \le 0\).
  • leaf_monotone (or in LeafControl): Enforces sign bounds on local linear leaf slopes (\(\beta_j \ge 0\) for \(+1\), \(\le 0\) for \(-1\)).
  • monotone: Sets both tree and leaf monotonicity simultaneously.
  • Interaction Constraints (interaction_groups):
  • Restricts root-to-leaf paths to features within the same group (LightGBM-style).
  • Supports column names (e.g. [["age", "income"], ["city", "zip"]]) as well as numeric column indices.
  • Weights (Row & Column):
  • Row weights: Pass via w, sample_weight, or row_weights to fit() or retrain().
  • Column weights: col_weights scales candidate split gains (\(gain \times W_j\)) and weights random feature subset sampling during col_sample.

Both are validated against reference implementations in examples/constraints_check.py (R gbm's var.monotone, LightGBM's interaction_constraints).

items.title: Inspection via text output
items.text:
print(model) reproduces rpart's print byte-for-byte: binary-heap node numbering, 2·depth indent, x< t / x>=t labels, format(signif(x,7)) columns, * terminal markers. Node ids in to_dot() match the text print.

Next: Metrics to evaluate, or the examples to see it all run.

items.title: Parameters Reference
items.text:
Comprehensive documentation for all hyperparameters, knobs, and training controls in mltreelib.

Inspired by the parameter architecture of CatBoost and LightGBM, every knob in mltreelib is typed, deterministic, and mapped directly to the underlying mltreelib-core Rust engine.

items.title: Quick Navigation
items.text:
• 1. Core Tree Architecture & Sizing
  • 2. Splitting & Search Space Controls
  • 3. Regularization, Purity Gates & Split Penalties
  • 4. Statistical Hypothesis Stopping & Pre-Selection
  • 5. Categorical Handling & Monotonicity Constraints
  • 6. Pruning, Honesty & Missing Value Routing
  • 7. Leaf Models, GLM Families & Penalized Solvers
  • 8. Growth and Leaf Controls
  • 9. Telemetry & Execution Controls

items.title: 1. Core Tree Architecture & Sizing
items.text:
Controls how deep and wide the tree can grow before termination.

Set the classification class count with GrowthControl(n_classes=...). Existing calls can supply n_classes as a flat constructor keyword, a fit keyword, or a legacy LeafControl setting.

Parameter Type Default Valid Range Description max_depth int 5 [1, 64] Maximum tree depth from root to any leaf. Set to 1 for decision stumps; increase to 8-12 to capture deep multi-way interactions. max_leaf_nodes int \| None None [2, \infty) Maximum number of terminal leaf nodes. If set, growth follows best-first priority queue until leaf limit is reached. min_rows int 50 [1, \infty) Minimum number of samples required to form a terminal leaf (minbucket in R / min_child_samples in LightGBM). Prevents overfitting to tiny sub-populations. minsplit int \| None None [2, \infty) Minimum number of samples required to attempt a split. If None, defaults to 2 * min_rows. minprob float 0.02 (0.0, 0.5) Minimum fraction of training rows required in a terminal node (\(N_{\text{leaf}} / N \ge \text{minprob}\)). Safeguards against isolated slivers. min_gain float 1e-9 [0.0, \infty) Minimum impurity reduction required to justify creating child nodes. Analogous to min_split_gain in LightGBM or gamma in XGBoost.

items.title: 2. Splitting & Search Space Controls
items.text:
Governs candidate generation, feature subsampling, and candidate evaluations.

Parameter Type Default Options Description gain str \| None None "entropy", "gini", "variance" Split evaluation objective. If None, automatically resolves to "entropy" for classification and "variance" for regression. split_eval str "fast" "fast", "exact" Split evaluation engine. "fast" utilizes SIMD vectorization and streaming histogram accumulators; "exact" re-evaluates all continuous thresholds without binning. split_precision int \| None 4 [1, 16] Decimal digit rounding applied to candidate thresholds. Rounds continuous splits (e.g. 3.1416 instead of 3.1415926535) to prevent floating-point overfitting and improve explainability. split_cols list[int] \| list[str] \| None None Feature subset Whitelist of features permitted to form splits. Useful when reserving specific features solely for leaf linear models. col_sample float \| None None (0.0, 1.0] Fraction of features randomly subsampled at each split decision (colsample_bytree in XGBoost / mtry ratio). Injects stochastic decorrelation across ensemble trees. col_weights list[float] \| None None Non-negative weights Prior weights determining the sampling probability of each feature during candidate selection. Higher weights bias search toward key business drivers. interaction_groups list[list[int \| str]] \| None None Feature sets Enforces interaction constraints: features may only appear on the same root-to-leaf path if they belong to a shared interaction group. Prevents disallowed cross-variable leakage. presort bool False True, False Whether to pre-sort continuous features at the root. Reduces per-node sort overhead at the cost of initial fit memory.

items.title: 3. Regularization, Purity Gates & Split Penalties
items.text:
Structural regularization mechanisms designed to suppress noisy split boundaries.

Parameter Type Default Valid Range Description purity_gate float \| None None (0.0, 1.0) Purity stopping criterion. If a node's target standard deviation or Gini impurity falls below this fraction of global variance, node splitting halts early. purity_gate_metric str "sd" "sd", "iqr", "mad" Metric for evaluating node purity: standard deviation ("sd"), interquartile range ("iqr"), or median absolute deviation ("mad"). tail_quantile float \| None None (0.0, 0.25) Extrema protection threshold. Penalizes splits that isolate extreme target quantiles into tiny leaves. imbalance_penalty float 0.0 [0.0, 1.0] Penalizes asymmetric splits where $ alpha float 0.0 [0.0, \infty) Structural complexity penalty subtracted from the candidate split gain (\(G' = G - \alpha\)). Forces simpler tree topologies.

items.title: 4. Statistical Hypothesis Stopping & Pre-Selection
items.text:
Replaces heuristic gain thresholds with formal statistical hypothesis testing (analogous to CHAID and partykit::ctree).

Parameter Type Default Options Description split_test str "none" "none", "f_test", "permutation" Formal statistical test evaluated on prospective splits. Halts recursion when null hypothesis of independence cannot be rejected. split_alpha float 0.05 (0.0, 1.0) Significance level threshold (\(p < \alpha\)) required to accept a split candidate. bonferroni bool False True, False Applies Bonferroni multiplicity correction (\(p < \alpha / P\)) adjusting for the number of tested feature candidates. Eliminates selection bias toward high-cardinality features. preselect str "none" "none", "variance", "correlation" Heuristic screening step executed before split scans to discard uninformative columns. min_relevance float \| None None [0.0, 1.0] Minimum correlation/mutual information required to include a feature in split search.

items.title: 5. Categorical Handling & Monotonicity Constraints
items.text:
Native handling of categorical variables and directional domain knowledge.

Parameter Type Default Options Description cat_order str \| None None "target", "frequency", "natural" Categorical level ordering strategy. "target" orders levels by target mean/rate, converting combinatorial \(2^{K-1}\) subset search into linear \(O(K)\) boundary scans (Fisher's exact theorem). cat_search str "cumulative" "cumulative", "exhaustive" Partition search algorithm across ordered levels. "cumulative" checks consecutive level subsets; "exhaustive" evaluates all partition subsets (small \(K\) only). monotone list[int] \| None None [-1, 0, +1] Monotonicity constraints per feature: +1 forces non-decreasing target response, -1 forces non-increasing, 0 unconstrained. tree_monotone list[int] \| None None [-1, 0, +1] Enforces monotonic split step direction across parent-child tree partitions. leaf_monotone list[int] \| None None [-1, 0, +1] Enforces non-negative/non-positive sign constraints on leaf GLM linear coefficients.

items.title: 6. Pruning, Honesty & Missing Value Routing
items.text:
Controls post-fit pruning, missing value handling, and sample splitting.

Parameter Type Default Options Description prune str "cp" "cp", "cost_complexity", "bic", "aic", "none" Post-pruning algorithm. "cp" matches CART/rpart complexity pruning; "bic" penalizes number of active parameters using Bayesian Information Criterion. cp_alpha float 5.0 [0.0, \infty) Complexity pruning penalty multiplier. Higher values produce shallower, more general trees. honesty bool False True, False Enables honest estimation (Wager & Athey 2018). Tree splits are learned on a training sub-sample, while leaf models are fitted on a held-out estimation sub-sample. Guarantees asymptotic normality. honesty_fraction float 0.5 (0.0, 1.0) Proportion of rows allocated to the split-learning sub-sample when honesty=True. maxsurrogate int 0 [0, 10] Number of surrogate split variables stored per node (CART style). When a primary split feature is missing during prediction, the highest-agreement surrogate variable routes the sample.

items.title: 7. Leaf Models, GLM Families & Penalized Solvers
items.text:
Defines the parametric or non-parametric local model fitted within each terminal leaf.

Parameter Type Default Options Description leaf str "linear" "linear", "mean", "median", "quantile", "huber", "mars", "knn" Mathematical formulation of the leaf model: piecewise linear OLS ("linear"), constant mean ("mean"), median ("median"), Huber robust regression ("huber"), adaptive splines ("mars"), or non-parametric nearest neighbors ("knn"). knn_k int 5 [1, \infty) Number of nearest neighbors queried at leaf inference time. knn_variant str "uniform" "uniform", "distance", "exponential", "dual", "double" Weighting scheme for leaf KNN: "uniform" (unweighted), "distance" (inverse distance \(1/(d+\epsilon)^p\)), "exponential" (\(\exp(-\gamma d)\)), "dual" (distance \(\times\) compactness), or "double" (DW-KNN: distance consistency \(\times\) neighbor reliability \(v_i\)). knn_metric str "euclidean" "euclidean", "manhattan", "chebyshev", "minkowski", "cosine", "correlation", "canberra", "braycurtis", "gower", "mahalanobis" Distance proximity metric across leaf feature coordinates. "gower" normalizes mixed continuous/categorical features and handles missing entries; "mahalanobis" applies diagonal variance scaling. knn_k_validity int 5 [1, \infty) Secondary neighborhood size for precomputing neighbor reliability \(v_i\) (DW-KNN) or local compactness during fit(). knn_gamma float \| None None (0.0, \infty) Exponential spatial decay rate parameter. If None, automatically calibrated by the inverse median neighbor distance within the queried leaf. knn_p float 2.0 (0.0, \infty) Power parameter \(p\) for Minkowski metric or inverse distance weighting (\(1 / (d + \epsilon)^p\)). leaf_family str "gaussian" "gaussian", "binomial", "poisson", "tweedie", "tobit", "softmax" Target distribution family for Generalized Linear Model (GLM) leaves. "gaussian" uses identity link, "binomial" uses logit link, "poisson" uses log link. leaf_solver str "irls" "irls", "lbfgs", "ccd", "cmaes", "shade", "nes", "ga" Local optimization solver for leaf regression models: Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares / exact normal Cholesky ("irls"), Quasi-Newton L-BFGS with Armijo line search ("lbfgs"), Cyclic Coordinate Descent with active set ("ccd"), or SOTA continuous evolutionary algorithms: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy ("cmaes"), Success-History Adaptive Differential Evolution ("shade"), Separable Natural Evolution Strategies ("nes"), or Real-Coded Genetic Algorithm with SBX crossover ("ga"). leaf_cols str "all" "all", "path_used" Feature policy for leaf linear models. "all" fits over all features (with L1/L2 shrinkage); "path_used" restricts the leaf model strictly to features split along that leaf's ancestry path (winnowing). l1 float 0.0 [0.0, \infty) Lasso regularization penalty on leaf linear coefficients. Drives irrelevant leaf weights strictly to zero. l2 float 0.5 [0.0, \infty) Ridge regularization penalty on leaf linear coefficients. Stabilizes collinear inversion matrices in high-dimensional leaves. tau float 0.5 (0.0, 1.0) Quantile level when leaf="quantile". Optimizes asymmetric pinball loss for conditional quantile forecasting. tweedie_p float 1.5 [1.0, 2.0] Power parameter \(p\) for Tweedie exponential dispersion modeling. Ideal for zero-inflated insurance claims (\(1 < p < 2\)). tobit_threshold float 0.0 \(\mathbb{R}\) Censoring threshold \(y_c\) when leaf_family="tobit". Models left-censored Gaussian variables via expectation-maximization. leaf_digest bool True True, False Maintains streaming \(t\)-digests in leaves. Enables fast empirical prediction intervals (predict_interval(coverage=0.9)) without distributional assumptions. mars_degree int 1 [1, 3] Maximum interaction degree for MARS spline hinge functions within leaves. mars_terms int 10 [2, 50] Maximum number of basis terms retained in leaf spline models. mars_penalty float 2.0 [0.0, 10.0] Generalized cross-validation (GCV) penalty per knot for MARS leaf models.

items.title: 8. Growth and Leaf Controls
items.text:
Use the growth settings in sections 1–6 to configure the partition. Use the leaf settings in section 7 to configure the model fitted in each region. Under constraints, tree_monotone governs splits and leaf_monotone governs leaf coefficients. Supply data, feature names, types, and row weights to fit.

Parameter Type Default Description growth_control GrowthControl \| dict \| None None Groups split search, stopping, feature sampling, honesty, and pruning settings. leaf_control / control LeafControl \| dict \| None None Groups the leaf form, family, solver, penalties, and other leaf settings. train_groups bool True Whether to preserve grouped hierarchical entities during leaf retraining. train_ids bool False Whether to index training entity row keys in leaf sample caches (leaf_samples()).

For solver selection inside a leaf control, use solver="lbfgs" or another compatible solver. Flat callers can continue to use leaf_solver. Some leaf models use a dedicated fitting method. See the model reference for typed, dictionary, and flat examples.

Leaf model Compatible explicit solver choices Gaussian linear irls, lbfgs, ccd, shade, cmaes, ga, nes Linear binomial, probit, Poisson, Gamma, Tweedie, or Tobit irls, lbfgs Leaves with a dedicated estimator Use the estimator selected by the leaf form and family.

Use L-BFGS with zero L1 penalty and no monotone leaf constraints. It supports ridge penalties. Specialized estimators reject explicit solver selections.

items.title: 9. Telemetry & Execution Controls
items.text: Parameter Type Default Options Description verbose int 0 0, 1, 2, 3 Training verbosity. 0 = silent; 1 = live depth progress, per-depth summaries, and fit complete summary; 2 = stream per-node split candidates, winning features, threshold, gain, and leaf reasons; 3 = stream leaf solver optimization (GLM convergence iterations, deviance step, linear fit stats). seed int 42 int Deterministic random seed controlling feature subsampling (col_sample) and honest partition splits.

items.title: API reference — Evaluation reports
items.text: What Metrics returns, field by field — the contract every learner is scored under. Reports are plain dicts; missing pairs are dropped from the math and counted in n_missing, never hidden.

items.title: Metrics().regression(y_true, y_pred) → dict
items.text: field meaning n, n_missing observed pairs; dropped missing pairs mean_error mean(actual − fitted) — signed bias mean_pred / mean_true (1.0 = unbiased) mae, mad mean / median absolute deviation mape absolute % error, non-zero targets only rmse, r2, max_error the usual explained_variance 1 − Var(error)/Var(y) deciles per-target-decile error profile — the DAR "bathtub" view

items.title: Metrics().classification(y_true, y_pred, probabilities=None) → dict
items.text: field meaning n, n_missing, n_classes observed pairs; classes seen accuracy overall accuracy macro_precision/recall/f1 unweighted mean over classes per_class precision/recall/f1/support per class confusion counts matrix auc, logloss, brier only with probabilities (P(class 1))

items.title: Grouped reports
items.text:
classification_by_group(keys, ...) / regression_by_group(keys, y_true, y_pred) return one report per group, as a dict keyed by the group label — the format ModelTree's group API consumes.

Real values for every field on real data: the Metrics & plots showcase and the Metrics page example.

items.text:
Every class and function with its exact signature and docstring — regenerated from the built module, so this never drifts from the code. Narrative guides with verified examples: Data · Model · Metrics · Reports · Visualization.

Scikit-Learn Compatibility

Classes in mltreelib (such as ModelTree) implement standard fit, predict, and predict_proba method signatures, but do not inherit from sklearn.base.BaseEstimator and are not fully scikit-learn compatible (clone and check_estimator are not supported).

items.title: API reference — Anomaly & density trees
items.text: Unified anomaly detection: AnomalyModel (tree-based and PCA/NMF reconstruction errors), density estimation, streaming mass scoring, CoDisp, and contextual surprise.

items.title: AnomalyModel
items.text:
class AnomalyModel(kind: 'str' = 'eif', max_depth: 'int | None' = None, min_rows: 'int' = 10, contamination: 'float' = 0.05, seed: 'int' = 42, *, extension_level: 'int | None' = None, subsample_size: 'int | None' = None, min_samples_split: 'int | None' = None, alpha: 'float' = 0.0, min_density_gain: 'float' = 0.0, window_size: 'int' = 250, initial_mass: 'float' = 0.0, sample_size: 'int' = 256, eta: 'float' = 0.1, prior_weight: 'float' = 1.0, alphabet_size: 'int' = 256, smoothing_discount: 'float' = 0.5, **params: 'Any')

Unified Tree and Component-Based Anomaly Detector.

Wraps multiple tree-based and component reconstruction anomaly engines: - "eif" or "isolation": Extended Isolation Tree (oblique hyperplanes, mixed types). - "det" or "density": Density Estimation Tree (piecewise constant density, mixed types). - "hst" or "half_space": Streaming Half-Space Tree (mass-based scoring). - "rct" or "random_cut": Random Cut Tree (co-displacement scoring). - "active": Active Anomaly Tree with expert feedback adaptation. - "context": Variable-Order Context Anomaly Tree for discrete sequences. - "pca": Principal Component Analysis subspace reconstruction error. - "nmf": Non-negative Matrix Factorization additive reconstruction error.

items.title: Parameters
items.text: kind : str, default="eif" Anomaly tree engine to use: "eif", "det", "hst", "rct", "active", or "context". max_depth : int, optional Maximum tree depth. min_rows : int, default=10 Minimum leaf samples. contamination : float, default=0.05 Expected proportion of anomalies in the dataset (used to calibrate binary predictions). If the cutoff splits a group of equal scores, the entire group is labeled as inliers. seed : int, default=42 Random seed for stochastic engines (EIF, HST, RCT, Active). extension_level, subsample_size : int, optional EIF hyperplane order and training subsample size. min_samples_split : int, optional DET minimum samples per split. Defaults to twice min_rows. alpha, min_density_gain : float DET density smoothing and minimum gain. window_size : int, default=250 HST stream window size. initial_mass : float, default=0 HST initial node mass. sample_size : int, default=256 RCT sample size. eta, prior_weight : float Active anomaly learning rate and prior leaf weight. alphabet_size : int, default=256 Context tree alphabet size. smoothing_discount : float, default=0.5 Context tree discount for smoothing symbol probabilities.
