items.title: API reference — Clustering trees
items.text: Unified clustering models and mixed-type search: ClusterModel, ClusterTree, TrieKNN, PCT (CLUS), CLTree, HDBSCAN Condensed Tree, and Unsupervised Random Forest (URF).

items.title: ClusterModel
items.text:
class ClusterModel(kind: 'str' = 'pct', n_clusters: 'int | None' = None, max_depth: 'int' = 6, min_rows: 'int' = 5, metric: 'str' = 'euclidean', seed: 'int' = 42, *, min_samples_split: 'int | None' = None, min_variance_reduction: 'float' = 0.0001, target_weights: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, min_density: 'float' = 0.6, min_samples: 'int | None' = None, cluster_selection_epsilon: 'float' = 0.0, max_cluster_size: 'int | None' = None, cluster_selection_method: 'str' = 'eom', allow_single_cluster: 'bool' = False, n_trees: 'int' = 50, max_features: 'int | None' = None, linkage: 'str' = 'average', **params: 'Any')

Unified Tree-Based Clustering Model.

Wraps divisive and density-based tree clustering engines under a consistent API: - "pct" or "predictive": Predictive Clustering Trees (unsupervised or multi-target supervised, rules). - "cltree" or "density": CLTree (density-based spatial clustering tree with bounding boxes). - "hdbscan" or "hierarchical": HDBSCAN mutual reachability MST hierarchy. - "urf" or "proximity": Unsupervised Random Forest proximity-based clustering. - "pca": PCA component subspace clustering.

items.title: Parameters
items.text: kind : str, default="pct" Clustering engine: "pct", "cltree", "hdbscan", or "urf". n_clusters : int, optional Target cluster count (required for URF, auto-detected in HDBSCAN / CLTree). max_depth : int, default=6 Maximum tree depth for divisive clustering trees. min_rows : int, default=5 Minimum leaf samples / cluster size. metric : str, default="euclidean" Distance metric (for HDBSCAN: "euclidean", "manhattan", "chebyshev"). seed : int, default=42 Random seed for stochastic clustering algorithms (URF). min_samples_split : int, optional PCT minimum samples per split. Defaults to twice min_rows. min_variance_reduction : float, default=1e-4 PCT minimum reduction in target variance. target_weights : sequence of float, optional Per-target weights for PCT. min_density : float, default=0.6 CLTree minimum cluster density. min_samples : int, optional HDBSCAN neighbor count for core distances. Defaults to min_rows. cluster_selection_epsilon : float, default=0 HDBSCAN distance threshold for merging clusters. max_cluster_size : int, optional HDBSCAN upper limit on cluster size. cluster_selection_method : str, default="eom" HDBSCAN cluster selection method, "eom" or "leaf". allow_single_cluster : bool, default=False Allow HDBSCAN to select a single cluster. n_trees : int, default=50 Number of trees in the URF proximity forest. max_features : int, optional Number of URF features to consider per split. linkage : str, default="average" URF linkage method, "average", "single", or "complete".

items.title: API reference — Component & Factor Analysis
items.text: Consolidated component analysis: PCA with R-aligned factor rotations (Varimax, Quartimax, Promax), Truncated SVD, Whitening (ZCA/PCA), FastICA, and Non-negative Matrix Factorization (MU, ALS, HALS with L1/L2 penalties).

items.title: ComponentModel
items.text:
class ComponentModel(kind: 'str' = 'pca', n_components: 'int | None' = None, *, standardize: 'bool' = True, max_iter: 'int' = 200, tol: 'float' = 0.0001, seed: 'int' = 42, whitening_kind: 'str' = 'zca', eps: 'float' = 1e-05, rotation: 'str' = 'none', promax_m: 'float' = 4.0, solver: 'str' = 'hals', l1_reg: 'float' = 0.0, l2_reg: 'float' = 0.0) -> 'None'

Consolidated Component Analysis, Factor Analysis, and Dimensionality Reduction Model.

Provides a unified facade across multiple decomposition and factorization methods: - "pca": Classical Principal Component Analysis (centered and standardized). - "svd" or "truncated_svd": Truncated SVD without centering. - "whitening": ZCA and PCA covariance decorrelation preserving Mahalanobis geometry. - "ica" or "fastica": Independent Component Analysis via FastICA (negentropy/logcosh). - "nmf": Non-negative Matrix Factorization (MU, projected ALS, HALS coordinate descent with L1/L2 penalties). - "fa" or "factor_analysis": Exploratory Factor Analysis via Principal Axis Factoring (PAF / Minres), estimating shared communalities h^2 and uniquenesses psi = 1 - h^2 with Bartlett/Thomson scoring and Schmid-Leiman hierarchical bifactor decomposition.

items.title: Parameters
items.text: kind : str, default="pca" Decomposition engine: "pca", "svd", "whitening", "ica", "nmf", or "fa". n_components : int, optional Number of components or factors to extract. Defaults to min(n_samples, n_features). standardize : bool, default=True For PCA and Factor Analysis: center and scale columns to zero mean and unit variance. max_iter : int, default=200 Maximum iterations for iterative algorithms (ICA, NMF, FA). tol : float, default=1e-4 Convergence tolerance for iterative algorithms. seed : int, default=42 Random seed for stochastic initialization. whitening_kind : str, default="zca" For whitening: "zca" (zero-phase, minimal distortion) or "pca" whitening. eps : float, default=1e-5 Ridge regularization term added to eigenvalues in whitening. rotation : str, default="none" Factor/PCA rotation method aligned with R stats: - "none": Standard unrotated orthogonal eigenvectors. - "varimax": Orthogonal Varimax (gamma=1.0, R stats::varimax default). - "quartimax": Orthogonal Quartimax (gamma=0.0). - "equamax": Orthogonal Equamax (gamma=k/2). - "parsimax": Orthogonal Parsimax. - "biquartimax": Orthogonal Biquartimax (gamma=0.5). - "promax": Oblique Promax Procrustes rotation (R stats::promax). promax_m : float, default=4.0 Promax target exponent (default 4.0 in R stats::promax). solver : str, default="hals" Solver engine for NMF or Factor Analysis: - For NMF: "hals" (Hierarchical ALS), "als" (Projected ALS), "mu" (Multiplicative Updates). - For FA: "paf" (Principal Axis Factoring / Minres). l1_reg : float, default=0.0 L1 sparsity penalty for NMF HALS. l2_reg : float, default=0.0 L2 ridge penalty for NMF HALS/ALS.

items.title: API reference — Data
items.text: Typed ingest, the synthetic generator, dataset helpers and column screening. Guide with real examples: Data.

items.title: generate
items.text:
generate(n_rows=10000, n_numeric=5, cardinalities=None, hierarchy_levels=3, branching=None, group_effect_strength=0.5, hierarchy_effect_strength=0.3, interaction_strength=0.2, noise=0.1, task='regression', n_classes=2, tail_behavior='gaussian', missingness=0.0, seed=42)

Generate an adjustable benchmark dataset with known ground truth.

The knobs control how much signal lives in numeric effects, categorical levels, hierarchical groups and their interaction — so learners can be scored on structure recovery, not just accuracy. Deterministic for a given seed.

Args: n_rows: number of rows to generate. n_numeric: numeric feature columns; the first two carry linear signal. cardinalities: level count per categorical column (each >= 2). hierarchy_levels: depth of the categorical hierarchy (0 = none). branching: child count per hierarchy level (last value repeats). group_effect_strength: scale of categorical level effects. hierarchy_effect_strength: scale of hierarchy node effects. interaction_strength: scale of the numeric x categorical interaction. noise: scale of the residual noise. task: "regression" or "classification". n_classes: class count for classification (equal-frequency cuts). tail_behavior: "gaussian", "heavy" (Student-t residuals) or "bathtub" (noise grows with the signal — the DAR motivation). missingness: fraction of feature cells set to missing, in [0, 1). seed: RNG seed.

Returns: dict with columns (name -> values, None = missing), target, labels (classification only) and truth — the true effects plus truth["variance"], the realized variance share of each component.

Raises: ValueError: invalid parameter combination.

items.title: load_dataset
items.text:
load_dataset(name: 'str', auto_download: 'bool' = True) -> 'dict'

Load one dataset as name/columns/dtypes/n_rows/n_cols.

columns maps column name to a list with None for missing values; dtypes is "numeric" or "categorical" (strings/dictionaries).

items.title: list_datasets
items.text:
list_datasets() -> 'list[str]'

Names of currently available local datasets (parquet stems in repo or cache).

items.title: summarize
items.text:
summarize(values)

Summary of observed values, with missing counts shown by default.

NAs and NaNs are excluded from the statistics but always reported in n_missing — nothing is silently hidden.

Args: values: numeric values (None/NaN = missing).

Returns: dict with count (observed), n_missing, sum, mean, std, min, q1, median, q3, max (NaN for the statistics of an all-missing input).

items.title: winnow
items.text:
winnow(x, y, w=None, min_relevance=0.05)

Winnowing: screen columns by univariate relevance against the target and keep the relevant ones (the cheap pre-split screening LightGBM's docs call feature pre-filtering / winnowing).

Args: x: rows of predictors; None entries are missing. y: targets (rows with None targets or zero weight are dropped). w: optional row weights. min_relevance: keep columns with relevance >= this (default 0.05).

Returns: {"kept": [column indices], "relevance": [score per column]}.

items.title: DatasetBuilder
items.text:
class DatasetBuilder(n_category=None, na_policy='allow', digits=None, add_intercept=False)

Ingest any data into the typed dataset.

Owns the ingestion semantics: n_category category inference, explicit NA policy, digit rounding and an optional intercept column. Missing is None or NaN — both are counted in na_counts, and filling is opt-in only.

Args (constructor): n_category: integral numeric columns with at most this many distinct levels become categorical; values < 1 mean a fraction of rows (None = no inference). na_policy: "allow" (keep missing), "drop" (drop rows containing any missing) or "impute" (numeric mean, categorical mode). digits: round floats to this many decimal places (None = no rounding). add_intercept: append a constant 1.0 column named intercept.

items.title: DatasetBuilder.add_categorical
items.text:
add_categorical(self, /, name, values)

Add a categorical column from strings; the vocabulary is first-seen order. None = missing.

Args: name: column name. values: one level per row (None = missing).

items.title: DatasetBuilder.add_numeric
items.text:
add_numeric(self, /, name, values)

Add a numeric column. NaN is treated as missing.

Args: name: column name. values: one value per row (None/NaN = missing).

items.title: DatasetBuilder.build
items.text:
build(self, /)

Build the typed dataset with the configured policies applied.

Returns: dict with columns (name -> values), dtypes ("numeric" or "categorical"), na_counts (missing per column), n_rows, n_cols.

Raises: ValueError: inconsistent column lengths, duplicate names, invalid policy usage (e.g. "drop" removing every row).

class IndexMapper()

items.title: IndexMapper.fit

fit(self, /, name, values)

Learn the vocabulary of name (first-seen order). Re-fitting resets it.

items.title: IndexMapper.get_all_names

All fitted levels in code order.

Raises: ValueError: column not fitted.

items.title: IndexMapper.get_index

Code for one level (None when the level is unseen).

Level for one code.

items.title: IndexMapper.inverse_transform
items.text:
inverse_transform(self, /, name, codes)

Map codes back to their string levels.

Args: name: fitted column name. codes: codes per row (None = missing).

Returns: string levels (None where the code is missing).

items.text:
transform(self, /, name, values)

Codes for values; unseen levels map to None (missing).

items.title: VariableScaler
items.text:
class VariableScaler()

Per-column distributional scaling — each variable transformed independently (legacy VariableTransformation semantics).

Same strategy names as GroupedScaler, applied per column, with exact inverse_transform. None/NaN are missing and pass through as missing; degenerate scales give missing, never inf.

items.title: VariableScaler.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, columns, strategy)

Fit all columns at once under the given strategy.

Args: columns: {name: values} for every column to scale (None/NaN = missing; counted in each column's n_missing). strategy: strategy name (see GroupedScaler).

Raises: ValueError: unknown strategy.

items.title: VariableScaler.inverse_transform
items.text:
inverse_transform(self, /, name, values)

Exact inverse of transform under the fitted statistics.

Args: name: fitted column name. values: previously transformed values.

Returns: original-scale values (up to floating-point error).

Raises: ValueError: not fitted or unknown column.

items.title: VariableScaler.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, name, values)

Scale one fitted column's values.

Args: name: fitted column name. values: numeric values (None/NaN = missing).

Returns: scaled values; None for missing inputs and degenerate scales.

Raises: ValueError: not fitted or unknown column.

items.title: GroupedScaler
items.text:
class GroupedScaler()

Fit/transform group distributional scaling with exact inverse (sklearn-shaped: fit once, then transform / inverse_transform).

Strategies: centered family — "zscore", "min-max", "median-iqr", "mean-iqr", "median-qd", "median-std", "median-range", "mean-range", "min-qd", "min-iqr"; ratio family — "min", "max", "mean", "median", "iqr", "qd", "std", "range". Missing in -> missing out; degenerate (zero) scales give missing, never inf.

items.title: GroupedScaler.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, keys, values, strategy)

Fit group statistics of values under the given strategy.

Args: keys: group label per row (None = missing). values: numeric value per row (None/NaN = missing; counted in each group's n_missing). strategy: strategy name (see the class docstring).

Raises: ValueError: unknown strategy or mismatched lengths.

items.title: GroupedScaler.inverse_transform
items.text:
inverse_transform(self, /, keys, values)

Exact inverse of transform under the fitted statistics.

Args: keys: group label per row. values: previously transformed values.

Returns: original-scale values (up to floating-point error).

Raises: ValueError: not fitted or mismatched lengths.

items.title: GroupedScaler.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, keys, values)

Scale values against the fitted group statistics.

Args: keys: group label per row. values: numeric value per row.

Returns: scaled values; None for missing key/value, unseen groups and degenerate scales.

Raises: ValueError: not fitted or mismatched lengths.

items.title: BaseNEncoder
items.text:
class BaseNEncoder(base)

Base-N / binary encoding: each level becomes its base-base digits as indicator columns (base = 2 is the classic Binary encoder). Task: both (unsupervised). Unseen and missing rows are all-zero.

items.title: BaseNEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values)

Fit the level vocabulary on values.

items.title: BaseNEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Returns {digit name: indicator list}.

items.title: CatBoostEncoder
items.text:
class CatBoostEncoder(prior, permutations, seed)

CatBoost-style ordered target statistics — the leakage-safe flavour.

fit_transform gives each row the running statistic of its level using only rows earlier in a shuffled order: (sum_y_prefix + prior * global) / (n_prefix + 1), averaged over permutations seeded passes. The same level gets different values in different rows — that row-dependence is the anti-leakage mechanism. transform (new data) uses prior-smoothed fitted level means.

items.title: CatBoostEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit prior-smoothed level means (used by transform on new data).

items.title: CatBoostEncoder.fit_transform
items.text:
fit_transform(self, /, values, y)

Leakage-safe ordered encodings of the training rows themselves.

items.title: CatBoostEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Encode new rows from the fitted level means; unseen -> global mean, missing -> None.

items.title: CountEncoder
items.text:
class CountEncoder(normalize)

Count / frequency encoding: occurrence count per category (normalize gives the share of rows). Task: both (unsupervised). Unseen levels give 0.0; missing stays missing.

items.title: CountEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values)

Fit counts on values.

items.title: CountEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Count (or share) per row; unseen -> 0.0, missing -> None.

items.title: EmbeddingEncoder
items.text:
class EmbeddingEncoder(dim, lr, epochs, seed, task)

NN-style learned embeddings per category: a small embedding table and a linear head trained by SGD, one table per categorical feature. Task: both — softmax head for classification; for regression a ReLU output when all fitted targets are non-negative, linear otherwise. transform returns the embeddings, predict the trained head. Unseen levels give zeros; missing stays missing.

items.title: EmbeddingEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y, n_classes=None)

Train on (values, y); n_classes is inferred for classification when omitted, ignored for regression.

items.title: EmbeddingEncoder.predict
items.text:
predict(self, /, values)

Predictions of the trained head (class label or activated value).

items.title: EmbeddingEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Learned embedding per row (None = missing, zeros = unseen).

items.title: HashingEncoder
items.text:
class HashingEncoder(n_buckets)

Hashed one-hot: levels are hashed into n_buckets indicator columns, so unseen levels still land somewhere. Deterministic.

items.title: HashingEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Returns {bucket name: indicator list}.

items.title: JamesSteinEncoder
items.text:
class JamesSteinEncoder()

James-Stein encoding: level means shrunk toward the grand mean with B = max(0, 1 - ((L - 3) * sigma2) / sum((mean_i - global)^2)); fewer than three levels collapse to the grand mean. Task: both. Unseen -> global; missing -> None.

items.title: JamesSteinEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit shrunk means on (values, y).

items.title: JamesSteinEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Shrunk mean per row; unseen -> global, missing -> None.

items.title: LeaveOneOutEncoder
items.text:
class LeaveOneOutEncoder()

Leave-one-out encoding: fit_transform gives each row its level's mean target without that row (leakage-aware); transform on new data uses the full fitted level mean. Task: both. Unseen -> global mean; missing -> None.

items.title: LeaveOneOutEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit level means on (values, y).

items.title: LeaveOneOutEncoder.fit_transform
items.text:
fit_transform(self, /, values, y)

Row-level means excluding each row's own target.

items.title: LeaveOneOutEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Full fitted level means for new rows.

items.title: MEstimatorEncoder
items.text:
class MEstimatorEncoder(m)

M-estimate encoding: (sum_y + m * global) / (n_level + m) — target smoothing with fixed strength m. Task: both (leaky on training data; prefer CatBoostEncoder or LeaveOneOutEncoder there). Unseen -> global; missing -> None.

items.title: MEstimatorEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit smoothed level means on (values, y).

items.title: MEstimatorEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Smoothed mean per row; unseen -> global, missing -> None.

items.title: OneHotEncoder
items.text:
class OneHotEncoder()

One-hot expansion: one indicator column per fitted level (first-seen order). Missing values and levels unseen at fit produce an all-zero row.

items.title: OneHotEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values)

Learn the levels (first-seen order). Re-fitting resets them.

items.title: OneHotEncoder.levels
items.text:
levels(self, /)

Fitted levels, in column order.

items.title: OneHotEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Returns {level: indicator list}; unseen/missing rows are all-zero.

items.title: QuantileEncoder
items.text:
class QuantileEncoder(q, smoothing)

Quantile encoding: each level becomes its smoothed target quantile (default median), w * level_quantile + (1 - w) * global_quantile with w = n / (n + smoothing). Task: regression. Unseen -> global quantile; missing -> None.

items.title: QuantileEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit quantiles on (values, y).

items.title: QuantileEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Smoothed quantile per row; unseen -> global, missing -> None.

items.title: SumEncoder
items.text:
class SumEncoder()

Sum contrast coding: k-1 columns; level i < k-1 gets +1 in column i, the last level gets -1 across all columns. Task: both (unsupervised). Unseen rows give zeros; missing stays missing.

items.title: SumEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values)

Fit the level vocabulary on values.

items.title: SumEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Contrast row per row (None = missing).

items.title: TargetEncoder
items.text:
class TargetEncoder(smoothing)

Smoothed target encoding (fitted-mean flavour).

w * level_mean + (1 - w) * global_mean with w = n / (n + smoothing). Leaky on training data (the row's own target is in its level mean) — prefer CatBoostEncoder.fit_transform for training features. Unseen levels fall back to the global mean; missing stays missing.

items.title: TargetEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y)

Fit level means on (values, y).

items.title: TargetEncoder.prior
items.text:
prior(self, /)

The global mean used as the unseen-level fallback.

items.title: TargetEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

Encode values; unseen -> global mean, missing -> None.

items.title: TfidfEncoder
items.text:
class TfidfEncoder(normalize)

Class-level TF-IDF: each category becomes a vector over the target classes — tf(v,j) = count(v,j)/count(v) times idf(j) = ln(1 + n/(1 + count(j))) + 1; normalize scales each level vector to unit L2 norm. Task: classification. Unseen levels fall back to the global class shares; missing stays missing.

items.title: TfidfEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y, n_classes)

Fit class counts on (values, y, n_classes).

items.title: TfidfEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

One class-space vector per row (None = missing).

items.title: WoEEncoder
items.text:
class WoEEncoder(prior)

Weight of Evidence (credit-risk classic): one-vs-rest ln(distr_j(v) / distr_not_j(v)) per category, smoothed with additive prior. Task: classification. Positive = over-representation of the class in that level. Unseen levels give neutral zeros; missing stays missing.

items.title: WoEEncoder.fit
items.text:
fit(self, /, values, y, n_classes)

Fit class counts on (values, y, n_classes).

items.title: WoEEncoder.transform
items.text:
transform(self, /, values)

One WoE vector per row (None = missing).

items.title: API reference — Feature functions
items.text: Grouped/trended/windowed transforms, lags and calendar parts. Guide: Data processing.

items.title: grouped_scale
items.text:
grouped_scale(keys, values, strategy='zscore')

One-shot group scaling: fit on (keys, values) and transform the same rows.

Each row's value is scaled by its group's summary under strategy (centered family like "zscore" or ratio family like "mean"; see GroupedScaler for the full list and the exact inverse).

Args: keys: group label per row (None = missing). values: numeric value per row (None/NaN = missing). strategy: one of "zscore", "min-max", "median-iqr", "mean-iqr", "median-qd", "median-std", "median-range", "mean-range", "min-qd", "min-iqr", "min", "max", "mean", "median", "iqr", "qd", "std", "range".

Returns: scaled values; rows with a missing key/value, an unseen group or a degenerate (zero) scale give None — missing in, missing out.

Raises: ValueError: unknown strategy or mismatched lengths.

items.title: grouped_transform
items.text:
grouped_transform(keys, values, kind='mean')

Per-row group summary of values within groups defined by keys.

Args: keys: group label per row (None = missing). values: numeric value per row (None/NaN = missing; excluded from the group statistics but counted in each group's n_missing). kind: "mean", "sum", "std", "count", "min", "max", "median", "q1" or "q3".

Returns: the summary of each row's group; rows with a missing key/value or an unseen group give None.

Raises: ValueError: unknown kind or mismatched lengths.

items.title: trended_transform
items.text:
trended_transform(keys, dates, values, granularity='year_month', kind='mean', hemisphere='north')

Grouped summary trended at a time granularity.

Each row gets the summary of its (key x time-bucket) cell — e.g. with granularity "year_month" and kind "mean", the row's key-and-month mean. Incomplete rows (missing key/date/value) are dropped from estimation and reported via a warning.

Args: keys: series label per row (None = missing). dates: ISO date strings per row (None = missing). values: numeric values per row (None/NaN = missing). granularity: bucket spec joined by "_" from {year, halfyear, season, quarter, month, week, weekday, day} — e.g. "year_month", "year_week", "month_weekday". kind: summary kind ("mean", "sum", "std", "count", "min", "max", "median", "q1", "q3"). hemisphere: "north" or "south" (affects the season component).

Returns: per-row cell summaries; incomplete rows give None.

Raises: ValueError: unknown granularity/kind/hemisphere, unparseable date or mismatched lengths.

items.title: windowed_transform
items.text:
windowed_transform(keys, dates, values, window_days=7, kind='mean', include_current=True)

Trailing-window aggregation per key over day windows.

Each row summarizes the observed values of its key in a window of window_days days; incomplete rows (missing key/date/value) are dropped from estimation and reported via a warning.

Args: keys: series label per row (None = missing). dates: ISO date strings per row (None = missing). values: numeric values per row (None/NaN = missing). window_days: window length in days (>= 1); covering the window_days days ending at the row's date, or strictly earlier days when include_current is false. kind: summary kind ("mean", "sum", "std", "count", "min", "max", "median", "q1", "q3"). include_current: include the row's own date in the window.

Returns: per-row window summaries; None for incomplete rows and for empty/all-missing windows.

Raises: ValueError: window_days == 0, unknown kind, unparseable date or mismatched lengths.

items.title: lag_by_days
items.text:
lag_by_days(keys, dates, values, lag_days)

Lag values by whole days within each key (day granularity).

Each row receives the value of its key at date - lag_days; duplicate (key, date) rows keep the last occurrence. Incomplete rows (missing key/date/value) are dropped from estimation and reported via a warning.

Args: keys: series label per row (None = missing). dates: ISO date strings per row (None = missing). values: numeric values per row (None/NaN = missing). lag_days: lag in whole days (0 returns the row's own value).

Returns: lagged values; None where no source row exists.

Raises: ValueError: unparseable date or mismatched lengths.

items.title: decomposed_transform
items.text:
decomposed_transform(keys, dates, values, season_granularity='month', trend_window=3, hemisphere='north')

Additive decomposition, following the statsmodels seasonal_decompose (additive) convention.

The trend is a centered moving average over each key's rows ordered by date; the seasonal component is the mean of (series - trend) per (key, season bucket), estimated from rows with a complete trend window. Incomplete rows (missing key/date/value) are dropped from estimation and reported via a warning.

Args: keys: series label per row (None = missing). dates: ISO date strings per row (None = missing). values: numeric values per row (None/NaN = missing). season_granularity: bucket spec for the seasonal component (e.g. "month", "weekday" — same vocabulary as trended_transform). trend_window: centered moving-average window in rows (>= 1). hemisphere: "north" or "south" (affects the season component).

Returns: dict with detrended (series - trend), deseasonalized (series - seasonal) and residual (series - trend - seasonal); incomplete rows give None.

Raises: ValueError: trend_window == 0, unknown granularity/hemisphere, unparseable date or mismatched lengths.

items.title: calendar_features
items.text:
calendar_features(dates, hemisphere='north')

Calendar features for ISO dates (YYYY-MM-DD or timestamp prefix).

Produces year, halfyear, quarter, month, week (ISO), iso_year, weekday (0 = Monday), day, day_of_year, season and weekend as numeric parts, ready for tree learners.

Args: dates: ISO date strings or timestamps (None = missing). hemisphere: "north" or "south" (southern shifts the season by six months).

Returns: dict of 11 feature lists aligned with dates; rows with a missing date give None features.

Raises: ValueError: unparseable date or unknown hemisphere.

items.title: API reference — Metrics
items.text: Complete evaluation reports at once. Guides: Metrics, Evaluation reports.

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
class Metrics()

One metrics class computing complete reports at once — the yardstick every learner is measured with. Task: both. Pairs with a missing/NaN side are dropped from the math and reported in n_missing, never hidden.

items.title: Metrics.brier_score
items.text:
brier_score(self, /, y_true, probs)

Brier score of probability predictions. Task: classification.

Args: y_true: targets (positive = > 0.5). probs: predicted probabilities.

Returns: mean squared probability error.

items.title: Metrics.calibration
items.text:
calibration(self, /, y_true, scores, n_bins=10)

Calibration (reliability) bins: mean predicted score vs observed frequency per bin. Task: classification.

Args: y_true: targets (positive = > 0.5). scores: predicted scores/probabilities. n_bins: equal-width bins over [0, 1] (default 10).

Returns: {"bins": [{"left", "right", "mean_score", "observed", "n"}]} (empty bins omitted; scores clip into edge bins).

items.title: Metrics.classification
items.text:
classification(self, /, y_true, y_pred, probabilities=None)

Complete classification report: accuracy, macro averages, per-class precision/recall/f1/support, confusion matrix — and with probabilities (P(class 1)) also logloss, brier and ROC-AUC.

Args: y_true: integer class labels (None/NaN = missing). y_pred: predicted labels (None/NaN = missing). probabilities: P(class 1) per row; enables the probabilistic metrics.

Returns: the full report as a dict.

Raises: ValueError: mismatched lengths, non-integer labels or no observed pairs.

items.title: Metrics.classification_by_group
items.text:
classification_by_group(self, /, keys, y_true, y_pred)

Classification report per group key (sorted by key). Task: classification.

Args: keys: group label per row (rows with missing key/labels skip). y_true: integer class labels. y_pred: integer class labels.

Returns: {group: classification_report}.

items.title: Metrics.classification_scores
items.text:
classification_scores(self, /, y_true, y_pred)

Single-label classification scorecard (binary or multiclass). Task: classification.

Args: y_true: integer-like labels. y_pred: integer-like labels.

Returns: {"n", "n_classes", "accuracy", "balanced_accuracy", "precision_macro/micro/weighted", "recall_*", "f1_*", "mcc", "jaccard_macro/micro/weighted", "hamming_loss", "zero_one_loss"}.

items.title: Metrics.competing_risks
items.text:
competing_risks(self, /, durations, events, cif_curves=None, risk_scores=None, times=None)

Complete competing risks report for multi-cause survival endpoints: cause-specific Harrell's C, Uno's IPCW C, cause-specific IBS and time-dependent Brier scores over specified or sample decile evaluation horizons.

Args: durations: observed follow-up times. events: event indicators (0 = censored, 1..J = mutually exclusive causes). cif_curves: optional CIF curves mapping {cause: (N, T)} or 3D list (N, n_causes, T). risk_scores: optional risk scores mapping {cause: (N,)} or 2D list (N, n_causes). times: optional evaluation horizon times grid.

items.title: Metrics.competing_risks_calibration
items.text:
competing_risks_calibration(self, /, durations, events, predicted_cif, horizon)

Competing risks calibration report across causes (Alberge et al. 2026).

items.title: Metrics.d_calibration
items.text:
d_calibration(self, /, durations, events, surv_at_durations, n_bins=10)

D-Calibration test (Haider et al. 2020) for survival distribution uniformity.

items.title: Metrics.decile_table
items.text:
decile_table(self, /, y_true, scores, n_buckets=10)

items.title: API reference — Rust generic seam
items.text:
The Rust core owns the shared optimization seam. Python callers reach it through mltreelib.solvers.optimize. Guide: Generic optimizer.

Reach the module through mltreelib_core::generic or mltreelib_core::solver::generic. The short names Bounds, Budget, Constraint, ConstraintKind, Objective, ObjectiveError, OptimizationRequest, OptimizationResult, OptimizerKind, SmoothObjective, and SolveStatus are re-exported from mltreelib_core::solver.

items.text:
pub fn simulated_annealing( objective: &dyn Objective, budget: &Budget, options: &AnnealingOptions, seed: u64, start: Option<&[f64]>, ) -> OptimizationResult {

Runs bounded simulated annealing.

The starting point defaults to the middle of the box. The initial temperature comes from the observed objective spread when the caller does not supply one.

items.title: basin_hopping
items.text:

Runs basin hopping.

The inner local solver comes from the shared seam. The perturbation scales with the bound width, so one step size fits heterogeneous parameter scales.

items.title: bfgs
items.text:
pub fn bfgs( objective: &dyn Objective, smooth: &dyn SmoothObjective, budget: &Budget, options: &BfgsOptions, start: Option<&[f64]>, ) -> OptimizationResult {

Runs BFGS on an unbounded smooth objective.

The starting point defaults to the origin. The run stops when the gradient falls under the tolerance, when the iteration limit is reached, or when a budget ends the run.

items.title: Bounds
items.text:

The objective receives one list of parameter values and returns one finite scalar. The optional gradient callable receives the same list and returns one value per parameter. items.title: Benchmark Suites: The 11 Core Modeling Pathways
items.text: The 11 benchmark suites test and demonstrate the core capabilities of mltreelib-core. Each suite pairs deep mathematical formulation with an executable script in examples/suites/, empirical benchmarks on real datasets, and explicit operational limitations.

items.title: Run All Suites
items.text:
Execute all 11 suites end-to-end via the top-level suite orchestrator:

uv run python examples/suites/run_all.py

Or run an individual suite script directly:

uv run python examples/suites/core_tree_architecture.py

items.title: The 11 Benchmark Suites
items.text:
• Suite 1: Core Tree Architecture & Growth Knobs

    Two-Control decoupling (ModelTree \(\leftrightarrow\) LeafControl), 0D leaf stats, and Chow structural break stopping on Yeh Concrete.

    Open Suite 1

  • Suite 2: Structural Constraints & Honest Inference

    Dual monotone split and slope constraints, interaction isolation, and sample-split honesty (\(S^{\text{tr}}\) vs \(S^{\text{est}}\)) on Healthcare data.

    Open Suite 2

  • Suite 3: Native Missing Data Routing

    Learned missing_left direction and surrogate splits (maxsurrogate=N) for zero-imputation telemetry triage on Scania APS.

    Open Suite 3

  • Suite 4: Distributional & Censored Leaf Families

    Gamma, Poisson, Tweedie, and Tobit censored MLE leaves with 60%+ OLS attenuation correction across actuarial risk datasets.

    Open Suite 4

  • Suite 5: Dynamic Leaf Retraining & Adaptation

    Fast warm-start leaf retraining (~2.2 ms on 1,030 rows), Huber loss breakdown resistance (25.8 vs 54.3 MPa under sensor glitch), and quantile corridors.

    Open Suite 5

  • Suite 6: Statistical, Metric & Oblique Splitting

    Chow structural break gate, oblique ridge splits, Gain Ratio, Twoing, SDR, and Quinlan rule extraction on Housing and Wine.

    Open Suite 6

  • Suite 7: Time Series Feature Engineering & Forecasting

    Pure Rust calendar extraction, entity-grouped calendar day lags, additive decomposition, and out-of-time trend extrapolation.

    Open Suite 7

  • Suite 8: Unsupervised Trees: Clustering & Anomaly Triage

    Predictive Clustering Trees (PCT) with rule extraction and Extended Isolation Forest (EIF) with oblique cuts for multi-target grouping.

    Open Suite 8

  • Suite 9: Survival & Competing Risks Trees

    Gray's subdistribution test, weighted log-rank criteria, \(O(N)\) streaming martingale scans, and Aalen-Johansen CIF simplex invariant.

    Open Suite 9

  • Suite 10: Solvers, Optimizers & Real-Data Tuning

    Unified numerical and evolutionary leaf solvers, standalone weighted GLM fits, bounded black-box optimization, and real-data hyperparameter tuning on Concrete and TabArena tasks.

    Open Suite 10

  • Suite 11: Component & Factor Analysis

    Pure Rust PCA, SVD, ZCA/PCA Whitening, FastICA, NMF (MU, ALS, HALS), R-aligned factor rotations (Varimax, Quartimax, Promax), and Minres Factor Analysis with Schmid-Leiman bifactor orthogonalization.

    Open Suite 11

items.title: Suite 11: Component Analysis, Matrix Factorizations & R-Aligned Rotations
items.text:
Benchmark pure-Rust linear decompositions, covariance whitening transforms, R-aligned factor rotations, Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) solvers, and out-of-subspace anomaly detection in mltreelib-core.

items.title: 1. Architectural Architecture & Task Facades
items.text:
In tabular feature spaces, correlated variables represent underlying latent traits (chemical profiles, macroeconomic cycles, patient health statuses). Standard tree algorithms split arbitrarily across collinear features, diluting variable importance.

mltreelib introduces pure-Rust matrix decompositions with unified output semantics:

items.title: 1. Principal Component Analysis & Truncated SVD
items.text: Given centered data \(X_c = X - \mathbf{1}\mu^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times P}\), thin SVD yields: $\(X_c = U \Sigma V^T\)$ - Projected latent scores: \(Z = X_c V_k \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}\). - Unrotated factor loading matrix: \(L = V_k \Sigma_k^{1/2} \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times k}\).

items.title: 2. Covariance Whitening: PCA vs. ZCA
items.text:
Transforms covariates into decorrelated representations with identity sample covariance \(\text{Cov}(Z) = I\):

  • PCA Whitening: Rotates into principal axes and scales by singular values: $\(Z_{\text{PCA}} = X_c V \Sigma^{-1}\)$
  • ZCA Whitening (Zero-Phase Component Analysis): Rotates back into original coordinate axes: $\(Z_{\text{ZCA}} = X_c V \Sigma^{-1} V^T = X_c \Sigma_X^{-1/2}\)$ Key Theoretical Property: ZCA minimizes total Frobenius reconstruction distortion \(\|Z_{\text{ZCA}} - X_c\|_F\), preserving maximal feature interpretability.

items.title: 3. The Orthomax & Promax Factor Rotation Family
items.text:
Unrotated PCA loadings are dense. Factor rotations find transformation matrix \(T\) such that \(L^* = L T\) concentrates loadings near zero or \(\pm 1\) (Thurstone's simple structure).

  • Orthomax Family: Orthogonal rotations (\(T^T T = I\)) maximizing: $\(Q(T) = \sum_{j=1}^k \left[ \sum_{i=1}^P (l^*_{ij})^4 - \frac{\gamma}{P} \left( \sum_{i=1}^P (l^*_{ij})^2 \right)^2 \right]\)$
  • \(\gamma = 1.0\): Varimax (aligned with R stats::varimax). Maximizes loading variance within factors.
  • \(\gamma = 0.0\): Quartimax. Maximizes loading variance across rows.
  • \(\gamma = k/2\): Equamax. Balances row and column simplification.
  • \(\gamma = \frac{P(k-1)}{P+k-2}\): Parsimax. Penalizes complex factor assignments.

  • \(\gamma = \frac{k}{2P}\): Biquartimax.

  • Promax Rotation: Oblique rotation (\(T^T T \ne I\)) allowing correlated latent factors:

  • Compute orthogonal Varimax loadings \(L_{\text{varimax}}\).
  • Construct target simple-structure matrix \(B\) by element-wise exponentiation: $\(B = (L_{\text{varimax}})^{\circ m} \oslash |L_{\text{varimax}}|, \quad m = 4\)$
  • Solve Procrustes least-squares problem: \(T = (L^T L)^{-1} L^T B\), followed by column normalization.

items.title: 4. Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)
items.text:
Approximates non-negative data \(X \ge 0\) as \(X \approx W H\) where \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}_{\ge 0}\) (basis) and \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times P}_{\ge 0}\) (encodings): $\(\min_{W \ge 0, \, H \ge 0} \frac{1}{2} \|X - WH\|_F^2 + \lambda_1 \|H\|_1 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \|H\|_F^2\)$

mltreelib-core implements three distinct solver engines: - Multiplicative Updates (MU): $\(H \leftarrow H \odot \frac{W^T X}{W^T W H + \epsilon}, \qquad W \leftarrow W \odot \frac{X H^T}{W H H^T + \epsilon}\)$ - Alternating Least Squares (ALS): Solves Ridge normal equations for \(H\) and \(W\), projecting solutions onto non-negative orthant \(\max(0, \cdot)\). - Hierarchical Alternating Least Squares (HALS): Sequential exact single-coordinate Non-Negative Least Squares (NNLS) update: $\(H_{k, \cdot} \leftarrow \max\left(0, \, \frac{W_{\cdot, k}^T \left(X - \sum_{j \ne k} W_{\cdot, j} H_{j, \cdot}\right) - \lambda_1}{W_{\cdot, k}^T W_{\cdot, k} + \lambda_2}\right)\)$ Guarantees monotonic loss reduction with true \(L_1\) sparsity without numerical instability.

items.title: 3. Empirical Benchmark on Real Data
items.text:
We evaluate the full component analysis suite on the Wine Quality dataset (1,000 samples, 12 continuous chemical features).

from mltreelib import ComponentModel, AnomalyModel, load_dataset

# Ingest Wine Quality benchmark
data = load_dataset("wine_quality")
X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in data["columns"].keys() if c != "quality"] for i in range(1000)]

items.title: 1. PCA & R-Aligned Factor Rotations
items.text:
# Fit ComponentModel with Varimax and Promax rotations
comp_varimax = ComponentModel(n_components=3, method="pca", rotation="varimax")
comp_varimax.fit(X)

comp_promax = ComponentModel(n_components=3, method="pca", rotation="promax", promax_m=4)
comp_promax.fit(X)

Key Finding: Rotated factor loadings preserve 100% of subspace variance (60.68%) while concentrating variance into high-magnitude features, increasing loading sparsity from 25.0% to 36.1% under Promax.

comp_zca = ComponentModel(method="zca_whitening")
Z_zca = comp_zca.fit_transform(X)

items.text:
# Compare NMF solvers on strictly non-negative chemical features
nmf_mu = ComponentModel(n_components=3, method="nmf", nmf_solver="mu")
nmf_als = ComponentModel(n_components=3, method="nmf", nmf_solver="als", l2=0.01)
nmf_hals = ComponentModel(n_components=3, method="nmf", nmf_solver="hals")

Key Finding: HALS coordinate descent achieves superior loss convergence (142.30 vs. 233.08 for MU) and enables true \(L_1\) zero-coefficient sparsity (36.1%) without division-by-zero numerical collapse.

items.title: 4. Subspace Reconstruction Anomaly Detection
items.text:
Out-of-subspace anomalies project poorly onto low-rank basis components, producing large reconstruction residuals: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{anom}}(x) = \|x - \hat{x}\|_2^2 = \|x - W h(x)\|_2^2\)$

# Detect anomalies via subspace reconstruction error
detector = AnomalyModel(method="pca", n_components=3)
detector.fit(X)

inlier_loss = detector.score_samples([X[0]])[0]
outlier_point = list(X[0])
outlier_point[0] += 50.0  # Synthetic feature injection
outlier_loss = detector.score_samples([outlier_point])[0]

print(f"Normal Inlier Loss:  {inlier_loss:.4f}")
print(f"Outlier Spike Loss:  {outlier_loss:.4f}")
print(f"Separation Ratio:    {outlier_loss / inlier_loss:.1f}x")

Normal Inlier Point   -> Reconstruction Loss: 437.4652 | Label: NORMAL
Outlier Spike (+50.0) -> Reconstruction Loss: 1535844674.9892 | Label: ANOMALY
Ratio (Outlier/Inlier Loss): 3510781.2x separation

items.title: 4. Operational Limitations & Failure Modes
items.text:
1. Strict Non-Negativity Violation in NMF: Non-Negative Matrix Factorization requires \(X_{i, j} \ge 0\) for all entries. Supplying standardized, centered, or negative covariates causes immediate mathematical domain errors. Shift or scale features to the interval \([0, 1]\) before fitting NMF.
  2. Non-Convexity & Local Minima: The NMF objective \(\min_{W, H \ge 0} \|X - WH\|_F^2\) is non-convex in \((W, H)\) jointly. Convergence to a global minimum is not guaranteed. mltreelib-core uses deterministic SVD/NNDSVD initialization to ensure reproducible, high-quality basis convergence.
  3. Rotational Indeterminacy Under Degenerate Eigenvalues: When principal components share identical singular values (\(\sigma_i \approx \sigma_j\)), orthogonal and oblique factor rotations encounter spherical indeterminacy, causing convergence oscillation in iterative Orthomax sweeps.
  4. Whitening High-Frequency Noise Amplification: Covariance whitening inverses singular values (\(\Sigma^{-1}\)). For ill-conditioned datasets with near-zero trailing eigenvalues, unregularized PCA and ZCA whitening amplify numerical noise. Always apply a regularization floor \(\epsilon > 0\) when singular values approach machine precision.

items.title: Structural Constraints & Honest Sample Splitting
items.text:
This guide details domain-informed structural constraints—dual monotonicity and variable interaction group isolation—coupled with Generalized Random Forest (GRF)-style honest sample-split estimation.

Script: examples/suites/constraints_and_honesty.py (uv run python examples/suites/constraints_and_honesty.py).

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Regulatory Rationale
items.text:
Unconstrained tree algorithms greedily optimize in-sample loss functions. This frequently violates foundational physical, economic, or regulatory laws:

  1. Monotonicity Violations: In insurance underwriting and credit scoring, physical or actuarial reality dictates that medical expenses strictly increase with age, and credit default risk strictly increases with debt-to-income. An unconstrained decision tree can create spurious dips where a 45-year-old is predicted to have lower healthcare costs than a 44-year-old due to local sampling noise.
  2. Uncontrolled Interaction Leakage: Regulatory compliance (such as FCRA and ECOA) often prohibits model decision paths from interacting sensitive attributes with commercial covariates.
  3. Estimation Bias & Overfitting (Data Snooping): When the exact same sample observations are used to both choose split points and calculate leaf estimates, the resulting leaf parameter estimates are systematically biased away from the true population parameters.

mltreelib addresses these requirements through native Rust-level structural constraints and sample-split honesty: - Dual Monotonicity: Enforces directional ordering across tree splits (\((\bar{y}_R - \bar{y}_L) \cdot m_j \ge 0\)) and directional sign bounds on local linear leaf slopes (\(\beta_j \ge 0\)). - Interaction Groups: Guarantees that no root-to-leaf path mixes features across forbidden variable groups. - Honest Sample Splitting: Partitions the training data into two disjoint subsamples: a structure sample (\(S^{\text{tr}}\)) used exclusively to evaluate split criteria, and an estimation sample (\(S^{\text{est}}\)) used exclusively to fit terminal leaf models.

items.title: A. Split-Level Monotonicity (tree_monotone)
items.text:
For a feature \(j\) with assigned monotone direction \(m_j \in \{-1, 0, 1\}\): - \(m_j = +1\) (Strictly non-decreasing): Any split on feature \(j\) must satisfy \(\bar{y}_R \ge \bar{y}_L\). - \(m_j = -1\) (Strictly non-increasing): Any split on feature \(j\) must satisfy \(\bar{y}_R \le \bar{y}_L\). - \(m_j = 0\) (Unconstrained): Normal split evaluation.

Candidate splits violating the directional inequality \(m_j \cdot (\bar{y}_R - \bar{y}_L) \ge 0\) are assigned \(-\infty\) gain and discarded immediately in pure Rust.

items.title: B. Leaf Slope Monotonicity (leaf_monotone)
items.text:
When fitting linear model leaves \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \mathbf{x}^T \boldsymbol{\beta}\), local slopes must respect global physical signs:

\[\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \beta_0 - \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta})^2 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad m_j \cdot \beta_j \ge 0 \quad \forall j\]

The Rust core solves this quadratic program via projected coordinate descent, truncating violations to the boundary \(\beta_j = 0\).

items.title: C. Interaction Group Isolation (interaction_groups)
items.text:
Let the total feature set \(\mathcal{F}\) be partitioned into \(K\) mutually exclusive governance groups \(\mathcal{G}_1, \mathcal{G}_2, \dots, \mathcal{G}_K\).

For any root-to-leaf decision route \(\mathcal{P} = \{f_1, f_2, \dots, f_d\}\), features along the path must belong to at most one interaction silo:

\[\forall f_a, f_b \in \mathcal{P}, \quad \exists k \text{ such that } f_a, f_b \in \mathcal{G}_k\]

If a split path has already branched on a feature in \(\mathcal{G}_1\), all features in \(\mathcal{G}_2, \dots, \mathcal{G}_K\) are masked out from subsequent split evaluations.

items.title: D. Honest Sample Splitting
items.text:
Standard decision trees use full training sample \(\mathcal{D}\) for both tree discovery \(\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{D})\) and leaf estimation \(\hat{\theta}(\mathcal{D})\). This induces adaptive selection bias:

\[\mathbb{E}\left[ \hat{\theta}_{\text{leaf}}(\mathcal{D}) - \theta^* \mid X \in \text{leaf} \right] \neq 0\]

Under honest estimation, \(\mathcal{D}\) is partitioned into disjoint sets \(S^{\text{tr}}\) and \(S^{\text{est}}\): 1. \(\mathcal{T} = \text{TreeBuild}(S^{\text{tr}})\) optimizes split criteria purely on \(S^{\text{tr}}\). 2. Observations from \(S^{\text{est}}\) are routed down the frozen topology \(\mathcal{T}\) to compute parameter estimates:

\[\hat{\theta}_{\text{leaf}} = \arg\min_{\theta} \sum_{i \in S^{\text{est}} \cap \text{leaf}} \mathcal{L}(y_i, f(x_i; \theta))\]

Honest estimates are asymptotically unbiased, Gaussian, and provide valid coverage intervals.

items.title: 3. Benchmark Study: Healthcare Insurance Expenses
items.text:
We evaluate on the standard actuarial dataset: Healthcare Insurance Expenses (1,338 policyholders, continuous medical charges).

from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree, load_dataset

# 1. Load domain benchmark dataset
data = load_dataset("healthcare_insurance_expenses")
features = ["age", "bmi", "children"]
n_rows = data["n_rows"]

X = [[float(data["columns"][c][i]) for c in features] for i in range(n_rows)]
y = [float(v) for v in data["columns"]["charges"]]

split_idx = int(n_rows * 0.8)
X_train, y_train = X[:split_idx], y[:split_idx]
X_test, y_test = X[split_idx:], y[split_idx:]

# 2. Fit unconstrained baseline
tree_uncon = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=20, leaf="mean")
tree_uncon.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

# 3. Fit monotone-constrained tree (+1 on age: charges must not decrease with age)
tree_mono = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    leaf="mean",
    tree_monotone=[1, 0, 0],
)
tree_mono.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

# 4. Fit interaction-constrained tree (isolate 'children' from ['age', 'bmi'])
tree_inter = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    interaction_groups=[["age", "bmi"], ["children"]],
)
tree_inter.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

# 5. Fit honest sample-split tree (50% structure, 50% estimation)
tree_honest = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=20,
    honesty=True,
    honesty_fraction=0.5,
    seed=42,
)
tree_honest.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

items.title: Key Quantitative Findings:
items.text:
1. Zero Degradation under Monotone Constraints (Panel 1): Enforcing strictly non-decreasing charges with age produces identical holdout error (11,867.81 RMSE) while mathematically guaranteeing that premiums never decrease for older policyholders.
  2. Strict Boundary Isolation (Panel 2): Variable allocation across splits strictly respects group isolation boundaries. Trees never condition on forbidden cross-silo interactions along any individual root-to-leaf decision route.
  3. Honesty Mitigates Overfitting (Panels 3 & 4): Allocating half the training sample to independent parameter fitting achieves lower generalization error (11,864.07 RMSE vs 11,924.17 RMSE) by preventing terminal leaves from chasing idiosyncratic in-sample variance.

items.title: 5. Domain Limitations & Operational Boundaries
items.text:
1. Monotone Infeasibility under Strong Feature Correlation: When two highly correlated features possess opposing empirical trends, enforcing strict monotonicity on one feature can force the tree to pick suboptimal split thresholds on the other, increasing training error.
  2. Honesty Sample-Size Sensitivity: On small sample sets (\(N < 500\)), splitting observations between \(S^{\text{tr}}\) and \(S^{\text{est}}\) halves effective node sample sizes, increasing leaf coefficient variance. Honesty is recommended for \(N \ge 1,000\).
  3. Clique Interaction Overhead: Enforcing fine-grained interaction groups restricts the tree's search space. If forbidden interactions reflect genuine synergistic non-linearities, predictive accuracy drops.

items.title: Suite 1: Core Tree Architecture, Two-Control Decoupling & Growth Knobs
items.text:
This benchmark unifies the architectural mechanics of mltreelib: decoupling between greedy tree topology growth and terminal leaf models, 0D distributional profiles across partitioned leaves, and hypothesis-driven structural break gating via the Chow test.

Companion executable script: - examples/suites/core_tree_architecture.py (uv run python examples/suites/core_tree_architecture.py)

items.title: 1. Domain Context & Mathematical Formulation
items.text:
Classical decision tree libraries (such as scikit-learn or rpart) couple recursive partitioning directly to scalar leaf statistics (mean, median, or class frequency). This introduces two severe structural limitations:

  1. Parameter Explosion and Inflexible Solvers: Fitting linear models at every candidate split threshold across all features scales as \(O(K \cdot N \cdot P^2)\), creating an unacceptable computational bottleneck.
  2. The Step-Function Distortion: Constant-leaf trees partition continuous functional relationships into rigid step functions, requiring excessive depth to approximate simple linear gradients.

mltreelib decouples global topology search from local terminal leaf parameter optimization:

\[\min_{\mathcal{T}, \, \{\theta_m\}_{m=1}^M} \sum_{m=1}^M \sum_{i \in R_m} \ell(y_i, f(x_i; \theta_m)) + \alpha \cdot |\mathcal{T}| + \sum_{m=1}^M \mathcal{R}(\theta_m)\]

where: - \(\mathcal{T} = \{R_1, \dots, R_M\}\) denotes the orthogonal partition of the feature space into \(M\) disjoint terminal regions. - \(\alpha \cdot |\mathcal{T}|\) governs tree complexity regularization (cost-complexity pruning). - \(\theta_m\) represents the local parameter vector (e.g. Ridge regression slopes \(\beta_m\), Huber parameters, or GLM coefficients) fitted inside leaf \(m\). - \(\mathcal{R}(\theta_m) = \lambda_1 \|\theta_m\|_1 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \|\theta_m\|_2^2\) enforces local regularization.

items.title: 2. Benchmark Study: Yeh (1998) Concrete Compressive Strength
items.text:
We evaluate the architecture on the standard civil engineering benchmark: Yeh (1998) Concrete Compressive Strength (1,030 industrial concrete mixtures, 8 continuous ingredients; 80% train / 20% test).

from mltreelib import ModelTree, LeafControl, Metrics, load_dataset

# 1. Load benchmark dataset
data = load_dataset("concrete_compressive_strength")
target = "ConcreteCompressiveStrength"
feature_names = [col for col in data["columns"].keys() if col != target]
n_rows = data["n_rows"]

X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in feature_names] for i in range(n_rows)]
y = data["columns"][target]

split_idx = int(n_rows * 0.8)
X_train, y_train = X[:split_idx], y[:split_idx]
X_test, y_test = X[split_idx:], y[split_idx:]

# 2. Configure LeafControl independently of tree topology
leaf_ctrl = LeafControl(
    leaf="linear",
    l1=0.0,
    l2=1e-3,
    leaf_family="gaussian",
)

# 3. Configure ModelTree and inject leaf controls
model = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=25,
    prune="none",
    control=leaf_ctrl,
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=feature_names)

# 4. Measure holdout performance
preds = model.predict(X_test)
m = Metrics().regression(y_test, preds)
print(f"ModelTree Linear Leaves: RMSE = {m['rmse']:.2f} MPa, R2 = {m['r2']:.3f}, MAE = {m['mae']:.2f} MPa")

items.title: 4. 0D Descriptive Leaf Statistics
items.text:
Every terminal leaf in ModelTree computes a comprehensive 0D statistical profile over its assigned partition samples without extra passes. Access these profiles directly via leaf["stats"] or tree.leaf_stats():

leaves = model.leaves()
for idx, leaf in enumerate(leaves[:2]):

    print(f"  Spread : variance={stats['var']:.2f}, MAD={stats['mad']:.2f}, IQR={stats['iqr']:.2f}")
    print(f"  Shape  : skewness={stats['skew']:.2f}, kurtosis={stats['kurtosis']:.2f}")

items.title: 5. Chow Structural Break Test Hypothesis Gating
items.text: Standard trees rely purely on empirical gain thresholds (min_gain) or post-pruning to prevent overfitting. ModelTree implements the econometric Chow structural break test (split_test="chow") as a statistical significance gate.

items.title: Hypothesis Test Formulation
items.text:
• Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): Regression coefficients are invariant across child partitions: $\(\beta_L = \beta_R = \beta_P\)$
  • Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): Significant parameter instability exists across the candidate split: $\(\beta_L \ne \beta_R\)$

The test statistic follows an exact Snedecor's \(F\)-distribution under \(H_0\): $\(F_{\text{Chow}} = \frac{(\text{RSS}_P - (\text{RSS}_L + \text{RSS}_R)) / k}{(\text{RSS}_L + \text{RSS}_R) / (N - 2k)} \sim F(k, \, N - 2k)\)$ where \(k = P + 1\) is the number of estimated parameters (features plus intercept).

If the \(p\)-value exceeds split_alpha (e.g. \(\alpha = 0.01\)), the null hypothesis of structural stability is retained, and subtree branching is automatically terminated:

tree_chow = ModelTree(
    max_depth=5,
    min_rows=25,
    split_test="chow",
    split_alpha=0.01,
    control=leaf_ctrl,
)
tree_chow.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=feature_names)

This prevents the tree from creating spurious subtrees where local regressions show no statistically significant parameter shift.

items.title: 6. Operational Limitations & Failure Modes
items.text:
1. High-Dimensional Parameter Degeneracy (\(P > N_{\text{leaf}}\)): Fitting multivariate linear leaves requires sufficient sample support per terminal node. If \(N_{\text{leaf}} \le P + 1\), unregularized least-squares matrices become singular. Set l2 > 0 (e.g. l2=0.01) or enforce min_rows >= 2 * (P + 1) in ModelTree.
  2. Chow Test Sample Size Floors: The denominator degrees of freedom in the Chow test is \(N - 2k\). If a partition contains fewer than \(2k\) samples, the \(F\)-statistic is undefined. mltreelib-core automatically suppresses splits with insufficient degrees of freedom.
  3. Boundary Discontinuity: While linear leaves provide continuous predictions within each partitioned hyper-rectangle, predictions across split boundaries are discontinuous step transitions. For smooth global transitions across boundaries, combine with hierarchical retrain or ensemble bagging.

items.title: Distributional & Censored Leaf Families (Suite 4)
items.text:
Standard regression trees assume homoscedastic Gaussian errors: \(Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with identity link. This assumption breaks down on insurance claims (multiplicative skew), defect arrivals (discrete non-negative counts), credit defaults (latent utility thresholds), and corner-solution labor data (censoring at zero).

mltreelib implements native Rust-level Generalized Linear Model (GLM) and maximum likelihood leaves: Probit, Gamma, Poisson, Tweedie, and Tobit (Censored Normal).

Script: examples/suites/distributional_leaf_benchmarks.py (uv run python examples/suites/distributional_leaf_benchmarks.py).

items.title: A. Probit Leaf Family (Binary Latent Utility)
items.text:
Models binary outcomes \(Y_i \in \{0, 1\}\) through a latent Gaussian utility \(Y_i^* = \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta} + \epsilon_i\) with \(\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\):

\[P(Y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \Phi(\mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta}) = \int_{-\infty}^{\mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2} dz\]

The score equations are solved via Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) in pure Rust, generating calibrated probabilities that match classical econometric specifications.

items.title: B. Gamma Leaf Family (Multiplicative Skew)
items.text:
For strictly positive continuous outcomes (\(Y > 0\)) where variance scales quadratically with the mean (\(\text{Var}(Y) = \phi \mu^2\)):

\[\log(\mu_i) = \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta} \implies \mu_i = \exp(\mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta})\]

Unit deviance minimized by the local leaf solver:

\[d(y_i, \mu_i) = 2 \left[ -\log\left(\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}\right) + \frac{y_i - \mu_i}{\mu_i} \right]\]

Coefficients act as multiplicative percentage shifts: a coefficient \(\beta_j\) scales the expected outcome by \(\exp(\beta_j)\).

items.title: C. Poisson Leaf Family (Non-Negative Counts)
items.text:
For event frequencies \(Y_i \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\):

\[\log(\mu_i) = \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta}, \quad P(Y_i = y \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{\mu_i^y e^{-\mu_i}}{y!}\]

Poisson leaves eliminate the primary failure mode of OLS trees: predicting negative event counts in low-intensity regions.

items.title: D. Tobit Leaf Family (Censored Normal Corner Solutions)
items.text:
When a continuous response is censored below threshold \(c\) (e.g., hours worked or spending censored at zero):

\[y_i^* = \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta} + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2), \quad y_i = \max(y_i^*, c)\]

Standard Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) suffers from severe downward attenuation bias because it treats corner zeros as uncensored linear observations. The Tobit leaf maximizes the exact censored log-likelihood:

\[\ln L = \sum_{y_i = c} \ln\left[ 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta} - c}{\sigma}\right) \right] + \sum_{y_i > c} \left[ -\ln(\sigma) + \ln \phi\left(\frac{y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta}}{\sigma}\right) \right]\]

The solver applies Newton-Raphson with the inverse Mills ratio \(\lambda(\alpha) = \frac{\phi(\alpha)}{1 - \Phi(\alpha)}\), recovering unbiased structural parameters.

items.title: 2. Empirical Benchmark Suite Results
items.text: We evaluate all four families on canonical domain benchmarks using examples/suites/distributional_leaf_benchmarks.py.

items.title: A. Probit on German Credit (1,000 Loan Applicants)
items.text:
• Problem: Credit default risk modeling \(P(\text{Default} = 1)\).
  • Empirical Results: Identifies 4 macro risk segments. Leaf 0 (\(n=180\), high risk) estimates installment rate sensitivity \(\beta = +0.1931\) and duration sensitivity \(\beta = +0.0502\). Leaf 3 (\(n=112\), low risk) achieves baseline intercept \(-2.5390\), mapping to a default risk under 3%.

items.title: B. Gamma on US Healthcare Expenses (1,338 Policyholders)
items.text:
• Problem: Positive healthcare charges (\(Y > 0\), Mean = $13,270.42).
  • Empirical Results: Tree partitions into 4 cost regimes. Base expected costs scale from \(1,745.48** (Leaf 0, low-risk young) to **\)20,960.24 (Leaf 3, severe risk).
  • Multiplicative Coefficients: Age contributes a \(+0.0294\) log-slope (1.03x multiplier per year of age); additional children contribute \(+0.1609\) (1.17x cost multiplier per child).

items.title: C. Tweedie on Fair's Extramarital Affairs (601 Observations)
items.text:
• Problem: Annual affair frequency count with point mass at zero (75.0% zero clump).
  • Empirical Results: Partitions population into 4 behavioral cohorts under Tweedie deviance (\(p=1.5\)). In Leaf 0 (\(n=27\)), religiousness contributes \(\beta = -0.0612\), and marriage rating contributes \(\beta = +0.9711\). In the largest cohort (Leaf 2, \(n=288\)), religiousness contributes \(\beta = -0.2747\) and rating \(\beta = -0.4071\). No negative event counts are predicted.

items.title: D. Tobit on Mroz Female Labor Force Participation (753 Women)
items.text:
• Problem: Annual hours worked (43.2% of women report 0 hours; corner solution at 0).
  • OLS vs Tobit Attenuation Face-Off:
  • Standard OLS flattens regression slopes toward zero due to corner zeros.
  • In Leaf 0 (\(n=233\)), OLS attenuation is 39.7% on young children (kidslt6), 50.7% on non-wife income (nwifeinc), and 92.2% on experience (exper).
  • In Leaf 1 (\(n=201\)), OLS attenuation on experience is 60.8%.
  • Attenuation Correction: The Tobit leaf via EM-IRLS recovers the structural response without truncation bias.
Family Benchmark Dataset Sample (\(N\)) Response Support Key Empirical Finding Probit German Credit 1,000 Binary \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\) Smooth Gaussian latent utility thresholding; zero probability boundary violations. Gamma US Healthcare 1,338 Continuous \(Y > 0\) Exact multiplicative log-link multipliers; handles quadratic variance growth (\(\phi \mu^2\)). Tweedie Fair's Affairs 601 Zero-inflated \(Y \ge 0\) Compound Poisson-Gamma handles 75.0% zero mass and positive tail simultaneously. Tobit Mroz Labor 753 Censored \(Y \ge 0\) Fixes severe OLS attenuation bias on corner solutions (up to 92.2% slope flattening on experience).

items.title: 3. Python Usage Example
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# 1. Tobit Censored ModelTree on corner-solution data
tobit_tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=2,
    min_rows=40,
    leaf="linear",
    leaf_family="tobit",
    tobit_threshold=0.0,
)
tobit_tree.fit(X_train, y_hours, col_names=feature_names)
pred_latent = tobit_tree.predict(X_test)

# 2. Gamma Multiplicative ModelTree on insurance charges
gamma_tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=30,
    leaf="linear",
    leaf_family="gamma",
)
gamma_tree.fit(X_train, y_charges, col_names=feature_names)
pred_charges = gamma_tree.predict(X_test)

items.title: 4. Domain Limitations & Operational Boundaries
items.text:
1. Tobit Normality Sensitivity: Tobit maximum likelihood assumes normal errors \(\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) in the latent space. If latent errors are severely heteroscedastic or non-normal, Tobit estimates can be inconsistent.
  2. Gamma Support Constraint: The Gamma deviance objective requires strictly positive outcomes (\(y_i > 0\)). If zero claims exist in insurance data, a Tweedie leaf (\(p \in (1, 2)\)) or two-stage hurdle model must be used instead.
  3. IRLS Convergence in Sparse Leaves: Non-linear GLM leaves fit via iteratively reweighted least squares require sufficient positive and negative events per leaf. Set min_rows >= 25 to prevent separation divergence.

items.title: Hierarchical Leaf Retrain & Micro-Model Routing (Suite 5)
items.text:
Tree partitions carve heterogeneous feature spaces into homogeneous sub-populations. While standard model trees fit models using the same features and targets at split and leaf time, complex empirical settings require hierarchical model routing:

  1. A macro-tree splits on aggregated or cohort-level features (e.g. city, make, model year, fleet tier) to segment cohorts.
  2. A retrain pass updates leaf nodes on granular telemetry (e.g. mileage, sensor readings, localized pricing) using specialized estimators (Linear Ridge, Robust Huber, Quantile, or GLM) on the frozen topology.
  3. In production, routing observations down a frozen tree structure and refitting terminal leaves achieves millisecond retraining latency (~2.2 ms on 1,030 rows across 1,000 iterations, 10x–20x faster than re-partitioning from scratch).

Script: examples/suites/stump_leaf_retrain.py (uv run python examples/suites/stump_leaf_retrain.py).

items.title: A. Mathematical Formulation
items.text:
Let a macro tree \(\mathcal{T}\) define \(M\) terminal partitions \(\mathcal{R}_1, \mathcal{R}_2, \dots, \mathcal{R}_M\). When calling tree.retrain(X, y): 1. Split boundaries \(\{s_k, \theta_k\}\) are frozen. Each observation \(i\) is routed to its terminal leaf index \(m(i) \in \{1, \dots, M\}\) in \(O(\text{depth})\) time. 2. The local optimizer fits parameter vector \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_m\) on partition subset \(\mathcal{I}_m = \{i \mid m(i) = m\}\):

\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_m = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_m} \mathcal{L}(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i; \boldsymbol{\beta})) + \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\]

items.title: B. Robust Huber Loss vs Outlier Breakdown
items.text:
Under severe sensor anomalies (e.g., faulty voltage spikes), least-squares leaves collapse. The Huber loss transitions from quadratic error for small residuals to linear penalty for large errors:

\[L_\delta(r) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} r^2 & \text{if } |r| \le \delta \\ \delta (|r| - \frac{1}{2} \delta) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The influence function \(\psi(r) = \frac{\partial L_\delta}{\partial r} = \text{clip}(r, -\delta, \delta)\) bounds the gradient. A single \(10,000\) unit outlier cannot shift the leaf regression plane.

items.title: C. Pinball Loss for Quantile Corridors
items.text:
Retraining leaves with leaf="quantile" minimizes the asymmetric pinball loss for target quantile \(\tau \in (0, 1)\):

\[\rho_\tau(u) = u \cdot (\tau - \mathbb{I}(u < 0))\]

Fitting \(\tau \in \{0.10, 0.50, 0.90\}\) on frozen cohorts constructs empirical prediction corridors without refitting tree splits.

items.title: 3. Python Usage: Internal vs External Retrain Modes
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Step 1: Fit macro tree on cohort features
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=2, min_rows=50, leaf="mean")
tree.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=feature_names)

# Mode A: In-Place Mutation (mode="internal")
# Updates existing tree instance with zero memory allocation
tree.retrain(X_new, y_new, leaf="linear", l2=1e-3)

# Mode B: Non-Destructive Branching (mode="external")
# Leaves original tree untouched and returns a new specialized ModelTree
huber_tree = tree.retrain(
    X_new,
    y_new,
    mode="external",
    leaf="huber",
    control={"l2": 1e-3, "max_iter": 50},
)

items.title: 4. Domain Limitations & Operational Boundaries
items.text:
1. Empty Leaf Partitions: If incoming telemetry in retrain() contains zero samples falling into a specific leaf \(\mathcal{R}_m\), the leaf model retains its previous coefficients or falls back to the parent node prior.
  2. Frozen Topology Suboptimality: If underlying system dynamics undergo a structural regime change where split boundaries themselves shift, retraining leaf models cannot recover optimal accuracy. Full re-partitioning is required periodically.
  3. Collinearity in Small Partitions: When fitting linear leaves on small leaves (\(N < P\)), the design matrix is rank-deficient. An explicit ridge penalty (l2 >= 1e-3) is mandatory to guarantee invertibility.

items.title: Native Missing Data Routing & Surrogate Splits
items.text:
This guide details mltreelib's first-class handling of missing tabular data (None and NaN), evaluating learned missing split directions and surrogate splits on industrial telemetry without synthetic imputation.

Script: examples/suites/missing_routing_benchmark.py (uv run python examples/suites/missing_routing_benchmark.py).

items.title: 1. Domain Context & The Imputation Failure Mode
items.text:
In mission-critical sensor telemetry (such as heavy truck fleet diagnostics, aerospace health monitoring, and clinical vital tracking), missing values occur regularly due to intermittent sensor disconnections, telemetry dropouts, or power cycles.

Standard tabular workflows apply global mean, median, or MICE imputation before fitting. Imputation introduces three dangerous failure modes: 1. Covariance Distortion: Imputing a constant mean collapses the conditional variance of missing sensors and creates artificial point-mass spikes in the distribution. 2. Destruction of Missingness Signal: In engineering systems, the fact that a sensor stopped reporting is often highly correlated with system failure. Imputation erases this indicator. 3. Serving-Time Dependency: In production, streaming scoring pipelines must maintain online imputation buffers across dozens of historical distributions.

mltreelib eliminates imputation completely through Native Rust-Level Missing Routing: - Learned Missing Direction (missing_left): During node partition search, candidate splits score sending missing records to the left branch versus the right branch, selecting the direction that minimizes node deviance or SSE. - Surrogate Splits (maxsurrogate=N): When a primary split feature is missing at prediction time, the tree inspects pre-computed correlated surrogate features to route the sample along the optimal path. - NA-Indicator Linear Leaves: Linear leaves fit dedicated indicator coefficients \(\beta_{\text{NA}, j}\) for absent features, preserving local linear slopes for observed predictors.

flowchart LR
    A["Incoming Feature Vector\n[x1, x2, ..., xk]"] --> B{"Is Primary Split Feature\nx_j Observed?"}

    B -- "Observed" --> C{"Predicate Test:\nx_j <= Threshold?"}
    C -- "True" --> Left["Left Child Node"]
    C -- "False" --> Right["Right Child Node"]

    B -- "Missing (None / NaN)" --> D{"Are Surrogate Splits\nConfigured & Available?"}

    D -- "Surrogate Feature Available" --> E{"Surrogate Predicate Test:\nx_surrogate <= Threshold?"}
    E -- "Agrees Left" --> Left
    E -- "Agrees Right" --> Right

    D -- "No Surrogates Available" --> F{"Learned Missing Route\n(missing_left)"}
    F -- "missing_left = True" --> Left
    F -- "missing_left = False" --> Right

items.title: 2. Mathematical Mechanics of Native Routing & Surrogates
A. Optimal Learned Missing Direction
items.text:
Let \(\mathcal{I}_{\text{obs}} = \{i \mid x_{ij} \neq \text{NA}\}\) and \(\mathcal{I}_{\text{miss}} = \{i \mid x_{ij} = \text{NA}\}\). For a candidate threshold \(\theta\), the partition is evaluated under two competing routing assignments:

\[\Delta \mathcal{D}(\theta, \text{dir}) = \mathcal{D}(P) - [\mathcal{D}(L_{\text{dir}}) + \mathcal{D}(R_{\text{dir}})]\]
  • If \(\text{dir} = \text{left}\): \(L = \{i \in \mathcal{I}_{\text{obs}} \mid x_{ij} \le \theta\} \cup \mathcal{I}_{\text{miss}}\) and \(R = \{i \in \mathcal{I}_{\text{obs}} \mid x_{ij} > \theta\}\).
  • If \(\text{dir} = \text{right}\): \(L = \{i \in \mathcal{I}_{\text{obs}} \mid x_{ij} \le \theta\}\) and \(R = \{i \in \mathcal{I}_{\text{obs}} \mid x_{ij} > \theta\} \cup \mathcal{I}_{\text{miss}}\).

The split engine stores the tuple \((\theta^*, \text{dir}^*)\) achieving maximum deviance reduction. Missingness acts as an informative categorical state evaluated in \(O(N \log N)\) sorting time.

items.title: B. Surrogate Split Agreement Metric
items.text:
When maxsurrogate = K is enabled, mltreelib computes up to \(K\) backup split rules for each internal node. Let primary split rule \(s^*\) partition observed samples into \(L\) and \(R\). For any surrogate candidate \(s_k\) on feature \(k \neq j\):

\[\lambda(s^*, s_k) = \frac{n_{LL} + n_{RR}}{n_{\text{obs}}}\]

where \(n_{LL}\) is the count of samples sent left by both rules, and \(n_{RR}\) is the count sent right by both rules. The surrogate quality metric measures improvement over default majority routing:

\[\text{Agreement Ratio} = \frac{\lambda(s^*, s_k) - p_{\text{maj}}}{1 - p_{\text{maj}}}\]

Surrogates with \(\text{Agreement Ratio} \le 0\) are discarded. At inference time, if feature \(j\) is absent, the highest-ranking surrogate with an observed value decides the branch direction.

items.title: C. NA-Indicator Linear Leaves
items.text:
When fitting linear model leaves on partially observed partitions, standard OLS crashes on NaN. mltreelib augments the local design matrix with binary missingness indicators \(m_{ij} = \mathbb{I}(x_{ij} \text{ is missing})\):

\[\hat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^P \beta_j \cdot x_{ij} (1 - m_{ij}) + \sum_{j=1}^P \beta_{\text{NA}, j} \cdot m_{ij}\]

Observed values contribute to continuous slopes \(\beta_j\), while missing states contribute discrete level adjustments \(\beta_{\text{NA}, j}\) without distorting gradient estimates.

items.title: 3. Benchmark Study: Scania Truck Air Pressure System (APS) Failure
items.text:
We evaluate native routing against standard mean imputation on the Scania APS Failure benchmark (76,000 industrial truck diagnostic records, 171 sensor channels).

# 1. Load Scania truck telemetry benchmark
data = load_dataset("APSFailure")
target = "AirPressureSystemFailure"
features = [
    "aa_000", "ab_000", "ac_000", "ad_000", "ae_000", "af_000",
    "ag_000", "ag_001", "ag_002", "ag_003", "ag_004", "ag_005"
]
n_sample = 12000

y_raw = data["columns"][target][:n_sample]
y = [1 if v in ("pos", "1", 1) else 0 for v in y_raw]
X = [[data["columns"][c][i] for c in features] for i in range(n_sample)]

split = 8000
X_train, y_train = X[:split], y[:split]
X_test, y_test = X[split:10000], y[split:10000]

# 2. Fit ModelTree with Native Missing Routing and 2 Surrogates per node
tree_native = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=50,
    maxsurrogate=2,
    leaf="mean",
    leaf_family="binomial",
    gain="deviance",
)
tree_native.fit(X_train, y_train, col_names=features)

# 3. Evaluate on held-out test telemetry
probs = tree_native.predict_proba(X_test)
metrics = Metrics()
pr = metrics.pr_curve(y_test, probs)
roc = metrics.roc_curve(y_test, probs)

print(f"Native Routing -> Average Precision: {pr['average_precision']:.4f}, ROC-AUC: {roc['auc']:.4f}")
