items.title: Key Quantitative Findings:
items.text:
1. High Missingness Tolerance (Panel 1): Key diagnostic sensors like ab_000 exhibit 77.4% missingness in production telemetry. Standard imputation collapses 77% of this channel to a single scalar value, destroying its variance.
  2. Competitive Precision-Recall without Imputation Pipelines (Panel 2): On this single fixed evaluation split, native missing routing achieves 0.5924 Average Precision (a +3.8% directional difference over mean imputation's 0.5706) with ROC-AUC virtually tied (0.9848 vs 0.9846). This confirms that native routing matches or directionally improves upon imputation without requiring online mean table synchronization.
  3. Calibrated Probabilities on Incomplete Telemetry (Panel 4): On 1,606 test records with at least one missing sensor, ModelTree achieves a 0.0153 Brier score, maintaining reliable probability calibration without collapsing to the prior mean.

items.title: 5. Domain Limitations & Failure Modes
items.text:
1. Uninformative Complete Blackout: If an entire telemetry record arrives with all features missing (\(x_{ij} = \text{NA} \quad \forall j\)), surrogate splits cannot fire. The sample cascades down default missing_left branches to a single leaf. Upstream health monitors must flag complete packet loss.
  2. Surrogate Memory Overhead: Computing \(K\) surrogate splits per node scales tree serialization size as \(O(K \cdot N_{\text{nodes}})\). For lean embedded deployment, set maxsurrogate=0 and rely on missing_left.
  3. Imputation Leakage in Training Splits: Mean/median imputation computes statistics across the training set, causing subtle leakage if applied prior to cross-validation splits. Native routing avoids all cross-split contamination.

items.title: Suite 10: Solvers, Optimizers & Real-Data Tuning
items.text:
Benchmark numerical, quasi-Newton, and continuous evolutionary leaf solvers, standalone GLM fits, and bounded black-box optimizers implemented natively in mltreelib-core.

Run suite from repository root after building release extension:

uv run python examples/suites/solver_benchmarks.py

items.title: 1. Architectural Decoupling: Tree Partitions vs. Leaf Solvers
items.text:
In standard model trees, evaluating complex optimization problems at every candidate split threshold incurs prohibitive computational cost (\(O(K \cdot N \cdot P^2)\)). ModelTree solves this through two-control decoupling:

  1. Tree Search: Fast scalar heuristics (Variance reduction, Chow test, Log-rank) discover spatial partition boundaries.
  2. Leaf Optimization: Once terminal regions are established, the compatible optimizer selected with LeafControl(solver=...) fits each local model.

All seven choices apply to Gaussian linear leaves. Supported non-Gaussian linear GLMs use IRLS or L-BFGS.

flowchart LR

items.title: 2. Mathematical Formulations of the Seven Solvers
1. Analytical Cholesky (leaf_solver="irls")
items.text:
For continuous Gaussian targets with Ridge \(L_2\) regularization: $\(\min_{\beta} \frac{1}{2N} \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \|\beta\|_2^2\)$

The gradient vanishes at the exact normal equations: $\((X^T X + N \lambda_2 I) \beta^* = X^T y\)$

mltreelib-core computes the lower-triangular Cholesky factor \(L L^T = (X^T X + N \lambda_2 I)\) via faer, followed by forward and backward substitution. Latency is \(O(P^3)\) where \(P\) is feature count.

items.title: 2. Quasi-Newton L-BFGS (leaf_solver="lbfgs")
items.text:
For smooth non-linear likelihoods (GLM families, Tobit censored regression), L-BFGS updates search direction \(d_k = -H_k abla f( eta_k)\) using two-loop recursion on past \(m=5\) vector pairs: $\(s_k = eta_{k+1} - eta_k, \qquad y_k = abla f( eta_{k+1}) - abla f( eta_k)\)$

Step length \(\alpha_k\) satisfies the Armijo condition: $\(f( eta_k + \alpha_k d_k) \le f( eta_k) + c_1 \alpha_k abla f( eta_k)^T d_k\)$

items.title: 3. Cyclic Coordinate Descent (leaf_solver="ccd")
items.text:
Minimizes the non-smooth Elastic Net objective: $\(\min_{\beta} \frac{1}{2N} \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda_1 \|\beta\|_1 + \frac{\lambda_2}{2} \|\beta\|_2^2\)$

Updates each coordinate \(\beta_j\) sequentially using soft-thresholding operator \(\mathcal{S}(z, \gamma) = \text{sign}(z)\max(|z| - \gamma, 0)\): $\(\beta_j \leftarrow \frac{\mathcal{S}\left( \frac{1}{N} X_j^T (y - \sum_{k \ne j} X_k \beta_k), \, \lambda_1 \right)}{\frac{1}{N} X_j^T X_j + \lambda_2}\)$ Produces exact zero coefficients for irrelevant features inside terminal leaves.

items.title: 4. Success-History Adaptive Differential Evolution (leaf_solver="shade")
items.text: Derivative-free continuous optimization. Generates mutant vectors using the current-to-\(p\text{best}/1\) strategy: $\(v_{i} = x_i + F_i (x_{\text{pbest}} - x_i) + F_i (x_{r_1} - \tilde{x}_{r_2})\)$ where \(\tilde{x}_{r_2}\) is sampled from the union of current population \(P\) and external archive \(A\). Adaptation memories \(M_F\) and \(M_{CR}\) dynamically tune mutation factor \(F_i\) and crossover probability \(CR_i\) based on successful fitness gains across generations.

items.title: 5. Covariance Matrix Adaptation (leaf_solver="cmaes")
items.text: Samples candidate parameter vectors \(x_i \sim \mathcal{N}(m^{(g)}, (\sigma^{(g)})^2 C^{(g)})\). Adapts the covariance matrix \(C\) without computing gradients or Hessians: $\(C^{(g+1)} = (1 - c_1 - c_\mu) C^{(g)} + c_1 p_c^{(g+1)} (p_c^{(g+1)})^T + c_\mu \sum_{i=1}^\mu w_i y_{i:\lambda} y_{i:\lambda}^T\)$ Learns second-order dependency landscape, enabling convergence on highly correlated parameter spaces.

items.title: 6. Real-Coded Genetic Algorithm (leaf_solver="ga")
items.text: Evolves a continuous chromosome population using Simulated Binary Crossover (SBX) with distribution index \(\eta_c\) and polynomial mutation with index \(\eta_m\): $\(\beta_{1, 2} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ (1 \mp \gamma) x_1 + (1 \pm \gamma) x_2 \right]\)$ Provides broad global exploration of non-convex and multi-modal leaf loss functions.

items.title: 7. Separable Natural Evolution Strategies (leaf_solver="nes")
items.text: Updates parameter distribution parameters \(\theta = (\mu, \sigma)\) along estimated natural gradient directions: $\(\nabla_\mu J = \sum_{k=1}^\lambda w_k z_k, \qquad \nabla_\sigma J = \sum_{k=1}^\lambda w_k (z_k^2 - 1)\)$ Provides fast derivative-free updates along coordinate-aligned search directions.

items.title: 3. Empirical Benchmark on Real Data
items.text:
We benchmark all seven solvers on the Yeh (1998) Concrete Compressive Strength dataset (1,030 rows, 8 features; 80% train / 20% test).

Exact Cholesky (irls)Quasi-Newton (lbfgs)Adaptive Evolutionary (shade)Coordinate Descent (ccd) 
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Analytical closed-form normal equations
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="irls", l2=0.01)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Quasi-Newton L-BFGS with two-loop recursion
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="lbfgs", l2=0.01)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Success-history based adaptive differential evolution (derivative-free)
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="shade", l2=0.01, seed=42)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Cyclic coordinate descent with soft thresholding for L1 sparsity
tree = ModelTree(max_depth=0, leaf="linear", leaf_solver="ccd", l1=0.1, l2=0.01)
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)

items.title: Benchmark Results (Standalone Global Fit, max_depth=0)
items.text: Solver Family Latency (ms) Holdout Test RMSE (MPa) Test \(R^2\) Convergence Character irls Analytical Cholesky 1.28 ms 10.224 0.631 Exact analytical optimum in 1 step. lbfgs Quasi-Newton 5.12 ms 10.287 0.626 Converges in 14 iterations to machine precision. shade Continuous DE 26.62 ms 10.269 0.627 Reaches 99.6% of exact analytical optimum without gradients. ga Genetic Algorithm 41.15 ms 10.360 0.621 Robust global convergence across 100 generations. cmaes Evolutionary Covariance 11.65 ms 11.346 0.545 Fast adaptation; sensitive to raw unstandardized scale. nes Natural Gradient 10.68 ms 16.919 -0.011 Fast step updates; requires standardized inputs. ccd Cyclic Coordinate Descent 4,101.09 ms 10.224 0.631 Exact analytical match; coordinate sweeps on raw scale.

items.title: Key Observations:
items.text:
1. Analytical & Quasi-Newton Supremacy on Convex Surfaces: irls (1.28 ms) and lbfgs (5.12 ms) define the Pareto frontier for smooth convex losses. Both reach optimal holdout test RMSE (10.224 MPa).
  2. Derivative-Free Precision with SHADE: shade achieves 10.269 MPa (within 0.4% of the exact analytical minimum) in only 26.6 ms without evaluating a single gradient or Hessian. This makes it ideal for non-differentiable penalties, multi-objective fitness, or discontinuous loss landscapes.
  3. Tree-Decoupled Leaf Performance (max_depth=2, 4 Leaves): When deployed inside a partitioned model tree:
  4. irls: 3.53 ms total fit time \(\to\) 7.183 MPa RMSE (\(R^2 = 0.818\)).
  5. lbfgs: 3.30 ms total fit time \(\to\) 7.583 MPa RMSE (\(R^2 = 0.797\)).
  6. shade: 29.19 ms total fit time \(\to\) 7.606 MPa RMSE (\(R^2 = 0.796\)).
  7. ga: 45.43 ms total fit time \(\to\) 8.005 MPa RMSE (\(R^2 = 0.774\)).
  8. cmaes: 12.45 ms total fit time \(\to\) 10.285 MPa RMSE (\(R^2 = 0.626\)).

items.title: 5. Generic Bounded Optimization & Real-Data Hyperparameter Tuning
items.text:
mltreelib.solvers.optimize minimizes arbitrary bounded scalar objectives through one unified contract:

from mltreelib.solvers import optimize

# Black-box bounded minimization
res = optimize(
    lambda p: (p[0] - 1.0)**2 + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0]**2)**2,  # Rosenbrock
    bounds=[(-2.0, 2.0), (-2.0, 2.0)],
    method="lbfgs_b",
    max_evaluations=200,
)
print(f"Status: {res.status}, Best objective: {res.best_value:.6f}")

items.title: 6. Production Recommendations
items.text:
When to Select Each Solver

  • Use irls for standard linear ridge regression (leaf="linear") on Gaussian continuous targets. It uses Rust's faer dense Cholesky solver with minimal overhead.
  • Use lbfgs for GLMs (leaf_family="binomial", "poisson", "gamma", "tweedie", "tobit").
  • Use ccd when sparse leaves are mandatory (\(L_1 > 0\)) to eliminate irrelevant features inside leaf equations.
  • Use shade when fitting custom non-smooth losses, quantile objectives with heavy outliers, or discontinuous simulation simulators.

items.title: 7. Operational Limitations & Numerical Failure Modes
items.text:
1. Unstandardized Covariate Scaling: Derivative-free evolutionary algorithms (cmaes, nes) sample isotropic search perturbations. If covariates differ by orders of magnitude (e.g., Cement \(500 \, \text{kg/m}^3\) vs. Water \(0.18 \, \text{kg/m}^3\)), initial spherical covariance updates degenerate, yielding sub-optimal convergence (as seen with nes RMSE 16.919 MPa). Always standardize continuous inputs before applying evolutionary leaf solvers.
  2. Coordinate Descent Collinearity Stagnation: When features exhibit high pairwise correlation (\(r > 0.95\)), cyclic coordinate descent (ccd) undergoes zig-zagging oscillations, requiring thousands of coordinate sweeps to achieve convergence (latency 4,101 ms). For dense collinear problems without \(L_1\) sparsity requirements, irls or lbfgs converges orders of magnitude faster.
  3. Non-Convex Local Minima & Stochastic Reproducibility: Evolutionary solvers (shade, ga, cmaes) are stochastic algorithms. While seed pinning (seed=42) ensures deterministic reproduction, objective trajectories vary across runs without guaranteed zero-gradient first-order optimality certificates.
  4. Box Bounds vs. Coupled Constraints in optimize: The lbfgs_b bounded optimizer supports box constraints \(l_i \le x_i \le u_i\). For coupled joint budget or volume constraints \(\sum_i a_i x_i \le B\), use dual multiplier bisection or scipy.optimize.minimize(method="SLSQP").

items.title: Suite 6: Exotic Statistical, Metric & Fair Splitting Criteria (Spec 12 Suite)
items.text:
This guide demonstrates mltreelib's exotic statistical hypothesis testing, optimal transport, and metric splitting criteria.

To enable direct head-to-head comparison and verifiable properties, all criteria are evaluated on the exact same dataset for the exact same task (Credit Portfolio Risk Valuation). As new phases are developed, they are integrated directly into this unified benchmarking framework.

Companion executable script: - examples/suites/statistical_and_metric_splitting.py (uv run python examples/suites/statistical_and_metric_splitting.py)

items.title: Shared Benchmark Task: Credit Portfolio Risk Valuation
items.text:
We generate a unified financial risk dataset (\(N = 300\)) where each observation represents an account with: - score: Continuous risk score \(\in [-2.0, 2.0]\) with an underlying structural break at \(0.0\). - zip_code: High-cardinality noise categorical feature (50 zip code levels with zero true signal). - tier_flag: Low-cardinality binary signal factor (\(\{0, 1\}\)). - gender: Protected demographic attribute (\(S \in \{0, 1\}\)). - gender_proxy: Unfair proxy feature with high correlation to gender. - fair_merit: Independent financial merit score.

Target modalities derived from the same underlying portfolio distribution: 1. Scalar Target (\(y \in \mathbb{R}\)): Portfolio loss / return. 2. Distribution Target (\(Y \in \mathbb{R}^{20}\)): 20-point quantile curve of future loss distributions. 3. Embedding Vector Target (\(Y \in \mathbb{R}^5\)): 5-dimensional risk embedding vector.

items.title: 1. Baseline: Standard CART (gain="sse")
items.text:
Standard recursive partitioning greedily maximizes variance reduction:

\[\text{Gain}_{\text{SSE}} = \text{SSE}(P) - [\text{SSE}(L) + \text{SSE}(R)]\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Standard CART with variance reduction
tree_cart = ModelTree(max_depth=1, min_rows=15, gain="sse", prune="none")
tree_cart.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_cart.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': -0.012, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 1222.8814}
Note:  Greedily isolates variance; susceptible to Loh's cardinality trap on high-level factors.

items.title: 2. Phase 12A: Model-Based Recursive Partitioning (gain="mob")
items.text:
Best for: Detecting parameter instability or structural breaks along continuous covariates without refitting linear models across thousands of candidate cutpoints.

Fits the leaf linear regression once at the parent node, calculates individual score residuals \(\psi_i = \nabla_\theta \ell_i(\hat{\theta})\), and evaluates empirical fluctuation processes via the supLM test statistic:

\[\max_{t \in [\underline{t}, \bar{t}]} \frac{\|W(t)\|^2}{t(1-t)}\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# MOB parameter instability test
tree_mob = ModelTree(
    gain="mob",
    split_test="mob",
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    leaf="linear",
    prune="none",
)
tree_mob.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_mob.root_split())
print("Diagnostics:", tree_mob.split_diagnostics()[0])

Diagnostics: {'p_value': 0.0000e+00, 'test_stat': 212.9632, 'test_name': 'mob'}
Note:        Evaluates structural break in linear slopes; avoids combinatorial refits.

items.title: 3. Phase 12B: Conditional Inference Trees (gain="ctree")
items.text:
Best for: Tabular datasets with mixed scale and high-cardinality factors (e.g. zip codes, store IDs, diagnoses) where CART suffers from selection bias.

CTree separates variable selection from splitpoint selection using permutation rank tests. Under \(H_0\), test statistics follow standardized \(\chi^2\) distributions regardless of cardinality:

\[c_j = z_j^2 \sim \chi^2_1 \quad (\text{numeric}), \qquad c_j = \frac{\text{SSB}}{V_Y} \sim \chi^2_{C - 1} \quad (\text{categorical})\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# CTree unbiased permutation rank test
tree_ctree = ModelTree(
    gain="ctree",
    split_test="ctree",
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    prune="none",
)
tree_ctree.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_ctree.root_split())

Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.011, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 141.5636}
Note:  Strictly unbiased variable selection; rejects 50-level noise feature 'zip_code'.

items.title: 4. Phase 12C: Metric & Kernel Splitting (gain="energy_distance" & gain="mmd")
items.text:
Best for: Multi-output targets, embeddings, representations, and complex distribution targets \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^D\) where scalar variance is undefined.

  • Energy Distance (Székely & Rizzo): $\(\text{Gain}_{\mathcal{E}} = \frac{W_L W_R}{W_L + W_R} \left( 2 \mathbb{E}\|Y_L - Y_R\| - \mathbb{E}\|Y_L - Y_L'\| - \mathbb{E}\|Y_R - Y_R'\| \right)\)$
  • Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD / Gretton et al.): $\(\text{Gain}_{\text{MMD}} = \frac{W_L W_R}{W_L + W_R} \left( \mathbb{E}[k(Y_L, Y_L')] + \mathbb{E}[k(Y_R, Y_R')] - 2 \mathbb{E}[k(Y_L, Y_R)] \right)\)$

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Energy Distance on 5D vector embeddings
tree_energy = ModelTree(gain="energy_distance", max_depth=1, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_energy.fit(X, y_vectors, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

# MMD with RBF Kernel
tree_mmd = ModelTree(gain="mmd", mmd_kernel="rbf", max_depth=1, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_mmd.fit(X, y_vectors, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Energy Split:", tree_energy.root_split())
print("MMD Split:   ", tree_mmd.root_split())

MMD Split:    {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.011, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 58.1626}

items.title: 5. Phase 12D.1: Wasserstein-2 Optimal Transport (gain="wasserstein")
items.text:
Best for: Target outcomes that are continuous distributions, quantile functions, or probability histograms (e.g., regional daily temperature profiles, financial yield curves, pollution distributions).

Maximizes Fréchet barycenter dispersion reduction:

\[\text{Gain}_{\mathcal{W}_2}(L, R) = \frac{W_L W_R}{W_L + W_R} \frac{1}{D} \sum_{d=0}^{D-1} (\bar{Y}_L[d] - \bar{Y}_R[d])^2\]

Leaves output the predicted Fréchet barycenter distribution via predict_vector.

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Wasserstein-2 Optimal Transport on 20-point quantile curves
tree_wass = ModelTree(gain="wasserstein", max_depth=1, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_wass.fit(X, y_quantiles, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_wass.root_split())

# Predict Fréchet barycenter distribution for new profiles
barycenter_preds = tree_wass.predict_vector([X[0]])
print(f"Leaf Fréchet Barycenter (len={len(barycenter_preds[0])}):", [round(v, 2) for v in barycenter_preds[0][:5]], "...")

Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.011, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 1221.0445}
Leaf Fréchet Barycenter (len=20): [-3.42, -3.11, -2.89, -2.71, -2.55] ...
Note: Directly splits and outputs continuous distribution curves.

items.title: 6. Phase 12D.2: Fairness-Constrained Splitting (gain="fair")
items.text:
Best for: High-stakes automated decisions (credit approval, hiring, insurance underwriting) subject to demographic parity compliance bounds.

Penalizes split quality by Total Variation disparity across protected attribute \(S\):

\[\text{Gain}_{\text{fair}} = \text{BaseGain}(L, R) - \lambda \cdot \text{Impurity}_{\text{parent}} \cdot |P(S=1 \mid L) - P(S=1 \mid R)|\]

When \(\lambda > 0\), candidate splits that create disparate impact on protected groups are penalized, forcing the tree to select clean, fair merit features.

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Demographic Parity Fair Tree (lambda = 1.0 on protected column 3 'gender')
tree_fair = ModelTree(
    gain="fair",
    fairness_penalty=1.0,
    protected_col=3,
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    prune="none",
)
tree_fair.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_fair.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': 0.107, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 1191.7879}
Note:  Penalizes proxy discrimination; narrows selection rate gap between protected groups.

items.title: 7. Phase 12E.1: Hellinger Distance Splitting (gain="hellinger")
items.text:
Best for: Highly imbalanced classification regimes (e.g. fraud detection, rare failure analysis) where rare positive events represent < 5% of data.

Evaluates the skew-invariant Hellinger affinity divergence between child partitions without suffering from the probability floor collapse of Gini or Shannon entropy:

\[H^2(L, R) = \sum_{k=1}^C \left(\sqrt{p_{L, k}} - \sqrt{p_{R, k}}\right)^2\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Hellinger Distance on rare catastrophic risk event (~5% prevalence)
tree_hellinger = ModelTree(gain="hellinger", max_depth=1, min_rows=5, prune="none")
tree_hellinger.fit(X, y_rare, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_hellinger.root_split())

Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': -1.409, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 70.7933}
Note:  Skew-invariant divergence; cleanly isolates rare tail catastrophe without score collapse.

items.title: 8. Phase 12E.2: Maximally Selected Rank Statistics (gain="maxstat")
items.text:
Best for: Continuous targets with nonlinear monotone distortion or outliers where order preservation matters more than squared distance.

Maximizes the standardized two-sample linear rank statistic \(T^2(s) = S_L^2 / \text{Var}(S_L)\) with strict invariance under monotonic scalings:

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# MaxStat Rank Splitting
tree_maxstat = ModelTree(gain="maxstat", max_depth=1, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_maxstat.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_maxstat.root_split())

items.title: Visual Execution Output
items.text:
Split: {'col': 'score', 'threshold': -0.012, 'missing_left': True, 'gain': 149.2552}
Note:  Standardized two-sample linear rank divergence; invariant to monotone target scalings.

items.title: 9. Phase 12F: SPORF Oblique Splitting (sporf_d=2)
items.text:
Best for: Non-axis-aligned data regimes where true boundaries are diagonal hyperplanes (\(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 \le c\)).

Sparse Projection Oblique Randomer Forest (Tomita et al. 2020) evaluates random linear combinations of \(d\) features with random signs:

\[Z = \sum_{k=1}^d \alpha_k X_{j_k}, \quad \alpha_k \in \{-1, +1\}\]

When an oblique projection beats the best univariate axis split, it is selected and exposed with full algebraic transparency in root_split()["oblique"]:

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# SPORF: 2-feature oblique projections (30 candidate hyperplanes)
tree_sporf = ModelTree(sporf_d=2, sporf_projections=30, max_depth=1, min_rows=15, seed=42, prune="none")
tree_sporf.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

root = tree_sporf.root_split()
print("Split:", root)
print("Oblique Equation:", root["oblique"]["equation"])

Oblique Equation: -1.00*score -1.00*gender_proxy <= -1.2379
Note:  Evaluates random linear combinations of 2 features; eliminates diagonal staircasing.

items.title: 10. Phase 12G: Equalized Odds Fairness Penalty (fairness_metric="equalized_odds")
items.text:
Best for: Regulatory and credit compliance where decision error rates (True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate) must not disproportionately penalize a protected demographic subgroup:

\[\text{Disparity}_{\text{EO}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( |\text{TPR}_1 - \text{TPR}_0| + |\text{FPR}_1 - \text{FPR}_0| \right)\] \[\text{Gain}_{\text{Fair}} = \max\left(0, \, \text{Gain}_{\text{Raw}} - \lambda \cdot \text{SSE}_{\text{parent}} \cdot \text{Disparity}_{\text{EO}}\right)\]

items.title: Code Run
items.text:
# Equalized Odds constrained splitting (protected attribute = col 3 'gender')
tree_eo = ModelTree(
    fairness_penalty=1.0,
    fairness_metric="equalized_odds",
    protected_col=3,
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    prune="none",

tree_eo.fit(X, y_fair, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_eo.root_split())

items.title: 11. Phase 12H: Extremely Randomized Splits / ExtraTrees (extratrees=True)
items.text:
Best for: Fast \(O(1)\) split evaluation during tree bagging and ensemble training, avoiding the \(O(N \log N)\) sorting and exhaustive cutpoint scan per continuous feature:

\[s \sim \text{Uniform}(\min X_j, \max X_j)\]

items.title: Code Run

tree_et = ModelTree(
    extratrees=True,
    seed=42,
    max_depth=1,
    min_rows=15,
    prune="none",
)
tree_et.fit(X, y_scalar, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

print("Split:", tree_et.root_split())

Note:  Evaluates exactly 1 random cut per continuous feature in O(1) time without sorting.

items.title: 12. Phase 12I: EBM FAST Interaction Screening (ebm_fast=True)
items.text:
Best for: Discovering non-linear pairwise interactions across all \(P(P-1)/2\) feature pairs without combinatorial model fitting:

\[\text{InteractionGain}(j, k) = \frac{\sum_{a,b \in \{0, 1\}} N_{ab} (\bar{y}_{ab} - \hat{y}_{\text{add}})^2}{\text{SSE}_{\text{parent}}}\]

items.title: Code Run

from mltreelib import fast_interaction_screen

# Standalone FAST screening over all candidate pairs
screened = fast_interaction_screen(X, y_inter, col_names=col_names, top_k=3, min_samples=15)
print("Top Screened Pairs:", [(s['col1_name'], s['col2_name'], s['score']) for s in screened])

# Tree fitted with FAST interaction constraint
tree_fast = ModelTree(ebm_fast=True, max_depth=2, min_rows=15, prune="none")
tree_fast.fit(X, y_inter, col_names=col_names, dtypes=dtypes)

items.title: 13. Operational Limitations & Practical Failure Modes
items.text:
1. Quadratic Complexity of Metric Criteria (\(O(N^2)\)): Exact sample evaluations of Energy Distance (gain="energy_distance") and MMD (gain="mmd") compute pairwise Euclidean or kernel distances across all partition observations. On partitions with \(N > 10,000\), exact pairwise evaluations become computationally prohibitive. In large-scale regimes, subsample candidate partitions or use random Fourier features.
  2. The Fairness-Accuracy Trade-off: Constraining demographic parity (gain="fair") or equalized odds (fairness_metric="equalized_odds") penalizes predictive features that correlate with protected demographic attributes. As fairness penalty \(\lambda\) increases, the tree shifts splits from predictive proxy features to uncorrelated merit features, which may increase general test MSE while guaranteeing regulatory compliance.
  3. Rank Invariance vs. Point Calibration: MaxStat (gain="maxstat") and CTree (gain="ctree") operate on rank transformations of continuous targets, providing strict invariance under monotonic scaling. However, terminal leaf point predictions are uncalibrated step constants. To restore accurate probabilistic calibration, pair with leaf retrain (tree.retrain(...)) or isotonic calibration.
  4. Oblique Projection Feature Dimensionality: SPORF (sporf_d=2) samples random 2D hyperplanes to overcome axis-aligned limitations. If candidate feature spaces contain hundreds of irrelevant variables, random projections may sample uninformative subspace combinations. Pre-screen features using CTree or EBM FAST prior to oblique tree training.

items.title: Suite 9: Survival & Competing Risks Trees
items.text:
This suite implements non-parametric Survival Trees and Competing Risks Trees in pure Rust (mltreelib-core) with thin Python bindings (mltreelib). It partitions heterogeneous survival cohorts into interpretable prognostic subgroups while rigorously accounting for right-censoring and multi-cause competing risks.

Companion executable script: - examples/suites/survival_and_competing_risks.py (uv run python examples/suites/survival_and_competing_risks.py)

items.title: 1. Survival Tree Structure & Decision Topology
items.text:
In survival analysis, observations are right-censored: study termination or patient dropout masks the true event time \(T_i^*\). The observed pair is \((T_i, E_i)\) where \(T_i = \min(T_i^*, C_i)\) and \(E_i = I(T_i^* \le C_i)\).

In competing risks, an observation can experience one of \(J\) distinct, mutually exclusive event types (\(E_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, J\}\), where \(E_i = 0\) denotes right-censoring).

items.title: High-Level Workflow Architecture
items.text:
flowchart LR
    Data["Cohort Ingestion: (X, (T, E))"] --> TargetType{"Target Setting"}

    TargetType -- "Single Event (E in {0, 1})" --> SingleEvent["Right-Censored Survival"]
    SingleEvent --> SplitCrit1["Split Criterion:\nlogrank | tarone_ware | peto | martingale | survival_brier | rmst"]
    SplitCrit1 --> LeafEst1["Leaf Estimators:\nKaplan-Meier S(t)\nNelson-Aalen Lambda(t)\nAFT / Cure / Spline"]

    TargetType -- "Competing Risks (E in {0, 1, ..., J})" --> CompRisks["Multi-Cause Competing Risks"]
    CompRisks --> SplitCrit2["Split Criterion:\ngray (Subdistribution Log-Rank)\ntarget_cause = c"]
    CompRisks --> LeafEst2["Leaf Estimators:\nAalen-Johansen CIF F_c(t)\nCause-Specific Hazard Lambda_c(t)"]

    LeafEst1 --> SimplexCheck["Verify Monotonicity:\nS(t) non-increasing"]
    LeafEst2 --> SimplexCheck2["Verify Simplex Invariant:\nsum_c F_c(t) + S(t) == 1.0"]

items.title: Native ModelTree Architecture & Graphviz Topology
items.text:
Rather than an abstract diagram, mltreelib exports the exact mathematical graph structure directly via ModelTree.to_dot(). You can render this directly with Graphviz (dot -Tsvg):

import subprocess
from mltreelib import ModelTree

# Export and render native ModelTree graphviz DOT representation
dot_graph = tree.to_dot()
subprocess.run(["dot", "-Tsvg", "-o", "docs/assets/suite9_survival_tree_model.svg"], input=dot_graph, text=True)

The resulting native decision topology shows split predicates, node sample counts \(N\), node deviances, and leaf response constants:

items.title: Individual Leaf Survival & Competing Risks Profiles
items.text: Behind each terminal node in the tree lives a complete multi-state survival distribution. The panel below illustrates the distinct Kaplan-Meier survival curves \(S(t)\) and Aalen-Johansen Cumulative Incidence Functions \(F_1(t)\) (Relapse) and \(F_2(t)\) (Competing Mortality) across all 5 leaves:

items.title: Why the Partitions Formed:
items.text:
1. Leaf 1 (Rule 4: biomarker <= -0.155 & age <= 5.751) — Favorable Long-Term (\(N=111\), Median = 5.68 yrs): Younger patients with low biomarker levels have minimal hazard. Primary relapse incidence \(F_1(t)\) plateaus below 10%, while competing mortality remains negligible, sustaining high long-term survival.
  2. Leaf 2 (Rule 1: biomarker <= -0.155 & age > 5.751) — Moderate-Low Risk (\(N=161\), Median = 1.99 yrs): Older patients with low biomarker levels experience moderate relapse (32.3%), but their competing risk mortality \(F_2(t)\) accumulates steadily due to age-related hazards, pulling overall survival down to a 1.99-year median.
  3. Leaf 3 (Rule 3: -0.155 < biomarker <= 1.471 & age <= 6.168) — Intermediate Risk (\(N=135\), Median = 2.97 yrs): Intermediate biomarker levels in younger cohorts produce a moderate, delayed relapse accumulation (24.4%), yielding a stable 2.97-year median survival.
  4. Leaf 4 (Rule 2: -0.155 < biomarker <= 1.471 & age > 6.168) — Elevated Risk (\(N=152\), Median = 1.62 yrs): Older patients with intermediate biomarker levels face a dual-hazard scenario: accelerated relapse incidence (48.0%) combined with substantial competing mortality (\(F_2(t) \approx 45\%\)).
  5. Leaf 5 (Rule 5: biomarker > 1.471) — Extreme Early Relapse (\(N=41\), Median = 0.76 yrs): High biomarker levels trigger a catastrophic relapse spike (\(F_1(t) = 85.4\%\) within the first 12 months). The tree immediately isolates this high-risk cluster at the root split, dropping median survival to 0.76 years.

items.title: 2. The 9 Survival Split Criteria
items.text:
Configure the split criterion using the gain parameter in ModelTree:

tree = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=20, gain="pseudo_value")
Criterion (gain=) Mathematical Formula Weighting Function \(w(t_j)\) Best Used For "logrank" Two-sample Mantel-Haenszel score: \(Z = \frac{\sum_j (d_{1j} - e_{1j})}{\sqrt{\sum_j V_j}}\) \(w(t_j) = 1\) Proportional hazards settings where treatment or risk effect is uniform over time. "tarone_ware" Weighted log-rank score test \(w(t_j) = \sqrt{n_j}\) (square root of risk set size) Moderate non-proportional hazards; balances sensitivity between early and late event horizons. "peto" Peto-Prentice weighted score test \(w(t_j) = \tilde{S}(t_j-)\) (Kaplan-Meier survival at previous time) High-risk early divergence; prioritizes splits that separate immediate mortality or early customer drop-off. "martingale" \(O(N)\) streaming scan on Cox null martingale residuals: \(M_i = E_i - \hat{\Lambda}_0(T_i)\) Residual difference: \(\Delta \text{SSE} = \frac{S_L^2}{N_L} + \frac{S_R^2}{N_R} - \frac{S^2}{N}\) Large-scale datasets where \(O(N \log N)\) sorting per candidate split is too slow. Splits at the speed of regression trees. "pseudo_value" Jackknife pseudo-observations \(\theta_i = N \hat{S}(t) - (N-1)\hat{S}_{-i}(t)\) Standard regression variance reduction Fast \(O(N)\) streaming splits on survival probability or restricted mean survival time. "rmst" Restricted Mean Survival Time area divergence: \(\Delta \text{RMST} = \int_0^\tau S_L(t) dt - \int_0^\tau S_R(t) dt\) Integrated area difference: \(\frac{N_L N_R}{N_L + N_R} (\text{RMST}_L - \text{RMST}_R)^2\) Crossing hazards settings where log-rank statistics lose statistical power. "aft_deviance" Parametric AFT log-likelihood deviance reduction Likelihood ratio reduction \(\Delta D\) Parametric survival model trees targeting smooth log-linear survival functions. "gray" Gray's (1988) subdistribution score test for cause \(c\) Subdistribution weight: \(w(t_j) = \frac{n_j - d_j}{n_j} \cdot \dots\) Competing risks (\(E_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, J\}\)). Evaluates cumulative incidence separation for target_cause. "survival_brier" Minimizes IPCW integrated Brier loss at quartile time horizons Integrated squared residual: \(\sum_k \text{BS}(t_k)\) Calibration-first trees where calibrated probability estimates \(S(t)\) matter more than rank-ordering.

items.title: 3. Leaf Estimators & Invariants
items.text:
Inside each leaf, mltreelib-core computes non-parametric step functions:

  1. Kaplan-Meier Survival Estimator: $\(\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right)\)$

  2. Nelson-Aalen Cumulative Hazard: $\(\hat{\Lambda}(t) = \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j}\)$

  3. Aalen-Johansen Cumulative Incidence Function (CIF): For cause \(c \in \{1, \dots, J\}\): $\(\hat{F}_c(t) = \sum_{t_j \le t} \hat{S}(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{cj}}{n_j}\)$ where \(d_{cj}\) is the number of cause-\(c\) events at time \(t_j\).

  4. The Simplex Invariant: At any time \(t \ge 0\), the sum of all cause-specific cumulative incidence probabilities plus overall survival equals exactly 1: $\(\sum_{c=1}^J \hat{F}_c(t) + \hat{S}(t) \equiv 1.0\)$ The engine enforces and tests this invariant down to machine precision (\(1.33 \times 10^{-15}\)).

items.title: Frontier Leaf Models
items.text:
Standard survival tree libraries fit flat step functions in leaves. mltreelib supports parametric and semi-parametric model leaves:

  • Parametric AFT Leaves (leaf_family="aft"): Fits smooth continuous accelerated failure time distributions inside leaves: $\(\ln T = \mu(X) + \sigma \epsilon\)$ Knobs: aft_dist="weibull" | "lognormal" | "loglogistic". When paired with leaf="linear", the survival curve \(S(t \mid x)\) varies smoothly with continuous covariates within the leaf partition.
  • Mixture Cure Rate Leaves (leaf_family="cure"): Models populations where a fraction \(\pi\) are cured and will never experience the event: $\(S_{\text{pop}}(t) = \pi + (1 - \pi) S_{\text{uncured}}(t)\)$ Knob: cure_fraction=0.2. As \(t \to \infty\), the survival curve plateaus at \(\pi > 0\).
  • Restricted Cubic Splines Leaves (leaf_family="spline"): Fits Royston-Parmar flexible spline log cumulative hazard functions: $\(\ln \Lambda(t \mid x) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \ln t + \sum_{k=1}^K \gamma_{k+1} v_k(\ln t) + \beta^T x\)$ Knob: spline_knots=3. Eliminates discrete stepping while avoiding rigid parametric distribution assumptions.

items.title: 4. Fitting & Predictions API
items.text:
Fit trees using the standard 2-tuple target (durations, events):

from mltreelib import ModelTree

# 1. Competing risks tree isolating Cause 1 (Relapse) with Gray's test
tree = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=25,
    gain="gray",
    target_cause=1,
)
tree.fit(X_train, (dur_train, ev_train))

# 2. Frontier parametric AFT tree with smooth Weibull linear leaves
tree_aft = ModelTree(
    max_depth=3,
    min_rows=15,
    gain="rmst",          # Area divergence splitting under non-proportional hazards
    leaf_family="aft",    # Parametric AFT distribution
    aft_dist="weibull",   # "weibull", "lognormal", or "loglogistic"
    leaf="linear",        # Linear covariate response inside each leaf
)
tree_aft.fit(X_train, (dur_train, ev_train))

Console Output:

>>> tree.fit(X_train, (dur_train, ev_train))
Tree fitted successfully! Total leaves: 5, depth: 3

>>> tree_aft.fit(X_train, (dur_train, ev_train))
AFT Tree fitted successfully! Total leaves: 6, depth: 3

items.title: Prediction Methods via kind
items.text:
Query predictions using the unified predict method:

# Select 3 sample test patients across prognostic risk strata
X_sample = X_test[:3]
time_horizons = [1.0, 2.0, 5.0]  # Evaluation horizons in years

# 1. Predicted median survival time (years)
median_days = tree.predict(X_sample, kind="response")

items.title: 5. Model Evaluation with Modern Calibration Metrics
items.text:
Evaluate models with classical IPCW concordance and frontier calibration metrics:

from mltreelib import (
    Metrics,
    d_calibration,
    integrated_calibration_index,
    one_calibration,
    competing_risks_calibration,
)

# 1. Classical Discrimination & Calibration
metrics = Metrics()
cif_all_c1 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=time_horizons, cause=1)
cif_all_c2 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="cif", times=time_horizons, cause=2)
risk_all_c1 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="risk", cause=1)
risk_all_c2 = tree.predict(X_test, kind="risk", cause=2)

report = metrics.competing_risks(
    durations=dur_test,
    events=ev_test,
    cif_curves={1: cif_all_c1, 2: cif_all_c2},
    risk_scores={1: risk_all_c1, 2: risk_all_c2},
    times=time_horizons,
)

print(f"Cause 1 Harrell C:  {report['cause_c_indices'][1]:.4f}")
print(f"Cause 1 Uno IPCW C: {report['cause_uno_c_indices'][1]:.4f}")
print(f"Cause 1 IBS:        {report['cause_ibs'][1]:.4f}")
print("Brier at horizons: ", {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in report['brier_at_horizons'][1].items()})

# 2. D-Calibration (Haider et al. 2020)
# Evaluates whether event occurrences are uniformly distributed across probability bins
surv_test_h = [row[1] for row in tree.predict(X_test, kind="survival", times=time_horizons)] # at t=2.0 yr
d_rep = d_calibration(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, n_bins=10)
print(f"D-Calibration: Chi2 = {d_rep['chi2_stat']:.3f}, p-value = {d_rep['p_value']:.4f}, Calibrated = {d_rep['is_calibrated']}")

# 3. Integrated Calibration Index (ICI) (Austin et al. 2020)
# IPCW-weighted mean absolute calibration error at horizon t_0
ici_rep = integrated_calibration_index(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, horizon=2.0)
print(f"ICI: {ici_rep['ici']:.4f}, E50: {ici_rep['e50']:.4f}, E90: {ici_rep['e90']:.4f}, Emax: {ici_rep['emax']:.4f}")

# 4. 1-Calibration Slope & Intercept
one_rep = one_calibration(dur_test, ev_test, surv_test_h, horizon=2.0)
print(f"1-Calibration: Intercept = {one_rep['intercept']:.3f}, Slope = {one_rep['slope']:.3f}")

# 5. Competing Risks Multi-Cause Calibration (Alberge et al. 2026)
cr_rep = competing_risks_calibration(
    dur_test,
    ev_test,
    {1: [r[1] for r in cif_all_c1], 2: [r[1] for r in cif_all_c2]},
    horizon=2.0,
)
print(f"Competing Risks: Cause 1 ICI = {cr_rep['cause_ici'][1]:.4f}, Cause 2 ICI = {cr_rep['cause_ici'][2]:.4f}")

items.title: 7. Assumptions & Limitations
items.text:
1. Conditionally Independent Censoring: \(T_i^* \perp C_i \mid X_i\). If unobserved health deterioration causes patients to drop out, Kaplan-Meier leaf estimates will overestimate survival.
  2. Competing Risks vs. Censoring: Do not treat competing events (e.g., organ transplant, accidental death) as right-censoring. Doing so overestimates the cumulative incidence of the primary event. Use gain="gray" and kind="cif".
  3. Cumulative Hazard vs. Instantaneous Hazard Rate: predict(kind="hazard") computes \(\hat{\Lambda}(t) = \int_0^t \lambda(u) du\) (dimensionless accumulated expected event count). It does not compute instantaneous hazard rate \(\lambda(t) = \frac{d\Lambda(t)}{dt}\).
  4. Tail Extrapolation: Beyond \(\max(T_i)\) in a leaf, non-parametric step curves remain flat at their last estimated value. For continuous tail extrapolation, use parametric AFT leaves (leaf_family="aft").

items.title: 8. Research Foundations & Benchmark Reproductions
items.text:
The implementation reproduces eleven key findings from classical (1988–2014) and frontier (2020–2026) survival analysis literature:

Reference & Paper Link Topic & Method Benchmark Dataset Original Paper Finding mltreelib Reproduction Result LeBlanc & Crowley (1992), (1993) Martingale residual splitting (\(O(N)\) streaming scan) Veterans' Lung Cancer (\(N=137\), 128 deaths) Primary prognostic split occurs on Karnofsky score \(\le 40\), yielding 3.1x mortality hazard jump. ModelTree(gain="martingale", max_depth=2) isolates primary cut at karno <= 40. Yields median survival of 30 days vs 111 days. Gray (1988) K-sample subdistribution log-rank test for competing risks Competing risks cohort (\(N=800\), Cause 1: 333, Cause 2: 366, Censored: 101) Naive Kaplan-Meier overestimates primary event incidence because it treats competing failures as independent censoring. gain="gray", target_cause=1 correctly estimates cause-specific CIF \(F_1(t)\), eliminating competing-event risk overestimation. Fine & Gray (1999) Subdistribution hazards model Mayo Clinic PBC cohort Serum bilirubin and albumin are dominant predictors of primary liver failure mortality. Tree rules isolate bili > 3.2 and albumin <= 3.1 with high subdistribution hazard and rapid CIF accumulation. Ishwaran et al. (2014) Aalen-Johansen leaf CIF estimator & simplex property Multi-cause oncology simulation (\(N=800\)) Competing risk probabilities and overall survival must satisfy the simplex identity \(\sum_{c=1}^J F_c(t) + S(t) = 1.0\). Verified across 1,000 grid points: maximum absolute error is \(1.33 \times 10^{-15}\) (machine epsilon). Uno et al. (2011) IPCW Concordance Index (\(C^{\text{Uno}}\)) Mayo Clinic FLCHAIN (\(N=7,874\), 2,172 deaths) Harrell's C is sensitive to study follow-up duration; Uno's IPCW C removes censoring bias via inverse Kaplan-Meier weights. Native Metrics().survival(...) computes Harrell's C (0.784) and Uno's IPCW C (0.781) on raw FLCHAIN data with 1,350 missing creatinine values. Graf et al. (1999) Integrated Brier Score (IBS) with IPCW censoring weights Simulation benchmark (\(N=800\)) IBS evaluates probability calibration across the full timeline \([0, t_{\max}]\) under arbitrary censoring. Benchmark across criteria yields IBS between 0.2136 (tarone_ware) and 0.2297 (peto). Liu & Li (2020), (2021) RMST area divergence splitting Crossing hazards simulation Standard log-rank test loses statistical power when hazards cross. RMST preserves power via integrated area differences. gain="rmst" maintains high split discrimination under crossing hazards where log-rank fails. Schenk et al. (2024) Jackknife pseudo-values for survival trees SurvSet benchmarks Pseudo-values transform right-censored outcomes into continuous pseudo-observations for \(O(N)\) split scanning. gain="pseudo_value" matches full martingale rank ordering with \(O(N)\) linear scans. Haider et al. (2020) D-Calibration for distribution uniformity SurvSet benchmark suite Well-calibrated survival estimators distribute event probabilities uniformly across probability bins: \(\chi^2\) test \(p > 0.05\). d_calibration(durations, events, surv, n_bins=10) outputs \(\chi^2\) statistic and uniformity hypothesis test. Austin et al. (2020) Integrated Calibration Index (ICI) & 1-Calibration GBSG2 Breast Cancer cohort ICI computes IPCW-weighted mean absolute error between predicted survival and observed status at horizon \(t_0\). integrated_calibration_index(durations, events, surv, horizon) outputs ICI, E50, E90, and Emax. Alberge et al. (2026) Multi-cause calibration divergence Mayo Clinic PBC cohort Competing risks calibration must evaluate cause-specific calibration divergences and Brier scores simultaneously. competing_risks_calibration(durations, events, cif_dict, horizon) evaluates per-cause ICI and Brier divergences.

items.title: Time Series Feature Engineering & Additive Forecasting (Suite 7)
items.text:
In enterprise demand planning and energy load forecasting, models face secular growth trends, intra-week cycles, and calendar shocks.

Standard flat decision trees fail out-of-sample on trending series because constant-leaf partitions cannot extrapolate beyond the maximum target value seen during training.

mltreelib implements a zero-allocation, pure Rust feature engineering engine—providing ISO calendar extraction, entity-grouped calendar day lags, windowed rolling statistics, and additive trend decomposition—coupled with piecewise-linear model trees that extrapolate trends out-of-time.

Script: examples/suites/timeseries_additive_forecasting.py (uv run python examples/suites/timeseries_additive_forecasting.py).

items.title: Why Flat Trees Fail on Time Series:
items.text:
1. The Step-Function Ceiling: Standard regression trees predict leaf sample means \(\bar{y}_{\text{leaf}}\). In a growing business where future sales exceed historical peaks, a constant-leaf tree predicts the historical maximum for all future dates.
  2. Calendar Offset Misalignment: Naive array row shifts (df['sales'].shift(7)) fail when store closures or holiday gaps omit records. Real forecasting requires shifting by elapsed wall-clock calendar days (\(t - 7 \text{ days}\)) grouped by entity.
  3. Imputation Distortion: Shifting introduces unobserved initial histories (None). Forcing median imputation erases autoregressive relationships.

items.title: 2. Mathematical Formulation of Pure Rust Transforms
A. Entity-Grouped Calendar Day Lags (lag_by_days)
items.text:
Given entity keys \(\mathbf{k}\), date timestamps \(\mathbf{t}\), and values \(\mathbf{y}\), the Rust engine computes:

\[L_k(t, \Delta d) = y(t') \quad \text{where } t' = t - \Delta d \text{ days, with } \text{entity}(t') = \text{entity}(t)\]

If no transaction occurred on exact calendar date \(t'\), the cell is assigned None and routed via ModelTree's native missing handler without distorting observed lags.

items.title: B. Additive Classical Time Series Decomposition (decomposed_transform)
items.text:
For periodic series with period \(m\) (e.g. \(m = 7\) for weekly retail cycles):

\[y_t = T_t + S_t + I_t\]
  1. Trend (\(T_t\)): Computed via two-sided moving average filter: $\(T_t = \frac{1}{m} \left( \frac{1}{2} y_{t - m/2} + \sum_{k = -m/2 + 1}^{m/2 - 1} y_{t+k} + \frac{1}{2} y_{t + m/2} \right)\)$
  2. Seasonality (\(S_t\)): Detrended averages normalized to sum to zero over the cycle: $\(\tilde{S}_k = \text{mean}(y_t - T_t \mid t \equiv k \pmod m), \quad S_k = \tilde{S}_k - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{j=1}^m \tilde{S}_j\)$
  3. Residual Irregularity (\(I_t\)): \(I_t = y_t - T_t - S_t\).

items.title: C. Continuous Trend Extrapolation via Linear Leaves
items.text:
In terminal leaf \(\mathcal{R}_m\), ModelTree fits local ridge regression:

\[\hat{y}(t, \mathbf{x}) = \beta_0 + \beta_{\text{trend}} \cdot t + \sum_{k=1}^P \beta_k \cdot L_k(t)\]

Because time \(t\) enters as an explicit continuous predictor with non-zero slope \(\beta_{\text{trend}}\), predictions continue along the secular trajectory beyond the training horizon.

items.title: 3. Benchmark Study: Multi-Store Retail Demand Panel
items.text:
We evaluate on a simulated multi-store retail panel (240 records across 2 stores over 120 days from 2025-01-01 to 2025-04-30) exhibiting weekly seasonality and strong upward secular growth. - Training Period: First 90 days (2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31, 180 records). - Out-of-Time Test Period: Final 30 days (2025-04-01 to 2025-04-30, 60 records).

from mltreelib import Metrics, ModelTree
from mltreelib.timefeat import calendar_features, decomposed_transform, lag_by_days, windowed_transform

# 1. Transform features in pure Rust
cal = calendar_features(dates)
lag_1 = lag_by_days(keys=stores, dates=dates, values=sales, days=1)
lag_7 = lag_by_days(keys=stores, dates=dates, values=sales, days=7)
win_7 = windowed_transform(keys=stores, dates=dates, values=sales, days=7, stat="mean")
decomp = decomposed_transform(values=sales, period=7, model="additive")

# 2. Build feature matrix and split out-of-time
X = list(zip(cal["weekday"], cal["month"], lag_1, lag_7, win_7, decomp["trend"]))
X_train, y_train = X[:180], sales[:180]
X_test, y_test = X[180:], sales[180:]

# 3. Fit standard CART step-function baseline
tree_cart = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=15, leaf="mean")
tree_cart.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_cart = tree_cart.predict(X_test)

# 4. Fit ModelTree piecewise linear model tree
tree_linear = ModelTree(max_depth=3, min_rows=15, leaf="linear", l2=1e-3)
tree_linear.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_linear = tree_linear.predict(X_test)

items.title: Key Quantitative Findings:
items.text:
1. Massive Out-of-Time Error Drop (66.9%): ModelTree reduces out-of-sample RMSE from 12.87 to 4.26 and lifts \(R^2\) from 0.787 to 0.977, accurately capturing post-March trend expansion.
  2. Elimination of the Flat Ceiling (Panel 2): Standard CART flattens into horizontal plateaus as test dates exceed training values. ModelTree linear leaves maintain positive trend derivatives across all store cohorts.
  3. Rust Transformation Latency: Feature engineering on the multi-store panel executes in compiled Rust, completely eliminating Python date-parsing and pandas groupby bottlenecks.

items.title: 5. Domain Limitations & Operational Boundaries
items.text:
1. Multi-Step Recursive Error Compounding: In multi-step autoregressive rollouts, errors in \(\hat{y}_{t+1}\) feed into lagged inputs for \(\hat{y}_{t+2}\). For horizons exceeding 30 days, direct forecasting or periodic re-anchoring is required.
  2. Trend Over-Extrapolation Risk: Linear leaves fit unconstrained local slopes. If historical growth was parabolic or transient, linear extrapolation will over-predict over long horizons. Setting l2 >= 1.0 or clipping leaf slopes bounds long-term drift.
  3. Irregular Calendar Gaps: When telemetry ceases for extended periods (e.g., store shutdown for 3 months), all day-lags up to \(\Delta d = 90\) become missing, routing records through the missing path.

items.title: Unsupervised Trees: Clustering & Anomaly Triage (Suite 8)
items.text:
Unsupervised machine learning faces a common dilemma: distance-based algorithms (like k-means and DBSCAN) do not provide human-readable assignment rules, while standard isolation forests produce coordinate-axis ghost artifacts in high dimensions.

mltreelib implements two specialized unsupervised tree architectures in pure Rust: 1. Predictive Clustering Trees (PCT): Groups observations by maximizing normalized multivariate variance reduction across multi-target profiles, generating white-box IF-THEN cluster rules. 2. Extended Isolation Forest (EIF): Replaces axis-aligned splits with random oblique hyperplanes, eliminating ghosting artifacts and accelerating anomaly isolation.

Script: examples/suites/unsupervised_trees.py (uv run python examples/suites/unsupervised_trees.py).

items.title: A. Predictive Clustering Trees (PCT)
items.text:
Given \(N\) samples with \(M\) continuous target dimensions \(\mathbf{y}_i \in \mathbb{R}^M\), the total sample variance in partition node \(\mathcal{S}\) is:

\[\text{Var}(\mathcal{S}) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{j=1}^M \frac{(y_{ij} - \bar{y}_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}\]

where \(\sigma_j^2\) is the global variance of feature \(j\). A candidate split \(s\) partitions node \(P\) into children \(L\) and \(R\). The split score maximizes normalized variance reduction:

\[\Delta \text{Var}(s) = \text{Var}(P) - \left[ \frac{N_L}{N} \text{Var}(L) + \frac{N_R}{N} \text{Var}(R) \right]\]

Because splits branch on readable feature predicates (\(x_j \le \theta\)), each cluster corresponds to an explicit, auditable IF-THEN rule.

items.title: B. Extended Isolation Forest with Oblique Cuts
items.text:
Standard Isolation Forests isolate points by picking a random feature \(j\) and a random threshold \(\theta \in [\min x_j, \max x_j]\). This creates ghost artifacts: empty regions aligned parallel to coordinate axes receive artificially short isolation paths.

Extended Isolation Forest (Hariri et al., 2019) branches using random normal hyperplanes:

\[(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p})^T \mathbf{n} \le 0\]
  • \(\mathbf{p} \sim \text{Uniform}(\min \mathbf{X}, \max \mathbf{X})\): A random pivot point in the bounding box.
  • \(\mathbf{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})\) with \(\|\mathbf{n}\|_2 = 1\): A unit normal vector pointing in an arbitrary spherical direction.

The anomaly score for sample \(\mathbf{x}\) across \(T\) trees is:

\[s(\mathbf{x}, n) = 2^{-\frac{\mathbb{E}[h(\mathbf{x})]}{c(n)}}\]

where \(h(\mathbf{x})\) is the observed isolation tree depth, and \(c(n) = 2 \ln(n - 1) + 0.5772156649 - \frac{2(n-1)}{n}\) is the average depth of unsuccessful binary searches. An anomaly score \(s \to 1.0\) indicates an unmistakable outlier, while \(s < 0.5\) indicates normal inlier space.

items.title: 2. Empirical Benchmark Results
items.text: We evaluate both algorithms using examples/suites/unsupervised_trees.py.

items.title: A. PCT Clustering on Wine Quality (1,500 Samples, 6 Chemical Dimensions)
items.text:
• Problem: Group wines by multi-target chemical similarity (fixed_acidity, volatile_acidity, citric_acid, residual_sugar, chlorides, alcohol).
  • Performance: Discovers 8 compact, homogeneous clusters in 11.48 ms fit latency.
  • Interpretability: Each leaf provides explicit chemical thresholds (e.g. alcohol <= 10.2 and volatile_acidity > 0.48), allowing domain chemists to audit segment boundaries directly.

items.title: B. Extended IF vs Axis-Aligned IF on 2D Mixture (600 Inliers, 40 Outliers)
items.text:
• Problem: Isolate 40 peripheral anomalies situated around two dense multimodal inlier clusters.
  • Empirical Comparison:
  • Axis-Aligned IF: Fit time = 1.46 ms. Outlier scores range from \(0.479\) to \(0.590\). Suffers from coordinate ghosting where empty quadrant intersections receive false anomaly spikes.
  • Extended Isolation Forest (Oblique Cuts): Fit time = 0.39 ms (3.7x faster). Outlier scores range from \(0.597\) to 0.751, cleanly separating peripheral anomalies without rectangular ghosting artifacts.
Algorithm Split Mechanism Fit Latency Anomaly Score on Outliers Artifacts Standard Isolation Forest Axis-Aligned (\(x_j \le \theta\)) 1.46 ms 0.479 – 0.590 Severe coordinate ghosting Extended Isolation Forest Oblique Hyperplanes (\(\mathbf{n}^T (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p})\)) 0.39 ms 0.597 – 0.751 Zero ghosting; radial symmetry Predictive Clustering Trees Multi-Target Variance (\(\Delta \text{Var}\)) 11.48 ms N/A (8 clusters) Fully interpretable IF-THEN rules

items.title: 3. Python Usage Example
items.text:
from mltreelib.cluster import ClusterTree
from mltreelib.anomaly import AnomalyTree

# 1. Predictive Clustering Tree (PCT)
pct = ClusterTree(kind="pct", max_depth=3, min_rows=20)
pct.fit(X_wine, col_names=feature_names)
cluster_ids = pct.predict(X_wine)
print(f"Cluster rules: {pct.rules()}")

# 2. Extended Isolation Forest (EIF) with oblique cuts
eif = AnomalyTree(kind="eif", max_depth=8, seed=42)
eif.fit(X_telemetry)
anomaly_scores = eif.predict_score(X_telemetry)

items.title: 4. Domain Limitations & Operational Boundaries
items.text:
1. PCT Target Scaling Dependency: Because PCT sums normalized variances across \(M\) target attributes, attributes with heavy tails can dominate split selection. Standardizing target columns to zero mean and unit variance before fitting is required.
  2. EIF High-Dimensional Projection Curse: In very high dimensions (\(P > 1,000\)), random normal vectors \(\mathbf{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})\) become nearly orthogonal to all coordinate axes, diluting cut selectivity. Subsetting random coordinate subspaces (e.g. 2–10 features per oblique cut) preserves discrimination.
  3. Cluster Size Imbalance: Greedy variance reduction can isolate tiny outlier clusters (\(n < 5\)). Enforce min_rows >= 25 to ensure discovered segments represent viable operational cohorts.
